chapters.title: Linearization and phase-plane analysis
chapters.summary: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium a nonlinear flow looks like its linearization: the Hartman–Grobman theorem gives a topological conjugacy and the stable manifold theorem produces curved versions of the eigenspaces. When an eigenvalue sits on the imaginary axis linearization can lie, and centre manifolds or conserved quantities decide. These tools, plus nullclines and index theory, let us draw complete phase portraits of predator–prey, competition and pendulum models.

refs: Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS GSM 140)
Hirsch, Smale & Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos

items.name: Nullclines
items.pic: For a planar system the curves ẋ = 0 and ẏ = 0 are drawn in two colours; their crossings are the equilibria, and the flow direction in each region between them is shown by a single arrow.

items.name: Hyperbolic equilibria
items.pic: Place an equilibrium and edit its Jacobian; it is flagged hyperbolic while no eigenvalue lies on the imaginary axis, shown in the eigenvalue plane beside the portrait.

items.name: Linearized stability (Lyapunov’s indirect method)
items.pic: Zoom into an equilibrium of a nonlinear system; the trajectories approach those of the linearization, and when all eigenvalues have negative real part a quadratic Lyapunov function from the linear part is drawn and works.

items.name: Stable manifold theorem
items.pic: At a saddle of a nonlinear system, the stable and unstable manifolds are computed by integrating backward and forward from the eigenvectors; they bend away from the straight eigenlines but stay tangent to them at the saddle.

items.name: Hartman–Grobman theorem
items.pic: Side-by-side portraits of a nonlinear flow and its linearization near a hyperbolic point, with a grid on one deformed into the other by the conjugating homeomorphism; make the point non-hyperbolic and the deformation tears.

items.name: Linearization fails at non-hyperbolic points
items.pic: A linear centre is perturbed by a cubic term a·r²; the slider for a turns the closed orbits into slow inward or outward spirals, though the linearization is the same centre in all cases.

items.name: Centre manifold reduction
items.pic: At an equilibrium with one zero eigenvalue, the centre manifold is approximated by a polynomial graph; the reduced one-dimensional flow on it decides stability, and the full trajectories hug the manifold.

items.name: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model
items.pic: Prey and predator populations cycle around a centre; the conserved quantity is computed along the simulation and stays constant, while adding prey self-limitation turns the cycles into an inward spiral.

items.name: Competitive Lotka–Volterra and competitive exclusion
items.pic: Adjust competition coefficients for rabbits and sheep; the nullclines either cross in a stable coexistence point or the saddle’s stable manifold splits the plane into basins where one species wins.

items.name: The nonlinear pendulum
items.pic: The cylinder phase space of a pendulum shows librations, rotations and the separatrix; a damping slider turns the centre into a spiral and makes almost every trajectory end at rest.

items.name: Heteroclinic and homoclinic orbits
items.pic: Tune a parameter until the unstable manifold of one saddle lands exactly on the stable manifold of another (or itself); the connection exists only at that value and breaks on either side.

items.name: Nonlinear centres in conservative systems
items.pic: At an isolated minimum of a conserved quantity, the nearby level curves are closed loops, so the equilibrium is a genuine centre even though linearization alone could not tell.

items.name: Nonlinear centres in reversible systems
items.pic: Reflect a trajectory in the symmetry line of a time-reversible system: the mirrored orbit is a backward trajectory, so orbits near a linear centre must close up; break the symmetry and they spiral.

items.name: Index of a closed curve
items.pic: Drag a closed curve over a phase portrait; the field direction at each point of the curve is tracked on a compass, and its net number of turns is the index, unchanged until the curve crosses an equilibrium.

items.name: Index theory: closed orbits must enclose equilibria
items.pic: Equilibria are labelled by index (saddles −1, nodes, spirals and centres +1); a closed orbit is drawn and its index +1 is verified against the sum of indices it encloses.

items.name: Poincaré–Hopf index formula on the sphere
items.pic: Place sources, sinks and saddles of a flow on a sphere; the readout adds their indices and always gets 2, and on a torus always 0.

items.name: SIR epidemic model and the threshold theorem
items.pic: Set the contact and recovery rates; the epidemic curve takes off only when R₀S(0) > 1, and the final susceptible fraction read from the conserved quantity matches the simulation.

chapters.title: Waves in space
chapters.summary: In higher dimensions, averaging over spheres reduces the wave equation to a one-dimensional problem. Kirchhoff’s formula in three dimensions shows that a signal is felt only on the sphere of radius ct — Huygens’ principle — while in two dimensions, obtained by descent, waves leave a lingering tail. Energy estimates give finite speed of propagation in every dimension, and sources radiate through retarded potentials.

refs: Strauss, Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction

items.name: Energy and causality in space: the light cone
items.pic: A 3D wave launched from a bump is shown with its space–time cone; the energy inside a shrinking backward cone never increases, as the flux readout through its side confirms.

items.name: Spherical means and the Euler–Poisson–Darboux equation
items.pic: Average a 3D solution over spheres of radius r around a point; r times that average is shown to solve the 1D wave equation in r, animated side by side.

items.name: Kirchhoff’s formula
items.pic: Click an observation point; the sphere of radius ct around it is drawn on the initial data and the solution is computed from averages over that sphere only.

items.name: Poisson’s formula in two dimensions (method of descent)
items.pic: Treat 2D data as 3D data independent of z; the sphere’s projection fills the whole disc, so the 2D solution averages over a disc with weight 1/√(c²t² − r²), shown as a shaded kernel.

items.name: Huygens’ principle: sharp in 3D, tails in 2D
items.pic: A short flash at the origin is recorded by a distant listener in 1D, 2D and 3D; the 3D signal is a clean pulse, the 2D signal has a long decaying tail and the 1D signal leaves a step.

items.name: Retarded potentials for waves with sources
items.pic: Move a source along a path; the field at an observer is built from the source’s past positions on the backward light cone, drawn as the retarded point.

items.name: Rays and geometric optics
items.pic: A high-frequency wave passes a lens-shaped region of lower speed; its wavefronts are computed and the rays (normal to the fronts) bend and focus as the eikonal equation predicts.

items.name: Free Schrödinger equation and spreading wave packets
items.pic: A Gaussian wave packet with adjustable momentum moves and spreads; |ψ|² keeps unit integral while its width grows, unlike the heat equation which also spreads but loses oscillations.

items.name: Lorentz invariance of the wave equation
items.pic: Apply a Lorentz boost with a velocity slider to a solution in the (x, t) plane; the boosted function still satisfies the wave equation (residual readout) and the light cone is mapped to itself.

items.name: Spherical waves and 1/r decay
items.pic: An outgoing radial wave F(r − ct)/r is animated; its amplitude falls like 1/r while the energy flux through spheres of every radius stays the same, read out as the wave expands.

chapters.title: Surfaces and surface integrals
chapters.summary: A parametrized surface comes with tangent vectors whose cross product is a normal and whose length is the local area factor. Surface area and integrals of scalar functions follow, along with a cautionary tale: inscribed triangulations need not converge to the area. Choosing a consistent unit normal orients a surface (the Möbius strip cannot be oriented), and the flux of a vector field through an oriented surface is the integral of its normal component.

refs: Schey, Div, Grad, Curl, and All That

items.name: Parametrized surfaces
items.pic: Map a square of parameters (u, v) into space as a sphere, torus or helicoid; the grid lines u = const and v = const ride on the surface as you drag a parameter point.

items.name: Tangent plane and normal of a parametrized surface
items.pic: At a draggable point the vectors T_u and T_v span the tangent plane and their cross product is the normal; at the pole of a sphere parametrization it collapses to zero even though the surface is smooth.

items.name: Surface area as ∬|T_u × T_v|
items.pic: Tile a surface with small parallelograms built from T_u and T_v; their total area converges to the integral, and the readout matches 4πr² for a sphere under any parametrization.

items.name: Schwarz lantern
items.pic: Triangulate a cylinder with m rings of n triangles each; refine m and n together and the triangulated area tends to the true area or to infinity depending on the ratio m/n², shown live.

items.name: Archimedes’ hat-box theorem
items.pic: Slice a sphere and its circumscribed cylinder between two draggable horizontal planes; the two zones always have equal area, whatever the height of the slab.

items.name: Integral of a scalar function over a surface
items.pic: Paint a temperature onto a curved shell; its total heat content is integrated patch by patch, and switching to a different parametrization of the same shell leaves the readout unchanged.

items.name: Orientation of a surface
items.pic: Carry a normal arrow around a closed surface along any loop you draw; it returns pointing the same way, defining an outward side and an inward side.

items.name: The Möbius strip is non-orientable
items.pic: Slide a normal arrow once around the centre line of a Möbius strip with an adjustable number of half-twists; with an odd number it comes back reversed.

items.name: Flux of a vector field through a surface
items.pic: Tilt and stretch a net in a steady flow; F·n is coloured on the net, and the flux readout is largest when the net faces the flow and zero when it lies along it.

items.name: Gauss–Bonnet theorem (for surfaces)
items.pic: Deform a closed surface by dragging control points; the integral of Gaussian curvature stays fixed at 4π for a sphere-like surface and 0 for a torus-like one, while the curvature map changes everywhere.

chapters.title: Isomorphisms
chapters.summary: Two groups are isomorphic when a bijection matches their multiplication tables. Isomorphisms preserve order, commutativity and cyclicity, so every cyclic group is $\mathbb Z$ or some $\mathbb Z_n$, and Cayley’s theorem places every group inside a group of permutations. Direct products build new groups from old — $\mathbb Z_m\times\mathbb Z_n\cong\mathbb Z_{mn}$ exactly when $m$ and $n$ are coprime — and internal direct products recognise such splittings inside a given group.

items.name: Group isomorphism
items.pic: Two Cayley tables, ℤ₄ and ⟨i⟩ ⊂ ℂ*: drag the labels of one to recolour its table until the colour patterns of the two tables coincide.

items.name: (ℝ, +) ≅ (ℝ⁺, ·) by the exponential map
items.pic: A slide rule: sliding one logarithmic scale along another adds lengths and multiplies the numbers printed on them.

items.name: Isomorphisms preserve order, commutativity and cyclicity
items.pic: Pairs such as ℤ₆ and S₃ or U(8) and ℤ₄ are run against a checklist of invariants (order, abelian, cyclic, element orders); a single mismatch proves them non-isomorphic.

items.name: Every infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to ℤ
items.pic: The powers 2ⁿ in ℚ* are hung above the integers n on a number line, and multiplying powers is seen as adding exponents.

items.name: Every cyclic group of order n is isomorphic to ℤₙ
items.pic: The powers of a generator of U(9), of a rotation of a hexagon and of 1 in ℤ₆ are laid around three clocks that turn in lockstep.

items.name: A group of prime order p is isomorphic to ℤₚ
items.pic: Groups of order 5 from a menu (rotations of a pentagon, the fifth roots of unity, ℤ₅) have their Cayley tables relabelled into ℤ₅’s.

items.name: Isomorphism is an equivalence relation on groups
items.pic: A pile of groups of orders 4 and 6 sorts itself into isomorphism classes as you draw isomorphism arrows, which can be reversed and composed.

items.name: Cayley’s theorem
items.pic: Each element g of a small group becomes the permutation “multiply on the left by g” of the group’s own elements, drawn as arrows on its Cayley graph, giving a copy of the group inside S_|G|.

items.name: The external direct product G × H is a group
items.pic: The elements of ℤ₂ × ℤ₃ sit on a 2 × 3 grid wrapped into a torus; adding pairs moves along the two directions independently.

items.name: The order of (g, h) is lcm(|g|, |h|)
items.pic: Two clocks of sizes r and s tick together; the pair of hands first returns to (0, 0) after lcm(r, s) ticks.

items.name: Orders in a product of several groups
items.pic: Several clocks of different sizes tick in unison, and their first common return time is the lcm of the sizes.

items.name: ℤₘ × ℤₙ ≅ ℤₘₙ iff gcd(m, n) = 1
items.pic: Walk diagonally by (1, 1) steps on an m × n torus grid: when m and n are coprime the walk covers every cell, otherwise it closes early.

items.name: Products of cyclic groups of pairwise coprime orders
items.pic: A diagonal walk on a three-dimensional torus grid of sizes n₁, n₂, n₃ fills every cell exactly when the sizes are pairwise coprime.

items.name: ℤₘ splits over the prime powers dividing m
items.pic: Factor m into prime powers and watch the m-hour clock unfold into a grid of smaller clocks, one per prime power.

items.name: Internal direct product
items.pic: Highlight two subgroups H and K of U(8) or D₆; the page checks G = HK, H ∩ K = {e} and hk = kh element by element.

items.name: An internal direct product is isomorphic to H × K
items.pic: The elements hk of D₆ are placed at coordinates (h, k), and multiplication in the group matches coordinatewise multiplication in the grid.

items.name: Internal direct products of several subgroups
items.pic: U(24) splits into three subgroups of order 2 drawn as the axes of a cube, with each of its eight elements at its own corner.

chapters.title: Induced representations
chapters.summary: Representations can be moved between a group and its subgroups: restriction forgets, induction builds the smallest representation of the big group generated by one of the subgroup. Frobenius reciprocity makes them adjoint, and Mackey’s criterion decides when an induced representation is irreducible. Artin and Brauer show that induced characters from small subgroups generate everything, and induction gives the representations of Frobenius groups and of GL₂ over a finite field.

refs: Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups

items.name: Restriction to a subgroup
items.pic: Restrict the irreducibles of S₄ to S₃ or to A₄; the restricted characters are decomposed and drawn as a branching diagram.

items.name: Induced representations
items.pic: Induce a character of the rotation subgroup C₃ up to S₃: the induced space is drawn as values on the two cosets, and group elements act by moving and twisting coset values.

items.name: Frobenius reciprocity
items.pic: For a subgroup and a pair of characters, ⟨Ind ψ, χ⟩ and ⟨ψ, Res χ⟩ are computed side by side and agree for every pair, filling a matrix of multiplicities.

items.name: Character of an induced representation
items.pic: The induced character at g is a sum over cosets fixed by g; the cosets are drawn and the fixed ones highlighted, matching the trace of the induced matrices.

items.name: Mackey’s irreducibility criterion
items.pic: For a character of a subgroup, its conjugates restricted to double-coset intersections are compared; when they are all disjoint the induced representation is irreducible, verified by ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 1.

items.name: Representations of a product G × H
items.pic: Irreducibles of ℤ/2 × S₃ are tensor products of irreducibles of the factors; the character table appears as the Kronecker product of the two tables.

items.name: Degrees are at most the index of an abelian subgroup
items.pic: For dihedral and other groups with an abelian subgroup A, every irreducible degree is checked against [G : A], with the bound attained in the 2-dimensional dihedral representations.

items.name: Semidirect products by abelian groups
items.pic: Orbits of the acting group on the characters of the abelian normal subgroup are drawn; each orbit with its stabilizer’s representation induces one irreducible, recovering all irreducibles of Dₙ and A₄.

items.name: Artin’s induction theorem
items.pic: Characters induced from cyclic subgroups are listed for a chosen group; a rational combination of them reproducing each irreducible character is found by linear algebra.

items.name: Brauer’s induction theorem
items.pic: Characters induced from one-dimensional characters of elementary subgroups generate all characters with integer coefficients; an integer solution is exhibited for S₄.

items.name: Frobenius’ theorem on Frobenius groups
items.pic: In a Frobenius group such as the affine group of 𝔽₅ or A₄, the elements fixing no point together with the identity are shown to form a normal subgroup, using characters induced from the complement.

items.name: Representations of GL₂(𝔽_q)
items.pic: Conjugacy classes of GL₂(𝔽_q) are sorted into four types; principal series are induced from the Borel subgroup, and the dimension count Σd² = |G| is checked for q = 3 and 5.

chapters.title: Urysohn, Tietze, Tychonoff and metrization
chapters.summary: Normality is exactly what is needed to build continuous functions separating closed sets (Urysohn) and to extend continuous functions from closed sets (Tietze). Countably many such functions embed a regular second-countable space in the Hilbert cube, which proves it metrizable. Tychonoff’s theorem — arbitrary products of compact spaces are compact — leads to the Stone–Čech compactification, and paracompactness and local finiteness give the general metrization theorems and partitions of unity.

items.name: Urysohn lemma
items.pic: Two disjoint closed sets in the plane: dyadic rationals index a nested family of open sets drawn as contours, and f(x) = inf{r : x ∈ U_r} is rendered as a heat map going from 0 on one set to 1 on the other.

items.name: Completely regular (Tychonoff) spaces
items.pic: For a point and a closed set, a continuous function equal to 0 at the point and 1 on the set is constructed and graphed; spaces where none exists are flagged with the obstruction.

items.name: Urysohn metrization theorem
items.pic: A regular second-countable space is embedded in the Hilbert cube by countably many Urysohn functions; adding functions one at a time, points that were glued in the image come apart.

items.name: Embedding in cubes
items.pic: Use all continuous functions from a space to [0,1] as coordinates: a sample space (an annulus) is mapped into a cube of growing dimension until the map separates points from closed sets and becomes an embedding.

items.name: Tietze extension theorem
items.pic: A continuous function given on a closed set (a few arcs and dots in a disc) is extended by successive Urysohn approximations; the error bound shrinks by a factor 2/3 per step, read out live.

items.name: Partitions of unity on normal spaces
items.pic: A finite open cover of a closed interval or disc; bump functions subordinate to it are stacked and sum to exactly 1, shown as a stacked area chart.

items.name: Compact manifolds embed in Euclidean space
items.pic: A partition of unity combines finitely many charts of a compact surface into one injective map into ℝᴺ; drop a chart and the map ceases to be injective, with a collided pair highlighted.

items.name: Tychonoff theorem
items.pic: A family of closed sets with the finite intersection property in a product of intervals is enlarged by Zorn’s lemma to a maximal one, and a point in all the sets is read off coordinate by coordinate; open one factor to (0,1] and the point escapes.

items.name: Tychonoff’s theorem implies the axiom of choice
items.pic: Add a point to each set in a family and give it a compact topology; the closed sets “coordinate i lies in Xᵢ” have the finite intersection property, and a point in all of them is a choice function.

items.name: [0,1]^[0,1] is compact but not sequentially compact
items.pic: Points of [0,1]^[0,1] are functions; the sequence fₙ(x) = n-th binary digit of x has no convergent subsequence, because for any subsequence a point x is built whose digits along it alternate.

items.name: The Hilbert cube and Cantor cube are compact metrizable
items.pic: A sequence in ∏[0, 1/n] is tamed by a diagonal argument, coordinate after coordinate, into a convergent subsequence, with the metric Σ|xₙ − yₙ| tracking the convergence.

items.name: Stone–Čech compactification
items.pic: Embed (0,1] via x ↦ (x, sin(1/x)) and take the closure, which adds a segment; add more bounded functions as coordinates and the remainder grows, βX being the compactification to which every bounded function extends.

items.name: Local finiteness and paracompactness
items.pic: Cover the line with intervals; a probe point counts how many sets meet a small neighbourhood of it, and a refinement tool shrinks a non-locally-finite cover into a locally finite one.

items.name: Metrizable spaces are paracompact (Stone)
items.pic: An open cover of a metric space (an open disc covered by sets crowding toward the boundary) is refined by Stone’s layered construction into a locally finite cover, with local counts read out.

items.name: Paracompact Hausdorff spaces have partitions of unity
items.pic: A locally finite cover of the line by intervals of shrinking size and bump functions summing to 1, drawn as a stacked area chart; remove local finiteness and the sum blows up.

items.name: Nagata–Smirnov metrization theorem
items.pic: A countably locally finite basis feeds Urysohn functions into a product with the uniform metric; layers of the basis are switched on one by one and the embedding becomes injective and open.

items.name: Smirnov metrization theorem
items.pic: Patch together local metrics on a paracompact, locally metrizable space using a partition of unity; the line with two origins fails the Hausdorff test and the patching visibly breaks there.

chapters.title: The Gauss map and curvature
chapters.summary: How a surface bends in space is recorded by how its unit normal turns: the Gauss map and its derivative, the shape operator. The shape operator is self-adjoint, so it has two principal curvatures in perpendicular directions; their product is the Gaussian curvature and their average the mean curvature. Points are elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic or umbilic according to these, and compact surfaces always have a point of positive curvature.

refs: do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces

items.name: Gauss map
items.pic: Paint a region of a surface and see its image on the unit sphere under the normal; a saddle region maps onto the sphere with reversed orientation.

items.name: The shape operator is self-adjoint
items.pic: At a point, the derivative of the normal is shown as a 2×2 matrix acting on tangent vectors; the readout checks ⟨Su, v⟩ = ⟨u, Sv⟩ for random pairs.

items.name: Second fundamental form
items.pic: The surface near a point is compared with its tangent plane: the height above the plane matches ½ II(v, v) to second order, shown as a graph over the plane.

items.name: Normal curvature and Meusnier’s theorem
items.pic: Curves on a surface through a point with the same tangent but different osculating planes: their curvatures differ, but the normal components all equal the normal curvature.

items.name: Principal curvatures and principal directions
items.pic: Rotate a normal plane around a point and plot the curvature of the slice against the angle; the maximum and minimum occur in perpendicular directions, matching the eigenvectors of the shape operator.

items.name: Euler’s formula for normal curvature
items.pic: The plot of normal curvature against angle is overlaid with κ₁cos²θ + κ₂sin²θ and they coincide for every point and every surface tried.

items.name: Gaussian and mean curvature
items.pic: Heat maps of K and H on a torus: positive on the outside, negative on the inside, zero on the top and bottom circles; the scale bar shows the extremes.

items.name: K as the area ratio of the Gauss image
items.pic: Shrink a disc around a point; the signed area of its Gauss image divided by its own area converges to K, with a log-scale plot of the ratio.

items.name: Elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic and umbilic points
items.pic: Probe points on a bumpy surface: the classification is shown together with the local shape — bowl, saddle, trough — and parabolic curves are traced where K changes sign.

items.name: Dupin indicatrix
items.pic: Slice a surface by planes parallel to the tangent plane just above and below a point; the scaled cross-sections approach ellipses or pairs of hyperbolas, the Dupin indicatrix.

items.name: Lines of curvature and asymptotic curves
items.pic: Integrate the principal-direction fields on an ellipsoid or a saddle to draw lines of curvature, and on a hyperbolic region the asymptotic curves where normal curvature vanishes.

items.name: Curvature in local coordinates
items.pic: For a patch you type, E, F, G and e, f, g are computed symbolically-numerically and K = (eg − f²)/(EG − F²) is evaluated, agreeing with the Gauss-map area ratio.

items.name: Curvature of a graph at a critical point
items.pic: Edit f(x, y) as a quadratic form plus cubic terms: at a critical point K equals the Hessian determinant, so bowls, saddles and troughs line up with the second-derivative test.

items.name: Curvature of surfaces of revolution
items.pic: Draw a profile curve and spin it: the meridian and parallel curvatures are computed, and their product is shown as a colour on the surface.

items.name: All-umbilic surfaces are pieces of planes or spheres
items.pic: Deform a sphere slightly; umbilic points become isolated, marked by the solver, and the ratio κ₁/κ₂ map shows they appear only where the surface is locally round.

items.name: The four umbilics of an ellipsoid
items.pic: Lines of curvature on a triaxial ellipsoid swirl around four umbilics located by the solver; make two axes equal and the umbilics merge in pairs at the poles.

items.name: Compact surfaces have an elliptic point
items.pic: Shrink a sphere around a compact surface until it first touches; at the contact point K ≥ 1/R², shown with both curvatures read out.

chapters.title: Differential forms and Stokes’s theorem
chapters.summary: Covectors are the objects one integrates along curves, and alternating multilinear forms generalize them to higher dimensions. Differential forms pull back under smooth maps, have an exterior derivative with d∘d = 0 that unifies gradient, curl and divergence, and interact with flows through Cartan’s formula. On an oriented manifold they can be integrated, and Stokes’s theorem equates the integral of dω over a region with the integral of ω over its boundary.

items.name: Covectors and the cotangent bundle
items.pic: A covector at a point is drawn as a stack of parallel level lines; evaluating it on an arrow counts how many lines the arrow crosses, and changing coordinates transforms the components inversely to vectors.

items.name: Differential of a function
items.pic: Level curves of a function f with df drawn as local line stacks at each point; df(v) matches the directional derivative of f along v read from the contours.

items.name: Line integrals of covector fields
items.pic: Draw a path through a covector field; the integral accumulates crossings of the level stacks along the way, and reparametrizing the path leaves it unchanged.

items.name: Conservative covector fields
items.pic: Integrate a covector field around closed loops you draw: for df every loop gives 0; for the angle form on the punctured plane, loops around the puncture give 2π.

items.name: Tensors and tensor fields
items.pic: A bilinear form on the plane is drawn by its effect on pairs of vectors; symmetric ones as ellipses or hyperbolas, alternating ones as signed areas, with components transforming under a draggable change of basis.

items.name: Alternating tensors and the wedge product
items.pic: The wedge of two covectors on the plane is evaluated on two arrows as the signed area of the parallelogram of their images; swapping the arrows flips the sign.

items.name: Differential forms on manifolds
items.pic: A 2-form on a surface is painted as oriented area density; integrating it over small parallelograms at a point recovers its value on the spanning vectors.

items.name: Pullback of forms
items.pic: Pull a 1-form back along a map from the plane to the sphere; the pulled-back stacks of lines are drawn in the parameter domain and evaluate consistently on pushed-forward vectors.

items.name: Exterior derivative; d² = 0
items.pic: For a 1-form, dω evaluated on a small square equals the circulation of ω around it to leading order, computed numerically; applying d twice gives zero up to round-off.

items.name: d unifies gradient, curl and divergence
items.pic: Translate a vector field on ℝ³ into a 1-form or 2-form and apply d; the result matches curl or divergence computed directly, and d∘d = 0 recovers curl grad = 0 and div curl = 0.

items.name: Interior multiplication
items.pic: Insert a vector field into a 2-form to get a 1-form: the area density becomes a flux density across curves, drawn as line stacks perpendicular to the field.

items.name: Cartan’s magic formula
items.pic: The Lie derivative of a form along a flow is computed by finite differences and compared with d ι_X ω + ι_X dω; for an area form it reduces to the divergence of X times the area form.

items.name: Orientations
items.pic: Pick an ordered basis at one point and transport it continuously over a manifold; on the torus the choice is consistent everywhere, on the Möbius band and ℝP² it flips.

items.name: The orientation covering
items.pic: Each point is doubled into its two orientations; for the Möbius band the result is a connected cylinder double-covering it, for an orientable surface two disjoint copies.

items.name: Volume forms
items.pic: A nowhere-vanishing top form is painted on a surface; its sign on ordered bases defines the orientation, and on the Möbius band any attempt must vanish somewhere.

items.name: Integration of differential forms
items.pic: Integrate a 2-form over a sphere by splitting it with a partition of unity into chart pieces; each piece’s integral and the total are shown, and changing the partition leaves the total unchanged.

items.name: Stokes’s theorem
items.pic: Choose a 1-form and a region with holes on a surface: the integral of dω over the region and of ω around its boundary are computed numerically and agree; reverse one boundary orientation and they disagree.

items.name: Green’s theorem and the classical Stokes theorem
items.pic: A vector field and a surface with boundary curve in ℝ³: the flux of the curl and the circulation are integrated side by side, and flattening the surface into the plane gives Green’s theorem.

items.name: Exact forms integrate to zero on closed manifolds
items.pic: Integrate dη over a sphere or torus for random η: the result is zero to machine precision, while the area form, which is closed but not exact, integrates to the area.

items.name: Invariant volume forms on Lie groups
items.pic: Translate a small volume element around SO(3) or SU(2) by left multiplication; its volume stays fixed, giving the Haar measure as a differential form.

chapters.title: Brownian Motion
chapters.summary: Brownian motion is constructed from its finite-dimensional laws and Kolmogorov's continuity criterion, and its paths are shown Hölder of every order below one half yet nowhere differentiable. The Markov property with the right-continuous filtration gives Blumenthal's 0-1 law, time inversion and recurrence in one dimension; stopping times and the strong Markov property lead to the reflection principle, the hitting-time process and Lévy's arcsine law. The martingales $B_t$, $B_t^2-t$ and $e^{\theta B_t-\theta^2t/2}$ compute exit probabilities, exit times and Laplace transforms, and the chapter ends with Itô's formula.

items.name: Brownian motion
items.pic: Seeded Brownian paths with draggable time points t₁ < t₂ < t₃: the increments are scattered pairwise (independent) and histogrammed against normals of variance tᵢ₊₁ − tᵢ.

items.name: Existence of the finite-dimensional Brownian laws
items.pic: Gaussian finite-dimensional laws at chosen times are sampled and checked consistent: dropping a time gives the lower-dimensional law.

items.name: Brownian paths are uniformly continuous on dyadics
items.pic: Refine a Brownian path level by level at dyadic times; the largest jump between neighbours at level n is plotted and shrinks like √(n2⁻ⁿ).

items.name: Kolmogorov continuity theorem
items.pic: A moment bound E|X_s − X_t|^β ≤ K|t − s|^{1+α} is set with sliders; the dyadic chaining construction yields paths whose Hölder exponent stays below α/β.

items.name: Dyadic chaining bound
items.pic: Two dyadic points q < r are joined by a chain of dyadic steps of decreasing size; the increment bound sums a geometric series, drawn step by step.

items.name: Brownian paths are Hölder continuous of order γ < 1/2
items.pic: The Hölder quotient |B_s − B_t|/|s − t|^γ over a fine grid is plotted for γ on either side of ½: bounded below, unbounded above.

items.name: Brownian paths are nowhere differentiable
items.pic: Zoom into a Brownian path at any point: the difference quotients (B_{t+h} − B_t)/h blow up as h shrinks, unlike for a smooth curve shown alongside.

items.name: Markov property of Brownian motion
items.pic: Restart seeded paths at a time s from their current positions: the future increments are fresh Brownian motions, compared by histogram with independent ones.

items.name: Germ information adds nothing: F_s⁺ versus F_s°
items.pic: Conditional expectations of a functional given the path up to s and given an infinitesimal peek beyond s are estimated and coincide.

items.name: Blumenthal’s 0-1 law
items.pic: Germ events at time 0, like "B is positive at times arbitrarily close to 0", are estimated on refining grids and have probability 0 or 1.

items.name: Brownian motion is immediately positive
items.pic: Zoom into a path near t = 0 at ever smaller scales: there is always a time where it is positive, on every seeded path.

items.name: Brownian motion returns to 0 immediately
items.pic: Zero crossings of a path started at 0 are marked; zooming toward t = 0 always reveals more of them.

items.name: Time inversion
items.pic: The process tB(1/t) is built from a seeded path and its increments are checked to be Brownian; its behaviour near 0 mirrors B at infinity.

items.name: Tail 0-1 law for Brownian motion
items.pic: Tail events such as "B_t > √t infinitely often" are estimated over long seeded runs and come out 0 or 1, the same for every start x.

items.name: lim sup B_t/√t = ∞
items.pic: B_t/√t is plotted on a log time axis over a long run and keeps reaching new heights and depths.

items.name: One-dimensional Brownian motion is recurrent
items.pic: Returns of a long seeded path to 0 are marked on a log time scale and keep coming at all scales.

items.name: Stopping time in continuous time
items.pic: Rules applied to a Brownian path ("first exit from (−1, 1)", "last zero before 1") are tested for whether {T ≤ t} can be decided from the path up to t.

items.name: Hitting times of open sets are stopping times
items.pic: For an open set G, {T < t} is decided by checking rational times only, illustrated on a path with a grid of rational checkpoints.

items.name: Decreasing limits of stopping times are stopping times
items.pic: Stopping times Tₙ ↓ T (exit times of shrinking neighbourhoods) are drawn on a path converging to T.

items.name: Increasing limits of stopping times are stopping times
items.pic: Hitting times of shrinking open neighbourhoods of a closed set increase to the hitting time of the set, marked on a seeded path.

items.name: Hitting times of closed sets are stopping times
items.pic: A closed set K and its 1/n-neighbourhoods: their hitting times climb to the hitting time of K on each path.

items.name: Dyadic approximation of stopping times
items.pic: A stopping time S is rounded up to the next dyadic time at level n; the discrete approximations Sₙ are drawn decreasing to S.

items.name: F_S ⊂ F_T when S ≤ T
items.pic: Two stopping times on a path, the first exit from (−1, 1) and from (−2, 2): information revealed by the first is visibly contained in that of the second.

items.name: F_T = ∩ F_{Tₙ} for Tₙ ↓ T
items.pic: Decreasing stopping times close in on T and the information sets shrink to the information at T, shown as nested path segments.

items.name: B_S is F_S-measurable
items.pic: The value of the path at the dyadic approximations Sₙ converges to B_S by continuity, drawn on a seeded path.

items.name: Strong Markov property of Brownian motion
items.pic: Restart seeded paths at the first hitting time of a level: the post-T increments are compared with fresh Brownian motions and match.

items.name: Hitting times T_a have stationary independent increments
items.pic: The first-passage process a ↦ T_a is extracted from a seeded path and drawn as an increasing jump process; its increments over disjoint levels are independent.

items.name: Reflection principle for Brownian motion
items.pic: A path is reflected after first hitting level a; the reflected path is equally likely, and P(T_a ≤ t) = 2P(B_t ≥ a) is confirmed by simulation.

items.name: Lévy’s arcsine law for the last zero
items.pic: The last zero of a Brownian path before time 1 is recorded over seeded runs and histogrammed against the arcsine density.

items.name: Optional stopping for continuous martingales
items.pic: A right-continuous martingale is stopped at a bounded stopping time; the averages of X_T over seeded runs equal EX₀.

items.name: Brownian motion is a martingale
items.pic: From a time s on each path, continuation simulations give the conditional mean of B_t, which sits at B_s.

items.name: Exit probabilities from an interval
items.pic: Drag a starting point x between a and b: the simulated probability of hitting a first lies on the line (b − x)/(b − a).

items.name: B_t² − t is a martingale
items.pic: The averages of B_t² − t over seeded paths stay at 0 while individual paths swing; dropping the −t makes the average climb linearly.

items.name: Mean exit time from an interval: E₀T = −ab
items.pic: Exit times from (a, b) are histogrammed over seeded runs and their mean compared with −ab as the endpoints are dragged.

items.name: Exponential martingale exp(θB_t − θ²t/2)
items.pic: Averages of exp(θB_t − θ²t/2) stay at 1 for every θ you choose, while the median path decays to 0.

items.name: Laplace transform of hitting times
items.pic: E₀e^{−λT_a} is estimated from simulated hitting times and plotted against exp(−a√(2λ)) as λ varies.

items.name: Space-time harmonic polynomials give martingales
items.pic: The polynomials obtained by expanding the exponential martingale in θ (x, x² − t, x³ − 3tx, …) are averaged along seeded paths and stay constant.

items.name: Second moment of the exit time: ET² = 5a⁴/3
items.pic: Exit times from (−a, a) are simulated and their second moment compared with 5a⁴/3 as a is dragged.

items.name: Itô’s formula
items.pic: For f you choose, f(B_t) − f(B_0) is compared along one seeded path with the left-point Riemann sum of f′(B)dB plus ½∫f″(B)ds, the gap shrinking as the mesh refines.

items.name: Weak convergence with uniformly converging integrands
items.pic: Discrete measures Σ(ΔB)²δ_{tᵢ} converge to Lebesgue measure on [0, t]; integrals of g along the path converge too.

items.name: Stochastic integrals are continuous martingales
items.pic: Riemann sums of g(B)dB along many seeded paths average to 0 at every time, and their variance matches E∫g(B_s)²ds.

items.name: Itô’s formula with time dependence
items.pic: For f(t, x) = e^{x − t/2} the Itô decomposition along a path has no drift term, while e^{x} picks up the ½∫ds term; both are checked numerically.

items.name: Multidimensional Itô’s formula
items.pic: For a 2-D Brownian path and f(x, y) = log|z| or x² + y², the Itô terms are accumulated along the path and compared with f(B_t) − f(B_0).

chapters.title: Card shuffling and spectral gaps
chapters.summary: Strong stationary times, random times at which the chain is exactly stationary and independent of the time itself, analyse card shuffles: top-to-random and random transpositions take order n log n moves, and seven riffle shuffles are needed for a 52-card deck. These chains drop to equilibrium abruptly — the cutoff phenomenon. For reversible chains the spectral gap controls mixing; Cheeger’s inequality relates it to bottlenecks, comparison and canonical paths transfer bounds between chains, and expanders mix in logarithmic time.

refs: Levin, Peres & Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times
Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

items.name: Strong stationary times
items.pic: In the top-to-random shuffle, mark the moment the original bottom card reaches the top and is reinserted; decks observed at that moment are perfectly shuffled, as the histogram over permutations of a small deck shows.

items.name: Strong stationary times bound separation and total variation
items.pic: Plot the tail P(τ > t) of a strong stationary time above the exact separation distance and TV distance for a small deck; the bound holds at every t.

items.name: Top-to-random shuffle mixes in n log n
items.pic: Shuffle a virtual deck by moving the top card to a random position; the bottom card’s climb is tracked and the number of moves to randomise n cards is plotted against n log n.

items.name: Seven riffle shuffles suffice (Bayer–Diaconis)
items.pic: The exact total-variation distance after k Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds riffles of a 52-card deck is computed from rising sequences; it stays near 1 for five shuffles and falls below 1/2 at seven.

items.name: Random transpositions mix in ½ n log n
items.pic: Swap two random cards at each step; the number of untouched cards and the distance to uniform are tracked, both dropping sharply near ½ n log n.

items.name: Cutoff phenomenon
items.pic: Overlay the distance-to-stationarity curves of the hypercube walk for n = 10, 100, 1000 with time rescaled by ½ n log n; the curves sharpen into a step function at 1.

items.name: Spectral decomposition of reversible chains
items.pic: Symmetrize a reversible transition matrix and display its real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenfunctions; Pᵗ is rebuilt as a sum of eigenvalue powers times projections.

items.name: Spectral gap and relaxation time
items.pic: Drag a parameter of a chain and watch the second-largest eigenvalue modulus approach 1 as a bottleneck forms; the relaxation time 1/gap is read off live.

items.name: Relaxation time controls the mixing time
items.pic: For several chains, measured t_mix is plotted between the lower bound (t_rel − 1)log 2 and the upper bound t_rel·log(4/π_min); all points fall inside the band.

items.name: Eigenvalues of walks on the cycle and the hypercube
items.pic: The discrete Fourier basis diagonalises the cycle walk and Walsh functions the hypercube walk; computed eigenvalues cos(2πk/n) and 1 − 2k/n are shown matching the numerical spectrum.

items.name: Dirichlet form and the variational spectral gap
items.pic: Paint a test function on the states; the ratio of its Dirichlet energy to its variance is computed, and minimising it by gradient steps converges to the spectral gap.

items.name: Cheeger’s inequality for Markov chains
items.pic: For random graphs and dumbbells, the conductance Φ is found by search and the gap computed; every point lands in the band Φ²/2 ≤ gap ≤ 2Φ.

items.name: Comparison of chains and canonical paths
items.pic: Route every transition of a known chain through paths in a new chain; the congestion of the busiest edge is displayed and converts one spectral gap into a bound on the other.

items.name: Expander graphs and rapid mixing
items.pic: Compare walks on a cycle, a grid and a random 3-regular graph with the same number of vertices; only the expander keeps a spectral gap bounded away from 0 and mixes in O(log n) steps.

items.name: Trailing the dovetail shuffle to its lair
items.pic: The paper’s table for a 52-card deck: total variation distance from uniform after k riffle shuffles — 1.000 for k ≤ 4, then 0.924, 0.614, 0.334, 0.167, 0.085, 0.043 for k = 5…10; the reader shuffles a virtual deck by the Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds model, counts rising sequences, and changes the deck size to watch the cutoff stay near (3/2) log₂ n shuffles.

chapters.title: Extremal Graph Theory
chapters.summary: How many edges force a given subgraph? Turán's theorem answers this exactly for complete graphs, and the Erdős–Stone theorem shows that for any H the extremal density is governed by its chromatic number alone. For minors and topological minors, average degree bounds (Mader, Kostochka–Thomason, Komlós–Szemerédi) and large girth force complete minors; Hadwiger's conjecture, which links chromatic number to complete minors, is proved for small cases. Szemerédi's regularity lemma partitions every large graph into random-like pairs; with the blow-up, counting and removal lemmas it proves Erdős–Stone, bounds Ramsey numbers of bounded-degree graphs, and yields Roth's theorem on three-term arithmetic progressions.

items.name: Extremal number ex(n, H) and Turán graphs
items.pic: Sliders for n and r: the Turán graph T^(r−1)(n) is drawn as r − 1 nearly equal classes completely joined, with its edge count t_{r−1}(n) shown.

items.name: Turán’s theorem
items.pic: Add edges to an n-vertex graph while the app forbids Kʳ; the edge counter peaks at t_{r−1}(n), and the unique extremal graph reached is the Turán graph.

items.name: Erdős–Stone theorem
items.pic: With εn² edges above the Turán number, random dense graphs are searched for a complete r-partite K_s^r; the app finds one and highlights its parts.

items.name: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits: extremal density is (χ − 2)/(χ − 1)
items.pic: Pick a graph H; its chromatic number sets the limit of ex(n, H)/(n choose 2), plotted against n for exact small values and the asymptote.

items.name: Turán graphs have edge density tending to (r − 2)/(r − 1)
items.pic: Plot t_{r−1}(n)/(n choose 2) against n for several r; the curves converge to (r − 2)/(r − 1).

items.name: Average degree 2^(r−2) forces a Kʳ minor
items.pic: Contract edges of a dense graph to keep it dense while shrinking it; a vertex’s neighbourhood becomes dense enough to contain a K^(r−1) minor by induction, and adding the vertex gives Kʳ.

items.name: Average degree 2^(r choose 2) forces a topological Kʳ
items.pic: Build a topological minor with r branch vertices one edge at a time, each new subdivided edge found by a density argument, while the average degree requirement halves each step.

items.name: Average degree c·r² forces a topological Kʳ
items.pic: In a graph of average degree 10r², the app finds a highly connected subgraph, chooses r branch vertices with many neighbours, and links them using linkedness.

items.name: Kostochka–Thomason: d(G) ≥ c·r√log r forces a Kʳ minor
items.pic: Plot the average degree needed to force a Kʳ minor against r: the bounds 2^(r−2) and c·r√log r, together with random graphs that show the latter is tight.

items.name: Large girth yields minors of huge minimum degree
items.pic: Choose far-apart centres in a high-girth graph, grow disjoint trees around them, and contract each tree: the resulting minor has enormous minimum degree.

items.name: Thomassen: large girth and δ ≥ 3 force a Kʳ minor
items.pic: For cubic graphs of growing girth, the app contracts local trees into a dense minor and finds a Kʳ minor inside it.

items.name: Kühn–Osthus: large girth, δ ≥ r − 1 force a topological Kʳ
items.pic: In graphs of large girth and minimum degree r − 1, the app locates a subdivided Kʳ, contrasting with dense graphs that need much larger degree.

items.name: Hadwiger’s conjecture
items.pic: For each small graph you draw, the app computes χ and the largest complete minor, plotting the pair; every point satisfies "χ ≥ r implies a Kʳ minor" so far.

items.name: No K⁴ minor: edge-maximal graphs are pasted triangles
items.pic: Build graphs by gluing triangles along edges (2-trees); adding any further edge creates a K⁴ minor, which the app highlights.

items.name: Edge-maximal graphs without a K⁴ minor have 2n − 3 edges
items.pic: Glue triangles one at a time: each adds one vertex and two edges, so the counter stays at 2n − 3.

items.name: Hadwiger’s conjecture holds for r = 4
items.pic: Graphs without a K⁴ minor are 3-coloured by colouring triangle by triangle along the pasting order.

items.name: Wagner’s structure theorem for graphs without a K⁵ minor
items.pic: Decompose an edge-maximal graph without a K⁵ minor along separating triangles and edges into plane triangulations and copies of the Wagner graph W, shown in a tree.

items.name: Graphs without a K⁵ minor have at most 3n − 6 edges
items.pic: Paste triangulations and Wagner graphs along triangles and edges; the edge counter never exceeds 3n − 6.

items.name: Hadwiger’s conjecture holds for r = 5
items.pic: Colour each planar piece with four colours and each Wagner graph with three, then permute colours to agree on the pasted triangles and edges.

items.name: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas: Hadwiger’s conjecture for r = 6
items.pic: A minimal counterexample would have an apex vertex over a planar graph; the app shows how removing the apex and 4-colouring the rest gives 5 colours.

items.name: Kühn–Osthus: Hadwiger for K_{s,s}-free graphs and large r
items.pic: For K_{s,s}-free graphs of large chromatic number, the app finds the predicted complete minor, compared with random graphs that contain K_{s,s}.

items.name: Large girth: chromatic number r forces a topological Kʳ
items.pic: In high-girth graphs of chromatic number r, a critical subgraph of minimum degree r − 1 is found and a subdivided Kʳ inside it is highlighted.

items.name: ε-regular pairs and ε-regular partitions
items.pic: Choose two vertex sets A, B and subsets X ⊆ A, Y ⊆ B with a slider for ε; the densities d(X, Y) and d(A, B) are compared, and the pair is flagged irregular when they differ by more than ε.

items.name: Szemerédi’s regularity lemma
items.pic: A large random-like graph with planted structure is partitioned iteratively; the adjacency matrix reorders into blocks of near-constant density, with irregular pairs marked.

items.name: Refining a partition does not decrease its index
items.pic: Refine a partition step by step; the index q, a mean square density, is plotted and never decreases.

items.name: An irregular pair splits to raise the index by ε⁴
items.pic: Given an irregular pair with witness sets X and Y, split A and B along them; the index of the pair jumps by at least ε⁴, shown numerically.

items.name: An irregular partition has a refinement of much larger index
items.pic: Apply all splitting witnesses at once and equalise part sizes; the index gains ε⁵/2, so after boundedly many rounds the partition must be regular.

items.name: ε-regular pairs: most vertices see large sets typically
items.pic: In an ε-regular pair, pick Y ⊆ B larger than ε|B|; vertices of A with fewer than (d − ε)|Y| neighbours in Y are coloured red and are always fewer than ε|A|.

items.name: Regularity graph
items.pic: From a regular partition, draw a vertex for each part and an edge for each ε-regular pair of density at least d, giving the reduced graph R.

items.name: Blow-up lemma
items.pic: Blow up each vertex of the regularity graph into a large set: a bounded-degree graph H mapped homomorphically into R is embedded vertex by vertex into G, keeping candidate sets large.

items.name: Uniform multipartite graphs have the expected clique count
items.pic: For a k-partite graph with uniform pairs of given densities, the number of k-cliques is counted and compared with the product of densities times the part sizes.

items.name: Counting lemma
items.pic: Count homomorphic copies of a small graph H in a graph built from uniform pairs; the count tracks the product of pair densities as ε shrinks.

items.name: Removal lemma
items.pic: Take a graph with few copies of H; the app deletes edges of irregular, sparse and small pairs of a regular partition, at most ρn² in total, and no copy of H survives.

items.name: Thinly spread copies of H force o(n²) edges
items.pic: For graphs where every edge lies in a bounded number of copies of H, plot edges against n²; the ratio drifts to zero as n grows.

items.name: Ruzsa–Szemerédi (6,3) theorem: one triangle per edge
items.pic: Build graphs in which every edge lies in exactly one triangle (from 3-AP-free sets); the edge density drops towards zero as n grows.

items.name: Szemerédi’s theorem on arithmetic progressions
items.pic: Choose a set of positive upper density on a number line (say, via a pattern); the app finds arithmetic progressions of the length you request, highlighted in colour.

items.name: Szemerédi’s theorem in density form: r_k(n) = o(n)
items.pic: Compute the largest subsets of {0, …, n − 1} without k-term progressions for small n; the density r_k(n)/n is plotted and slowly decreases.

items.name: Roth’s theorem: r₃(n) = o(n)
items.pic: A set without 3-term progressions is turned into a tripartite graph in which every edge lies in exactly one triangle; the removal lemma then caps its size, shown with Behrend-type examples.

chapters.title: Integer partitions
chapters.summary: Partitions of an integer are counted by Euler’s infinite product, and that product turns bijections between Ferrers diagrams into identities between series. Euler’s odd–distinct theorem, the pentagonal number theorem with Franklin’s involution, the Jacobi triple product and the Rogers–Ramanujan identities are the classical highlights. Restricting partitions to a box brings back the q-binomial coefficients, and stacking them in three dimensions gives plane partitions.

items.name: Euler’s generating function for partitions
items.pic: Multiply the factors 1/(1 − xᵏ) one at a time; the coefficient table fills in with p(n), and each factor’s contribution is shown as the number of parts equal to k.

items.name: Conjugation of partitions
items.pic: Reflect a Ferrers diagram in its diagonal; the number of parts and the largest part swap, so the two counts agree for every n.

items.name: Euler: distinct parts equal odd parts
items.pic: List partitions of n into distinct parts beside partitions into odd parts; repeatedly halving even parts or merging equal pairs carries one list onto the other.

items.name: Glaisher’s bijection
items.pic: Choose d and match partitions with no part divisible by d to partitions with no part repeated d or more times by splitting and merging parts; both columns are counted.

items.name: Euler’s pentagonal number theorem
items.pic: Franklin’s involution moves the smallest part onto the staircase slope or back; distinct-part partitions cancel in pairs except at pentagonal numbers, where the leftover diagram is drawn.

items.name: Euler’s recurrence for p(n)
items.pic: Compute p(n) up to a thousand with the pentagonal recurrence, timing it against brute-force enumeration and plotting log p(n) against √n.

items.name: Jacobi triple product identity
items.pic: Truncate both sides of the triple product as two-variable series in z and q; the coefficient arrays agree entry by entry, and specialising z recovers the pentagonal theorem.

items.name: Rogers–Ramanujan identities
items.pic: Count partitions of n whose parts differ by at least 2 and partitions into parts ≡ 1, 4 (mod 5); the two counts are listed side by side up to n = 100 and never differ.

items.name: Partitions in a box and Gaussian coefficients
items.pic: Fit Ferrers diagrams inside a k × (n − k) box; the size distribution is plotted and matches the coefficients of [n choose k]_q, which can also be traced as lattice paths along the boundary.

items.name: Unimodality of Gaussian coefficients
items.pic: Choose n and k; the coefficient sequence of [n choose k]_q is drawn as bars that rise to a single peak and fall symmetrically, with any failure of unimodality flagged in red.

items.name: MacMahon’s plane partition generating function
items.pic: Stack cubes in a corner to form plane partitions of n, viewed in 3D; the counts 1, 1, 3, 6, 13, 24, … agree with the coefficients of ∏(1 − xᵏ)⁻ᵏ.

chapters.title: Farey fractions, continued fractions and Pell’s equation
chapters.summary: Fractions between 0 and 1 arranged by size and denominator have a rigid structure, visible in Farey sequences, Ford circles and the Stern–Brocot tree. Continued fractions encode a number by the steps of Euclid’s algorithm; their convergents are the best rational approximations, and they are eventually periodic exactly for quadratic irrationals. That periodicity solves Pell’s equation x² − dy² = 1, and the statistics of partial quotients of a typical number follow the Gauss–Kuzmin law.

refs: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers
Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

items.name: Farey sequences and the mediant property
items.pic: Grow the Farey sequence of order n by inserting mediants; neighbours a/b < c/d always satisfy bc − ad = 1, checked for every adjacent pair.

items.name: Ford circles
items.pic: Place a circle of diameter 1/q² tangent to the line at each fraction p/q; circles never overlap, and neighbouring Farey fractions give tangent circles.

items.name: Stern–Brocot tree
items.pic: Descend the Stern–Brocot tree toward a target number by L/R moves; each rational appears exactly once, and the run lengths of the path are the continued fraction digits.

items.name: Simple continued fractions and convergents
items.pic: Type a rational or a real number; the integer part is split off and the remainder inverted repeatedly, and the resulting partial quotients match the quotients of Euclid’s algorithm.

items.name: Recurrences for convergents
items.pic: A table builds pₙ and qₙ by the recurrences pₙ = aₙpₙ₋₁ + pₙ₋₂; the determinant pₙqₙ₋₁ − pₙ₋₁qₙ alternates ±1 in every row.

items.name: Infinite continued fractions converge
items.pic: Plot convergents of √2, e or π on a number line; they alternate around the target with errors below 1/(qₙqₙ₊₁), shrinking geometrically.

items.name: Convergents are the best approximations
items.pic: For each denominator q up to 1000, the best fraction p/q for a chosen α is found by brute force; record-setting approximations are exactly the convergents (like 355/113 for π).

items.name: Lagrange: periodic continued fractions are quadratic irrationals
items.pic: Enter √d or (a + √d)/b; the expansion is computed in exact arithmetic, the repeating block is boxed, and a purely periodic expansion is folded back into its quadratic equation.

items.name: Pell’s equation
items.pic: Draw the hyperbola x² − dy² = 1 over the integer grid; lattice points on it are rare and spread out exponentially, as a log-scale view shows.

items.name: Pell’s equation is solved by the continued fraction of √d
items.pic: Expand √d up to the end of its first period; the convergent there solves x² − dy² = ±1, even for d = 61 where the smallest solution has ten digits.

items.name: All Pell solutions are powers of the fundamental one
items.pic: Multiply (x₁ + y₁√d) by itself repeatedly; each power is a new solution, and a search confirms there are no others in between.

items.name: The negative Pell equation and odd periods
items.pic: Tabulate d up to 1000 by the parity of the period of √d; x² − dy² = −1 is solvable exactly in the odd-period rows.

items.name: Euler’s continued fraction for e
items.pic: The partial quotients of e are computed to high precision and display the pattern [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, …], while those of π show no pattern.

items.name: Gauss–Kuzmin distribution of partial quotients
items.pic: Pick random reals and tally their partial quotients; the frequencies of 1, 2, 3, … converge to log₂(1 + 1/(k(k + 2))), with about 41.5% ones.

items.name: Khinchin’s and Lévy’s constants
items.pic: For a random real, the geometric mean of its partial quotients approaches 2.685… and qₙ^(1/n) approaches e^(π²/(12 ln 2)), while e and √2 visibly miss both limits.

chapters.title: Axiomatic set theory
chapters.summary: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory avoids the paradoxes by letting sets be formed only by specific operations: pairing, union, power set, and carving subsets out of sets already known. From these axioms and the axiom of infinity one builds the natural numbers, ordered pairs, functions and eventually all of ordinary mathematics. Foundation says every set is built in stages from the empty set.

refs: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic

items.name: Extensionality, pairing, union and power set
items.pic: Sets drawn as nested boxes: apply pairing, union and power set to small sets and see the results, with extensionality merging boxes that have identical contents.

items.name: Separation and replacement schemas
items.pic: Pick a set and a formula to carve out a subset (separation), or a definable operation to apply elementwise (replacement); the result is computed and shown to stay inside the universe of sets.

items.name: There is no set of all sets
items.pic: Given any set A you build, separation forms {x ∈ A : x ∉ x}, and the checker proves this new set is not a member of A — so A could never have contained everything.

items.name: Ordered pairs, relations and functions as sets
items.pic: The Kuratowski pair {{a},{a,b}} is drawn as nested boxes; swap a and b and the boxes change unless a = b, and a function appears as a set of pairs with one pair per input.

items.name: Infinity and the von Neumann natural numbers
items.pic: Build 0 = ∅, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0, 1}, … as nested boxes; each number is literally the set of smaller numbers, and the successor operation adds one more box.

items.name: Transitive sets
items.pic: Draw a membership diagram; the checker tests whether every member’s members are already members, and offers the transitive closure that would make it so.

items.name: Axiom of foundation
items.pic: Draw membership arrows among a few sets; for each nonempty collection the checker finds an ∈-minimal element, and an attempt to draw x ∈ x or an infinite descending chain is rejected.

items.name: Classes versus sets
items.pic: Formulas define collections; the tool sorts examples (all sets, all ordinals, all singletons, the subsets of ω) into sets and proper classes, with the Russell-style argument shown for each proper class.

items.name: Building ℕ, ℤ, ℚ and ℝ inside set theory
items.pic: Follow one number through the tower: integers as classes of pairs of naturals, rationals as classes of pairs of integers, reals as Dedekind cuts; a cut for √2 is drawn on the rational line.

items.name: Hereditarily finite sets and Ackermann coding
items.pic: Each natural number codes a hereditarily finite set through its binary digits; toggle bits and the nested-box picture updates, so membership becomes “the k-th bit is 1”.

items.name: Untersuchungen über die Grundlagen der Mengenlehre I
items.pic: Zermelo’s seven axioms as switches: the reader builds sets from ∅ by pairing, union, power set and separation, and the universe grows level by level; switch Separation back to unrestricted comprehension and Russell’s {x : x ∉ x} is formed and the contradiction lights up, while with the axioms on Zermelo’s argument shows every set has a subset that is not a member — so there is no set of all sets.

chapters.title: Numerical integration
chapters.summary: Quadrature rules integrate an interpolant instead of the function. Composite Newton–Cotes rules converge at rates set by their degree, the Euler–Maclaurin formula explains the error of the trapezoidal rule and why it is spectacular for periodic functions, and Richardson extrapolation turns it into Romberg integration. Gauss quadrature chooses the nodes as well as the weights, integrating polynomials of twice the degree exactly; Clenshaw–Curtis, based on Chebyshev points, is nearly as good and easier to compute.

refs: Süli & Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice

items.name: Newton–Cotes rules: trapezoidal and Simpson
items.pic: Integrate a function you draw with the trapezoidal and Simpson rules on one panel; the areas of the interpolating line and parabola are shaded against the exact area.

items.name: Composite rule error rates
items.pic: Error against number of panels on log–log axes for the composite midpoint, trapezoidal and Simpson rules; the slopes −2, −2 and −4 appear and degrade for a function with a kink.

items.name: Peano kernel theorem
items.pic: The Peano kernel of a quadrature rule is plotted; when it does not change sign the error equals a constant times a single derivative value, checked on test functions.

items.name: Euler–Maclaurin formula
items.pic: The trapezoidal error is expanded in even powers of h with Bernoulli-number coefficients; each correction term is added and the remaining error drops by the predicted factor.

items.name: The trapezoidal rule is spectral for periodic functions
items.pic: Integrate e^{cos θ} over a full period with the trapezoidal rule; the error falls geometrically to machine precision in about 20 points, while for a non-periodic integrand it falls like N⁻².

items.name: Romberg integration
items.pic: Build the Romberg table by applying Richardson extrapolation to trapezoidal estimates with halved steps; the diagonal converges rapidly, with errors shown in each cell.

items.name: Adaptive quadrature
items.pic: Integrate a function with a sharp spike; subintervals are split recursively where the local error estimate is large, and the final mesh, drawn as tick marks, crowds around the spike.

items.name: High-order Newton–Cotes rules are unstable
items.pic: Plot the weights of closed Newton–Cotes rules as the degree grows; negative weights appear and their sum of absolute values explodes, amplifying rounding errors in the computed integral.

items.name: Gauss quadrature: exact to degree 2n − 1
items.pic: Place n nodes freely and choose weights to integrate polynomials; the highest exactly integrated degree is read out and reaches 2n − 1 only when the nodes sit at the zeros of the Legendre polynomial.

items.name: Positive weights and convergence of Gauss quadrature
items.pic: Gauss weights are shown to be positive and to sum to the interval length; applied to a merely continuous function, the quadrature error is plotted converging to zero.

items.name: Golub–Welsch algorithm
items.pic: Gauss nodes and weights for a chosen weight function are computed as eigenvalues and squared first eigenvector components of the Jacobi matrix, and checked by integrating test monomials.

items.name: Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature
items.pic: Integrate the Chebyshev interpolant exactly by summing its coefficients; the weights are computed by FFT and are all positive, shown as a bar chart.

items.name: Clenshaw–Curtis is nearly as good as Gauss
items.pic: Errors of Gauss and Clenshaw–Curtis are plotted against n for analytic, smooth and kinked integrands; the two curves nearly coincide except for very smooth integrands, despite Gauss’ factor-of-two degree advantage.

chapters.title: Eigenvalue algorithms
chapters.summary: Power iteration finds the dominant eigenvector at a rate set by the ratio of the top two eigenvalues; shifting and inverting targets any eigenvalue, and updating the shift with the Rayleigh quotient gives cubic convergence for symmetric matrices. Iterating a whole basis at once is simultaneous iteration, which in disguise is the QR algorithm; with shifts and deflation on a Hessenberg matrix it is one of the great algorithms of the twentieth century. Jacobi rotations, bisection, divide and conquer and Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization complete the toolkit.

items.name: Power iteration
items.pic: Repeatedly multiply a vector by a 2×2 or 3×3 matrix and normalize; the iterates swing toward the dominant eigenvector, drawn as a fixed line, with the angle error plotted on a log scale.

items.name: Convergence of power iteration: rate |λ₂/λ₁|
items.pic: Slide λ₂ toward λ₁; the measured slope of the log-error line matches log|λ₂/λ₁| and flattens to no convergence when the two have equal modulus.

items.name: Inverse iteration with a shift
items.pic: Drag a shift μ along the real axis among the eigenvalues; inverse iteration converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue is nearest μ, and faster the closer μ is.

items.name: The Rayleigh quotient
items.pic: Move a unit vector around the circle for a symmetric 2×2 matrix; the Rayleigh quotient is plotted against the angle, stationary at the eigenvectors, and its error is quadratic in the angle error.

items.name: Rayleigh quotient iteration
items.pic: Use the current Rayleigh quotient as the shift for inverse iteration; the digits of accuracy triple each step in a readout table, compared with linear convergence of power iteration.

items.name: Simultaneous (orthogonal) iteration
items.pic: Iterate a pair of orthonormalized vectors in 3D; the plane they span converges to the dominant invariant plane, shown with the eigenvectors fixed in the background.

items.name: The QR algorithm without shifts
items.pic: Factor A = QR, form RQ, and repeat; the subdiagonal entries of the iterates shrink geometrically as an animated heat map, revealing the eigenvalues on the diagonal.

items.name: QR algorithm is simultaneous iteration in disguise
items.pic: Run simultaneous iteration on the identity and the QR algorithm in lockstep; the accumulated Q matrices coincide at every step, displayed side by side.

items.name: Shifted QR algorithm with deflation
items.pic: Add a Rayleigh shift to each QR step on a tridiagonal matrix; the last subdiagonal entry plunges to machine precision in a few steps, the matrix deflates, and the counter of total iterations is about 2 per eigenvalue.

items.name: Wilkinson shift
items.pic: On the symmetric matrix [[0, 1], [1, 0]] the Rayleigh shift stalls forever; switching to the Wilkinson shift from the trailing 2×2 block breaks the symmetry and converges at once.

items.name: Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm
items.pic: Annihilate the largest off-diagonal entry of a symmetric matrix by a plane rotation at each step; the off-diagonal Frobenius norm decreases monotonically on a log plot.

items.name: Bisection with Sturm sequences
items.pic: For a symmetric tridiagonal matrix, count sign changes of the leading principal minors at a trial x; the count tells how many eigenvalues lie below x, and bisection pins down any chosen one.

items.name: Divide and conquer for symmetric eigenproblems
items.pic: Split a tridiagonal matrix into two halves plus a rank-one correction; the secular equation is plotted and its roots, lying between the eigenvalues of the halves, are the eigenvalues of the whole.

items.name: Computing the SVD: Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization
items.pic: Alternate left and right Householder reflections to reduce a matrix to bidiagonal form, then iterate; the singular values emerge on the diagonal and match those computed from AᵀA only for well-conditioned inputs.

items.name: PageRank as a power iteration
items.pic: Edit a small web graph; power iteration on the damped link matrix converges to the ranking vector, and lowering the damping factor speeds convergence as |λ₂| shrinks.

items.name: The QR transformation
items.pic: Iterate A ← RQ on a small matrix: the reader watches the subdiagonal entries decay like (λᵢ₊₁/λᵢ)ᵏ and the diagonal settle on the eigenvalues; turning on shifts collapses the iteration count and deflation peels off one eigenvalue at a time.

paper.title: The QR Transformation: A Unitary Analogue to the LR Transformation — Part 1

chapters.title: Linear programming and the simplex method
chapters.summary: A linear program attains its optimum at a vertex of its feasible polyhedron, and vertices correspond to basic feasible solutions. Dantzig’s simplex method walks from vertex to adjacent vertex, always improving the objective, until reduced costs certify optimality. It is fast in practice but exponential in the worst case (Klee–Minty), degeneracy can make it cycle without an anti-cycling rule, and its dual variables have the economic meaning of prices.

items.name: Standard form and basic feasible solutions
items.pic: Convert a 2D LP to standard form with slack variables; each choice of basis is solved and plotted, feasible bases landing exactly on the vertices of the polygon and infeasible ones outside it.

items.name: Fundamental theorem of linear programming
items.pic: For random LPs the optimal value is computed over all vertices and over a fine grid of feasible points; the best vertex always matches the best grid point.

items.name: The simplex method
items.pic: Watch the simplex method walk along edges of a 3D polytope from vertex to vertex, with the tableau, entering and leaving variables and objective value updated at each pivot.

items.name: Reduced costs certify optimality
items.pic: At the current vertex the reduced cost of each non-basic variable is shown along its edge; the method stops when all are nonnegative, and the corresponding dual vector is displayed as a certificate.

items.name: Degeneracy, cycling and Bland’s rule
items.pic: On a degenerate LP where several constraints meet at a vertex, the textbook pivoting rule loops through the same bases forever; switching to Bland’s smallest-index rule breaks the cycle.

items.name: Phase I: finding a feasible starting vertex
items.pic: Add artificial variables and minimize their sum; the auxiliary simplex run drives them to zero and lands on a vertex of the original polytope, or proves the LP infeasible.

items.name: Klee–Minty cube: exponential worst case
items.pic: On a squashed cube in n dimensions, Dantzig’s rule visits all 2ⁿ vertices before reaching the optimum; the pivot counter is plotted against n on a log scale.

items.name: Dual simplex method
items.pic: After a new constraint cuts off the current optimum, the dual simplex restores feasibility by pivoting through dual-feasible bases, shown on the polygon as a walk back into the feasible region.

items.name: Transportation and assignment problems
items.pic: Edit supplies, demands and shipping costs between depots and stores; the optimal flows are drawn as arrows of varying width and the solution is integral when the data are.

items.name: Shadow prices in production planning
items.pic: A factory allocates scarce resources to products; the dual price of each resource is read out and predicts exactly how profit changes when a little more of that resource is supplied.

items.name: Maximizing a linear function subject to linear inequalities
items.pic: The simplex method on a three-variable production-planning problem: pivots move from vertex to vertex of the feasible polytope along improving edges, the tableau updating beside the 3-D picture; the reader chooses entering variables by different rules and sees the path and the number of pivots change.
