chapters.title: Bayesian inference
chapters.summary: Bayesian inference treats the parameter as uncertain and updates a prior distribution into a posterior by Bayes’ theorem. Conjugate families turn the update into adding counts, Jeffreys priors address invariance, and de Finetti’s theorem explains why priors appear at all once observations are exchangeable. The Bernstein–von Mises theorem reconciles Bayesian and frequentist answers in large samples, while Lindley’s paradox shows where they part ways. Hierarchical models let groups borrow strength, and Monte Carlo methods — importance sampling, Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs — compute posteriors in practice.

items.name: Bayes’ theorem for densities
items.pic: Prior, likelihood and posterior share one axis; the reader shapes the prior by dragging control points, and the posterior is computed pointwise as their normalized product.

items.name: Posterior predictive distribution
items.pic: Future observations are simulated by drawing θ from the posterior and then data from the model; the predictive histogram is wider than the plug-in fit, and the gap closes as data accumulate.

items.name: Conjugate prior
items.pic: For an exponential-family likelihood the prior’s hyperparameters are displayed as pseudo-observations that each new datum increments, and the posterior curve stays in the same family throughout.

items.name: Beta–binomial updating
items.pic: Flip a seeded coin one toss at a time and watch the Beta posterior narrow toward the true p; its mean is always a weighted average of the prior mean and the observed proportion, with the weights shown.

items.name: Laplace’s rule of succession
items.pic: After s successes in n trials under a uniform prior the predicted chance of another success is (s + 1)/(n + 2); simulating many coins with p drawn uniformly confirms that these predictions are calibrated.

items.name: Normal–normal model and precision weighting
items.pic: Drag the prior mean and variance: the posterior mean slides between prior mean and sample mean in proportion to their precisions, and the posterior precision is drawn as the sum of the two.

items.name: Gamma–Poisson model
items.pic: Accumulate Poisson counts and update a gamma posterior for the rate; the marginal distribution of a new count is the negative binomial, visibly more dispersed than any single Poisson.

items.name: Credible intervals: equal-tailed and HPD
items.pic: On a skewed posterior the equal-tailed and highest-density intervals are shaded with equal 95% area; the HPD is shorter, and a bimodal posterior splits the HPD set into two pieces.

items.name: Frequentist coverage of credible intervals
items.pic: Fix a true θ and repeat: the 95% credible interval under a confident prior centred far from the truth covers well under 95%, while drawing θ afresh from the prior on each repeat restores exactly 95%.

items.name: Jeffreys prior
items.pic: A flat prior on p becomes a lopsided prior on the log-odds after reparametrizing, while the Jeffreys prior ∝ √I(θ) transforms into the Jeffreys prior of the new parameter; both pairs are drawn and compared.

items.name: Bernstein–von Mises theorem
items.pic: As n grows, posteriors from three very different priors merge onto the normal curve centred at the MLE with variance 1/(nI); a total-variation readout tracks the merger, and a prior that excludes the truth never joins.

items.name: De Finetti’s representation theorem
items.pic: A Pólya urn generates exchangeable 0–1 sequences: different runs settle on different limiting frequencies whose histogram is the mixing Beta law, and within a run the sequence passes for iid coin flips with that frequency.

items.name: Bayes factor
items.pic: The prior predictive densities of two models are drawn and their ratio at the observed data is the Bayes factor; the simpler model wins when the data land where its predictive mass is concentrated.

items.name: Lindley’s paradox
items.pic: Hold the z-statistic at 2.5 while n grows: the p-value stays at 0.012, but the Bayes factor for the point null against a diffuse alternative swings to favour the null, both plotted against n.

items.name: Hierarchical models and partial pooling
items.pic: Eight schools with noisy effect estimates: slide the between-school standard deviation from zero to infinity to move from complete pooling to no pooling, with the marginal likelihood showing which values the data support.

items.name: Importance sampling
items.pic: Estimate a far-tail probability by sampling from a shifted proposal and reweighting: the variance readout shows large gains for a good proposal and the effective sample size collapsing when the proposal’s tails are lighter than the target’s.

items.name: Metropolis–Hastings sampling of posteriors
items.pic: A random-walk chain explores a banana-shaped posterior with accepted and rejected proposals marked; the proposal-scale slider produces sticky chains when too large and slow diffusion when too small, while the running histogram converges to the target.

items.name: Gibbs sampling of posteriors
items.pic: Alternating draws from the two full conditionals of a bivariate normal trace an axis-parallel staircase; raising the correlation to 0.99 shrinks the steps and slows mixing, quantified by the autocorrelation readout.

items.name: Improper priors and posterior propriety
items.pic: A flat prior on a normal mean gives a proper posterior after a single observation, but a flat prior on the log of a group-level standard deviation in a hierarchical model does not: the running integral of the unnormalized posterior keeps growing as the integration range is widened.

items.name: Essay towards solving a problem in the doctrine of chances
items.pic: Bayes’s table: a first ball thrown at random fixes an unknown position p; each later ball lands to its left or right; the reader throws balls and watches the posterior for p — the beta density Bayes evaluated as an area — narrow around the hidden truth, and reads off the chance that p lies between any two bounds.

items.name: Sampling-based approaches to calculating marginal densities
items.pic: Gibbs sampling a one-way variance-components model, the kind of hierarchical example the paper worked through: the reader alternates draws from each full conditional, watches marginal posterior densities emerge — raw histograms and the smoother Rao–Blackwellised averages of conditional densities — and compares them with numerically integrated answers.

chapters.title: The VC-Dimension
chapters.summary: Size is not what makes a class learnable: thresholds on the line form an infinite class that ERM learns from log(2/δ)/ε examples. What matters is shattering — the largest set on which the class realizes every labelling — and a class of infinite VC-dimension is unlearnable by the No-Free-Lunch argument. The fundamental theorem of statistical learning shows the converse: finite VC-dimension, uniform convergence, agnostic and realizable PAC learnability, and the success of every ERM are all equivalent, with sample complexity governed by the VC-dimension. The proof runs through the Sauer–Shelah–Perles lemma, which caps the growth function polynomially, and a uniform convergence bound in terms of the growth function.

collectionSource.author: Shai Shalev-Shwartz & Shai Ben-David
collectionSource.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms

items.name: Threshold functions on the line
items.pic: Drag a threshold a along a line of labelled points: points left of a are labelled 1, the rest 0, and the training error of every threshold is drawn as a staircase underneath.

items.name: Thresholds are PAC learnable from log(2/δ)/ε examples
items.pic: The two intervals of mass ε on either side of the true threshold are shaded; over many samples the app counts how often one of them receives no sample point and compares the frequency with 2e^{−εm}.

items.name: Restriction of H to a finite set
items.pic: Place three points on a line and list, as rows of 0/1 vectors, the labellings realized by thresholds, by intervals and by unions of two intervals.

items.name: Shattering
items.pic: A shattering game: the reader places points in the plane and demands labellings; the app tries to realize each with an axis-aligned rectangle and lights all 2^|C| cells when the set is shattered.

items.name: Shattered sets of size 2m defeat learners using m examples
items.pic: The No-Free-Lunch adversary works on a shattered set of size 2m, so its targets stay inside the class; any learner’s error on the unseen half hovers near 1/4 on average.

items.name: VC-dimension
items.pic: For a chosen class the app searches for the largest shattered point set; the reader proposes a set one point larger and the app exhibits a labelling the class cannot produce.

items.name: Infinite VC-dimension implies not PAC learnable
items.pic: For the class of sign patterns of sin(θx), sets of every size are shattered; whatever m the reader chooses, a shattered set of size 2m is produced and the learner’s failure rate stays above 1/7.

items.name: VC-dimension of thresholds and of intervals: 1 and 2
items.pic: Try to shatter two points with thresholds or three with intervals: the impossible labellings (0, 1) and (1, 0, 1) are flashed, and no slider position reaches them.

items.name: Axis-aligned rectangles have VC-dimension 4
items.pic: Four points in a diamond are shattered by rectangles, all 16 labellings shown; add a fifth point and the app picks the leftmost, rightmost, lowest and highest points and shows that labelling only them positive is impossible.

items.name: Finite classes: VCdim(H) ≤ log₂|H|
items.pic: Thresholds on k grid points: |H| = k grows with the slider while the VC-dimension stays 1, and log₂|H| climbs away from it.

items.name: VC-dimension is not the number of parameters
items.pic: A single frequency θ is tuned, by a binary-expansion recipe, so that the sign of sin(θx) matches any labelling the reader clicks on the points 10^{−1}, …, 10^{−d}: one parameter, infinite VC-dimension.

items.name: The fundamental theorem of statistical (PAC) learning
items.pic: Six equivalent conditions — uniform convergence, ERM agnostic learner, agnostic PAC, PAC, ERM PAC learner, finite VC-dimension — form a diagram; the reader picks a class and the app evaluates each condition, all lighting up together or not at all.

items.name: The fundamental theorem: quantitative version
items.pic: For halfspaces in d dimensions, the sample size ERM needs to reach excess error ε is measured and plotted on log axes against ε and d, beside the agnostic rate (d + log 1/δ)/ε² and the realizable rate (d log(1/ε) + log 1/δ)/ε.

items.name: Growth function
items.pic: For intervals and for halfplanes, the number of distinct labellings of m random points is counted and plotted against m beside 2^m.

items.name: Sauer–Shelah–Perles lemma
items.pic: The growth function of a class of VC-dimension d bends away from 2^m right after m = d and stays under Σ_{i≤d} C(m, i) ≤ (em/d)^d; the inductive proof’s split of H_C into Y₀ and Y₁ is shown on a small table.

items.name: Uniform convergence from a small growth function
items.pic: The symmetrization trick is animated — a ghost sample S′ is drawn and paired points are swapped by random signs — and the measured expected worst gap stays under (4 + √log τ_H(2m))/√(2m).

chapters.title: Infinite width: Gaussian processes and kernels
chapters.summary: As the width of a randomly initialized network grows, its output at any finite set of inputs becomes jointly Gaussian, so the network prior is a Gaussian process. Under the standard parametrization, training then barely moves the weights: the network stays close to its linearization, governed by a fixed neural tangent kernel, and gradient descent reduces to kernel regression with a spectral bias toward smooth functions. Other parametrizations keep features learning in the limit — the mean-field picture of two-layer networks and the maximal-update parametrization that lets hyperparameters transfer across widths.

items.name: Wide random networks are Gaussian processes
items.pic: Thousands of random shallow networks of growing width are sampled and their outputs at two inputs scattered: the cloud becomes a bivariate normal ellipse whose covariance matches the limiting kernel.

items.name: Gaussian process regression
items.pic: Click to add observations: the posterior mean and 95% band of a Gaussian process with the network-limit kernel update instantly, pinching at the data and widening between them.

items.name: Neural tangent kernel
items.pic: For a chosen network, the inner products of parameter gradients at pairs of inputs are drawn as a kernel heat map; at large width, different random seeds give nearly identical maps.

items.name: Lazy training: the NTK freezes at infinite width
items.pic: Networks of growing width are trained and the relative change of their weights and of their NTK is tracked; both shrink like 1/√width, so wide networks stay close to their linearization.

items.name: Wide-network training is kernel regression
items.pic: The function learned by a very wide trained network is overlaid with kernel regression using its NTK: the curves coincide, while a narrow network departs visibly from the kernel prediction.

items.name: Random features (random Fourier features)
items.pic: A Gaussian kernel is approximated by averaging cosines with random frequencies drawn from its Fourier transform; the maximum error of the approximate kernel matrix falls like 1/√D as features are added.

items.name: Spectral bias toward low frequencies
items.pic: A target made of low- and high-frequency sines is fitted while the Fourier amplitudes of the network output are tracked: low frequencies are learned first, in the order of the kernel’s eigenvalues.

items.name: Lazy versus feature learning
items.pic: Scale the network’s output multiplier: in the lazy regime hidden representations barely move and the kernel is frozen, in the rich regime the first-layer features visibly rotate toward the target’s relevant direction.

items.name: Mean-field limit of two-layer networks
items.pic: Each hidden unit is a particle in (input weight, output weight) space; as width grows, the particle cloud trained by gradient descent follows a smooth density flow that is reproducible across seeds.

items.name: Maximal-update parametrization and transfer
items.pic: The learning rate is swept for widths 64 to 4096: under the standard parametrization the optimal rate drifts with width, while under μP the loss-versus-rate curves line up at the same optimum.

chapters.title: Instruments, bounds and natural experiments
chapters.summary: An instrument moves the treatment without otherwise touching the outcome, so its effects on the two can be divided to recover a causal effect even with unmeasured confounding — exactly under homogeneity, and for the compliers under monotonicity. Weak instruments make this fragile, and without such extra assumptions only bounds are available, which the instrumental inequality can sometimes refute outright. Natural experiments — parallel trends, sharp cutoffs and genetic variants — supply the instruments and comparisons in practice.

refs: Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If

items.name: Instrumental variable
items.pic: On an editable DAG a candidate instrument is checked against the three conditions — it moves treatment, shares no cause with the outcome, and reaches the outcome only through treatment — with violating paths highlighted.

items.name: The Wald (IV) estimand under homogeneity
items.pic: The instrument’s effect on the outcome divided by its effect on treatment recovers the true effect in a simulated linear model with a hidden confounder, while ordinary regression is biased; an exclusion-violation slider biases the ratio.

items.name: Two-stage least squares
items.pic: Treatment is regressed on the instrument, then the outcome on the fitted treatment; both stages are drawn as scatters, and the second-stage slope matches the true effect over repeats.

items.name: Weak instruments
items.pic: Shrink the instrument’s effect on treatment: the 2SLS estimates spread out, drift toward the confounded OLS estimate and lose interval coverage, with the first-stage F-statistic shown alongside.

items.name: Compliance types and principal strata
items.pic: A population is split into compliers, always-takers, never-takers and defiers by their potential treatments under each assignment; the observed cells are mixtures of these strata, which the reader can see but the data cannot.

items.name: Local average treatment effect (LATE)
items.pic: Under monotonicity the Wald ratio equals the compliers’ average effect, as the simulated strata confirm; allowing defiers breaks the equality.

items.name: Manski’s no-assumption bounds
items.pic: With no assumptions, the average effect of a binary treatment on a binary outcome is only bounded to an interval of width one; the bounds are drawn from simulated data and shrink as assumptions such as monotone response are added.

items.name: Balke–Pearl bounds with an instrument
items.pic: A linear program over response types gives the tightest bounds on the effect consistent with the observed instrument–treatment–outcome table; the interval shrinks as the instrument strengthens, drawn against the true effect.

items.name: The instrumental inequality
items.pic: Edit the observed joint distribution of instrument, treatment and outcome; once the inequality is violated a warning shows that no valid instrumental model could have produced the data.

items.name: Difference-in-differences
items.pic: Treated and control groups are tracked before and after a policy; the counterfactual trend copied from the controls yields the effect, and a slider that bends the pre-trends shows the estimate absorbing the difference.

items.name: Regression discontinuity design
items.pic: Treatment switches on at a cutoff of a running variable; local linear fits on each side measure the jump, a bandwidth slider shows the bias–variance trade-off, and bunching of units just past the cutoff breaks the design.

items.name: Mendelian randomization
items.pic: Genetic variants serve as instruments for an exposure; per-variant ratio estimates are plotted as slopes through the origin, and adding a pleiotropic variant with a direct effect pulls it visibly off the common line.

chapters.title: String algorithms
chapters.summary: Finding a pattern in a text can be done in linear time by refusing to re-read characters. Rabin–Karp compares rolling fingerprints and checks only on a hash match; finite automata and Knuth–Morris–Pratt use the pattern’s self-overlaps to slide forward without backtracking in the text. Suffix arrays index every substring of a text at once, are built by repeated rank doubling, and become far more useful once the longest common prefixes of neighbouring suffixes are known. Boyer–Moore skips ahead by reading the pattern backwards, and Aho–Corasick matches a whole dictionary at once.

refs: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.)

items.name: String matching and the naive matcher
items.pic: Type a text and a pattern; the pattern slides along the text with character comparisons marked green or red at each shift, and the total is compared with (n − m + 1)m.

items.name: Rabin–Karp with a rolling hash
items.pic: A window slides over the text while its fingerprint updates in constant time by dropping the leading digit and adding the next; hits are verified, and a small-modulus slider makes spurious hits visible.

items.name: Random fingerprints rarely collide
items.pic: Pick two different strings of length m and sweep every base modulo a small prime p; the bases where their polynomial fingerprints agree are marked, never more than m − 1 of the p choices.

items.name: String matching with finite automata
items.pic: Type a pattern and its matching automaton is drawn with one state per matched prefix; feeding the text moves a token through the states, reaching the accepting state at every occurrence.

items.name: The prefix (failure) function
items.pic: For a typed pattern each position shows π[q], the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of the first q characters, drawn as a pair of matching brackets.

items.name: Knuth–Morris–Pratt
items.pic: Run KMP on a typed text and pattern: on a mismatch the pattern jumps by the failure function, and a potential meter (the current match length) shows total work never exceeding 2n.

items.name: Computing the prefix function in linear time
items.pic: The pattern is matched against itself: the π table fills left to right, fallback jumps are drawn as arcs, and an amortization counter keeps the total number of steps below 2m.

items.name: Tries and suffix tries
items.pic: Insert words into a trie letter by letter as shared prefixes merge into common branches, then switch to the suffix trie of a typed word where every substring is a path from the root.

items.name: Suffix arrays
items.pic: All suffixes of a typed string are listed and sorted, the array of their starting positions appears alongside, and a pattern query binary-searches the sorted list with its matching range highlighted.

items.name: Suffix array construction by prefix doubling
items.pic: Pairs of ranks for the first 2ᵏ and next 2ᵏ characters are radix-sorted round by round, and the number of distinct ranks rises until every suffix is separated after about log₂ n rounds.

items.name: LCP array in linear time (Kasai)
items.pic: Suffixes are visited in text order and each one’s common prefix with its sorted predecessor is measured; a counter that drops by at most one per step proves O(n) work, and the maximum entry reveals the longest repeated substring.

items.name: Boyer–Moore–Horspool: skipping with the bad-character rule
items.pic: The pattern is compared right to left; on a mismatch it jumps ahead by the distance stored for the text character under its last position, and a counter shows far fewer than n comparisons on natural-language text.

items.name: Aho–Corasick dictionary matching
items.pic: A trie of several patterns gains failure links computed breadth-first, generalizing the prefix function; one pass of the text moves a token through the automaton and reports every occurrence of every pattern.

chapters.title: Pushdown automata and the limits of context-free languages
chapters.summary: Adding a stack to a finite automaton gives exactly the power of context-free grammars. A pumping lemma for parse trees shows what that power cannot do — match three counts, or copy a string — and explains why context-free languages are closed under union but not under intersection or complement. Determinism matters here, unlike for finite automata: deterministic pushdown automata, the basis of practical parsers, recognize a strictly smaller class.

refs: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation

items.name: Pushdown automaton
items.pic: Run a PDA for 0ⁿ1ⁿ on typed input: the stack grows with each 0 and shrinks with each 1; for even palindromes the computation branches at every possible guess of the middle.

items.name: From grammar to pushdown automaton
items.pic: The PDA simulates a leftmost derivation: its stack holds the unexpanded part of the sentential form, matched against the input as the reader steps.

items.name: From pushdown automaton to grammar
items.pic: A variable A_pq is created for each pair of states; a run of the PDA from p to q that starts and ends with an empty stack is shown split into the rule that generates it.

items.name: PDAs recognize exactly the context-free languages
items.pic: Round trip: grammar → PDA → grammar; strings up to a chosen length are checked to have the same membership in all three descriptions.

items.name: Pumping lemma for context-free languages
items.pic: A tall parse tree must repeat a variable on some root-to-leaf path; the repeated subtree is highlighted and pumping it derives uvⁱxyⁱz for the i the reader chooses.

items.name: aⁿbⁿcⁿ and ww are not context-free
items.pic: Play the pumping game for aⁿbⁿcⁿ: wherever the opponent places the window vxy, pumping unbalances at least one letter count, shown by three bars.

items.name: Ogden’s lemma
items.pic: Mark positions in a string; the pumped pieces are forced to contain marked positions, defeating a language that the plain pumping lemma cannot rule out.

items.name: No closure under intersection or complement
items.pic: Two grammars generate {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} and {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} in two panels; the strings in both are exactly aⁿbⁿcⁿ, the non-context-free language just proved.

items.name: Context-free ∩ regular is context-free
items.pic: A PDA and a DFA run in lockstep inside a product machine: the stack belongs to the PDA, the extra state coordinate to the DFA, and verdicts are checked on test strings.

items.name: Deterministic pushdown automata
items.pic: A DPDA for balanced brackets runs with never more than one possible move; the tool flags any state where the reader’s machine has a choice.

items.name: Deterministic CFLs are closed under complement
items.pic: A DPDA is completed so it always reads its whole input, then its accept states are flipped; the verdicts on test strings invert, unlike the same trick on a nondeterministic PDA.

items.name: Palindromes need nondeterminism
items.pic: Every deterministic attempt at even palindromes is shown failing on some input because it must commit to a middle point; the nondeterministic PDA succeeds by guessing.

items.name: Parikh’s theorem
items.pic: Letter-count vectors of all strings of a context-free language up to some length are plotted in the plane; they form a finite union of linear sets, the same shapes a regular language produces.

items.name: Chomsky–Schützenberger theorem
items.pic: A context-free language is shown as the image of bracket words intersected with a regular language; pick a string and the bracketed word it came from is displayed.

chapters.title: Interactive proofs
chapters.summary: An interactive proof lets a powerful prover convince a randomized, polynomial-time verifier through conversation. Graph non-isomorphism, not known to be in NP, has a simple interactive proof; public coins turn out to be as good as private ones. Arithmetization — reading a Boolean formula as a polynomial — and the sum-check protocol show that interaction captures all of PSPACE, and with two non-communicating provers, all of nondeterministic exponential time.

refs: Arora & Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach

items.name: Interactive proof systems and IP
items.pic: A message diagram between prover and verifier steps through rounds; the reader plays a cheating prover and watches the verifier’s acceptance rate stay below the soundness bound.

items.name: Interactive proof for graph non-isomorphism
items.pic: The verifier secretly permutes one of two graphs and asks which it was; for isomorphic graphs the reader, as prover, can only guess, and the success rate settles at one half.

items.name: Arthur–Merlin games: AM and MA
items.pic: Arthur’s coins are shown face up to Merlin; message diagrams for MA (Merlin first) and AM (Arthur first) are compared on the same problem.

items.name: Goldwasser–Sipser: public coins suffice
items.pic: Set lower-bound protocol: a random hash function maps a large set onto a target and a small set rarely hits it; the reader resizes the set and watches the hit rate separate.

items.name: Graph isomorphism is not NP-complete unless PH collapses
items.pic: Graph non-isomorphism in AM would put coNP in AM if GI were NP-complete, and the chain of inclusions animates the polynomial hierarchy collapsing to level two.

items.name: Arithmetization
items.pic: Type a Boolean formula: AND becomes multiplication, NOT x becomes 1 − x, and the resulting polynomial agrees with the formula on every 0/1 input in the table.

items.name: Sum-check protocol
items.pic: The prover sends a univariate polynomial each round and the verifier checks it at a random point; a lying prover is caught with high probability, tallied over repeated runs.

items.name: coNP ⊆ IP (Lund–Fortnow–Karloff–Nisan)
items.pic: Counting satisfying assignments of a formula becomes a sum of its arithmetization over the cube; the sum-check rounds certify the count zero for an unsatisfiable formula.

items.name: IP = PSPACE (Shamir)
items.pic: Quantifiers become products and sums, and degree-reduction steps keep polynomials small; the degree of each round’s polynomial is plotted with and without linearization.

items.name: MIP = NEXP (Babai–Fortnow–Lund)
items.pic: Two provers are questioned in separate rooms; cross-checking their answers catches inconsistent strategies, as a match-rate meter shows for strategies the reader designs.

items.name: Program checking (Blum–Kannan)
items.pic: A buggy sorting or gcd routine is wrapped in a checker that tests its outputs on random self-related inputs; planted bugs are detected at the predicted rate.

chapters.title: Continuous sources and the Gaussian channel
chapters.summary: For continuous variables, differential entropy plays the role of entropy — it can be negative, but differences and mutual information keep their meaning. The Gaussian has the largest entropy for a given variance, which makes Gaussian noise the hardest and gives the additive white Gaussian noise channel its capacity ½ log(1 + SNR). With the sampling theorem this becomes the Shannon–Hartley law for band-limited channels, sets the ultimate limit on energy per bit, and tells how to share power across parallel channels.

refs: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms

items.name: Differential entropy
items.pic: Draw a density; h(X) is computed by numerical integration, goes negative for narrow densities and shifts by log a when the density is stretched by a.

items.name: Differential entropy as a limit of quantized entropy
items.pic: Quantize a density with bin width Δ; H(X_Δ) + log Δ converges to h(X) as the reader shrinks Δ.

items.name: The Gaussian maximizes entropy for a given variance
items.pic: Densities with the same variance — uniform, Laplace, mixtures the reader sketches — are compared; the Gaussian’s entropy ½ log(2πeσ²) beats them all.

items.name: Maximum-entropy distributions
items.pic: Toggle constraints — bounded support, fixed mean, fixed variance — and the maximum-entropy density is computed as an exponential family: uniform, exponential, Gaussian.

items.name: Entropy power inequality
items.pic: Convolve two densities the reader draws; the entropy power of the sum is compared with the sum of entropy powers, with equality only for Gaussians.

items.name: Capacity of the Gaussian channel
items.pic: Codewords of power P sit near a sphere and noise blurs each into a ball; counting non-overlapping noise balls inside the received sphere gives ½ log(1 + P/N) as the reader varies SNR.

items.name: Shannon–Hartley theorem
items.pic: Capacity W log(1 + P/(N₀W)) is plotted against bandwidth W and saturates at P/(N₀ ln 2) in the wideband limit.

items.name: The Shannon limit on energy per bit
items.pic: Spectral efficiency is plotted against Eb/N₀ with the capacity boundary at −1.59 dB; modulation schemes the reader toggles all land to its right.

items.name: Water-filling for parallel Gaussian channels
items.pic: Pour a power budget into vessels whose floors are the noise levels; the water level settles so total power matches, and the noisiest channels stay dry.

chapters.title: One-way functions and the foundations
chapters.summary: Almost all of private-key cryptography rests on a single assumption: functions that are easy to compute but hard to invert. From any one-way function one can extract a hard-core bit (Goldreich–Levin), build pseudorandom generators, stretch them arbitrarily, turn them into pseudorandom functions (GGM) and permutations (Luby–Rackoff). Conversely each of these implies one-way functions, and their existence would imply P ≠ NP — mapping cryptography onto Impagliazzo’s possible worlds.

refs: Katz & Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography
Boneh & Shoup, A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography

items.name: One-way functions
items.pic: Multiply two random primes instantly, then try to factor the product by trial division; the times are plotted against bit length, one flat and one exploding.

items.name: Candidate one-way functions
items.pic: Integer multiplication, modular exponentiation and subset sum are each computed forward and attacked backward by the best simple algorithms, with timings on a log scale.

items.name: One-way functions imply P ≠ NP
items.pic: Inverting a function is an NP search problem: with a hypothetical fast SAT solver the reader inverts a toy one-way function bit by bit via self-reduction.

items.name: Hard-core predicates
items.pic: For a toy permutation, the reader tries predictors for candidate bits of x given f(x); success rates stay near ½ for the hard-core bit and climb for leaky bits.

items.name: Goldreich–Levin theorem
items.pic: A predictor for ⟨x, r⟩ that is right only slightly more than half the time is turned, by local list decoding of the Hadamard code, into a short list of candidates containing x.

items.name: Pseudorandom generators from one-way permutations
items.pic: Output f(s) followed by the hard-core bit of s: one bit of stretch, with a distinguisher for the output shown converted into a predictor for the hard-core bit.

items.name: Increasing the expansion of a generator
items.pic: Iterate a one-bit-stretch generator, emitting one bit per step; a hybrid argument across the output positions is drawn as a row of panels.

items.name: Generators from any one-way function (HILL)
items.pic: A one-way function that is not a permutation is turned into a generator by hashing and entropy accumulation; the pipeline is drawn with the entropy of each stage annotated.

items.name: GGM pseudorandom functions from generators
items.pic: A length-doubling generator is applied down a binary tree; the input bits choose left or right halves, and the leaf reached is the output, with the path highlighted.

items.name: Luby–Rackoff: three Feistel rounds give a pseudorandom permutation
items.pic: Distinguishers that break one- and two-round Feistel networks are run and win; against three rounds with independent random functions their advantage collapses toward zero.

items.name: Private-key cryptography is equivalent to one-way functions
items.pic: A graph of primitives — one-way functions, generators, pseudorandom functions and permutations, MACs, CPA-secure encryption — with arrows for each construction showing they stand or fall together.

items.name: Impagliazzo’s five worlds
items.pic: Algorithmica, Heuristica, Pessiland, Minicrypt and Cryptomania are drawn as regions; toggling hypotheses (P = NP, average-case hardness, one-way functions, public-key) moves a marker between them.

chapters.title: Byzantine agreement
chapters.summary: When faulty processes can lie, agreement requires more than three times as many processes as faults and a network with enough disjoint paths; the classic argument shows three generals cannot tolerate one traitor. Exponential information gathering and the phase-king algorithm achieve the bound; digital signatures remove it. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance adds quorums and partial synchrony, and Nakamoto’s blockchain replaces identities with proof of work.

items.name: The Byzantine generals problem
items.pic: A commander sends orders to lieutenants, some of whom may be traitors sending contradictory messages; the reader picks traitors and their lies.

items.name: Byzantine agreement needs n > 3f
items.pic: Three generals with one traitor: copies of the processes are arranged in a hexagon so that each loyal pair sees a consistent scenario, yet the scenarios force contradictory decisions.

items.name: Exponential information gathering (Lamport–Shostak–Pease)
items.pic: Each process builds a tree of “A said that B said that …” values over f + 1 rounds and resolves it bottom-up by majority; tree size and the resolved decisions are shown for small n.

items.name: Phase-king algorithm
items.pic: In each phase a designated king breaks ties; once a loyal king has ruled, all loyal processes hold the same value, highlighted, using polynomial-size messages.

items.name: Byzantine agreement needs connectivity 2f + 1
items.pic: On a graph the reader draws, a vertex cut of size 2f lets traitors on the cut tell each side a different story; adding paths restores agreement.

items.name: Authenticated Byzantine agreement (Dolev–Strong)
items.pic: Values travel with growing chains of signatures that cannot be forged; any number of traitors is tolerated in f + 1 rounds, as runs with many traitors confirm.

items.name: Byzantine quorums
items.pic: With n = 3f + 1, any two sets of 2f + 1 processes overlap in at least f + 1, so in at least one honest process; the reader drags quorums and the overlap is counted.

items.name: Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT)
items.pic: Pre-prepare, prepare and commit phases run in a message diagram among four replicas; make the primary lie and the view-change protocol replaces it.

items.name: Nakamoto consensus: proof of work and the longest chain
items.pic: Miners extend a block tree at rates proportional to hash power; forks resolve to the longest chain, and an attacker with a share the reader sets catches up with probability that falls exponentially in confirmations.

items.name: The Byzantine Generals Problem
items.pic: Recreate the paper’s three-general figures: make the commander or a lieutenant a traitor and see why no oral-message algorithm can work, then add a fourth general and run OM(1) to agreement.

paper.authors: Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak and Marshall Pease
paper.title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
paper.venue: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4 (3): 382–401

chapters.title: Subtyping and objects
chapters.summary: Subtyping lets a value of a more specific type be used where a more general one is expected. Records may lose or refine fields, and functions are contravariant in their arguments — a rule whose violation, as in covariant mutable arrays, breaks safety. Algorithms decide subtyping without the subsumption rule, and joins and meets type conditionals. Objects can be modelled as records with open recursion through self, leading to Featherweight Java and the contrast between nominal and structural typing.

items.name: Subtyping and the subsumption rule
items.pic: A function expecting a point record is given a coloured-point record; the derivation uses subsumption to bridge the gap, highlighted in the tree.

items.name: Record subtyping: width, depth and permutation
items.pic: Drag fields in and out of two record types; the tool decides whether one is a subtype of the other and names the rules used.

items.name: Function subtyping is contravariant in the argument
items.pic: Try substituting functions with narrower and wider argument types; the covariant choice lets a caller pass a value the function cannot handle, and the run gets stuck.

items.name: Covariant mutable arrays are unsound
items.pic: Treat an array of cats as an array of animals and store a dog in it; reading it back as a cat fails, reproducing Java’s run-time store check.

items.name: Top and Bottom types
items.pic: The subtype lattice of a few base, record and function types is drawn with Top above everything and Bottom below; the reader adds types and the lattice re-forms.

items.name: Algorithmic subtyping
items.pic: A syntax-directed checker decides S <: T without guessing intermediate types; its run is compared with the declarative derivation, which uses transitivity freely.

items.name: Joins and meets
items.pic: The two branches of a conditional have different record types; their least common supertype is computed and highlighted in the subtype lattice.

items.name: Coercion semantics for subtyping
items.pic: Each subtyping step is compiled into an explicit conversion function; two derivations of the same judgment give coercions that the reader checks produce equal results.

items.name: Objects as records with open recursion
items.pic: A counter object is a record of methods closing over a state cell; a subclass overrides a method and calls through self, and the late-bound dispatch is traced.

items.name: Featherweight Java
items.pic: A tiny class table is edited; field access, method invocation and casts reduce step by step, and a downcast that fails at run time is the only way to get stuck.

items.name: Nominal versus structural typing
items.pic: Two classes with identical members are compatible under structural typing but not nominal; the reader toggles the regime and watches the checker’s verdicts change.

chapters.title: Geometric search structures
chapters.summary: Many applications ask the same geometric query again and again: which points lie in this rectangle, which face contains this point, which objects does this ray hit? Kd-trees, range trees, trapezoidal maps, interval and segment trees, binary space partitions, quadtrees and bounding volume hierarchies trade preprocessing and storage for fast queries. In high dimensions their advantages fade — the curse of dimensionality.

refs: de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld & Overmars, Computational Geometry
Pharr, Jakob & Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering

items.name: Kd-trees and orthogonal range queries
items.pic: Points are split alternately by vertical and horizontal medians; a query rectangle visits only cells it overlaps, and visited nodes are counted against √n + k.

items.name: Range trees and fractional cascading
items.pic: A tree on x stores associated trees on y; a query decomposes into O(log n) canonical subsets, and cascading pointers remove one log factor, shown by query counters.

items.name: Trapezoidal maps for point location
items.pic: Segments are inserted in random order into a trapezoidal map with its search DAG; a query point descends the DAG to its trapezoid, and depth is plotted for many orders.

items.name: Interval trees and segment trees
items.pic: Intervals are stored at the node whose split value they contain; a stabbing query walks one root-to-leaf path and reports all intervals containing the query point.

items.name: Binary space partitions and the painter’s algorithm
items.pic: Segments are split recursively by lines through them; traversing the BSP tree back to front from the viewer paints the scene correctly, with fragmentation counted.

items.name: Quadtrees and non-uniform mesh generation
items.pic: A quadtree refines near the reader’s boundary curves and is balanced so neighbouring cells differ by at most one level; cells are then triangulated into a graded mesh.

items.name: Bounding volume hierarchies
items.pic: Triangles are grouped into nested boxes by the surface-area heuristic; a ray traverses the tree, and the number of boxes and triangles tested is compared with brute force.

items.name: The curse of dimensionality in nearest-neighbour search
items.pic: As the dimension slider rises, distances between random points concentrate and a kd-tree visits nearly every leaf; the ratio of nearest to farthest distance tends to one.

chapters.title: Electric current
chapters.summary: Moving charge is described by a current density obeying the continuity equation, the local form of charge conservation. In most conductors the current is proportional to the field (Ohm’s law), which the Drude picture explains as drift against collisions; the dissipated power heats the wire. Circuits are governed by Kirchhoff’s laws, steady currents arrange themselves to minimize dissipation, and resistor networks connect to random walks.

refs: Feynman, Leighton & Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II

items.name: Current and current density
items.pic: Charges stream through a pipe of varying cross-section: the current counter through any cut is the same, while the current density J brightens where the pipe narrows.

items.name: Continuity equation
items.pic: A cloud of charge flows under a velocity field you draw: the rate of change of charge in any box equals minus the net flux of J through its walls, checked cell by cell.

items.name: Ohm’s law
items.pic: Sweep the field across a sample and plot J against E: a straight line for a metal, a curved diode characteristic for a junction, showing where the law holds and where it does not.

items.name: Drude model of conduction
items.pic: Electrons accelerate in a field and are randomly reset by collisions: their mean drift settles at eEτ/m, tiny compared with their thermal speed, and the slope of J against E gives the conductivity.

items.name: Resistance and resistivity
items.pic: Stretch and thicken a wire: its resistance follows ρL/A, while the resistivity readout stays fixed for a given material.

items.name: Joule heating
items.pic: Current through a resistor warms it: dissipated power I²R is shown against the kinetic energy collisions hand to the lattice in the Drude simulation.

items.name: Electromotive force
items.pic: A battery as a charge escalator: the non-electrostatic force pushes charges uphill inside it and the electrostatic field drives them around the external circuit, with the loop integrals of each shown.

items.name: Kirchhoff’s circuit laws
items.pic: Build a circuit by dragging resistors and batteries onto a grid: node currents and loop voltages are solved live and each junction’s inflow and each loop’s voltage sum read zero.

items.name: Steady currents minimize dissipation
items.pic: Redistribute current between parallel branches with a slider: total power dissipated has its minimum exactly at the split Kirchhoff’s laws pick.

items.name: Surface charges steer the current
items.pic: Bend a current-carrying wire: the solver places surface charges along it whose field turns the current around the corner, and removing them sends current into the wall.

items.name: Charge relaxation inside a conductor
items.pic: Inject a blob of charge into a conductor: it decays everywhere as e^{−t/τ} with τ = ε₀/σ and reappears on the surface; a conductivity slider changes τ by orders of magnitude.

items.name: RC circuit
items.pic: Close a switch on a resistor and capacitor: the voltage climbs to the battery value with time constant RC, and the energy split shows exactly half the battery’s work lost as heat.

items.name: Drift is slow, signals are fast
items.pic: Close a switch on a long circuit: electrons creep along at fractions of a millimetre per second, yet the bulb lights almost at once because the field rearranges at nearly c — both speeds are read out side by side.

items.name: Resistor networks and the infinite grid
items.pic: Grow a square grid of unit resistors and measure the resistance between neighbours: it converges to R/2, while between distant points it grows like log distance.

items.name: Random walks and effective resistance
items.pic: Random walkers released at one node of a network: the fraction reaching a target before returning matches the escape probability computed from the effective resistance.

chapters.title: Interference and coherence
chapters.summary: Coherent waves add amplitudes, not intensities, and the cross term makes fringes: Young’s slits, thin films and Newton’s rings, and interferometers that split and recombine beams to measure lengths, spectra and refractive indices. Multiple-beam interference sharpens fringes into the narrow resonances of Fabry–Pérot cavities and dielectric mirrors. Real light is only partly coherent, and the visibility of fringes measures how far its phase memory reaches in time and space — enough to measure the diameters of stars.

items.name: Interference of two coherent waves
items.pic: Two waves with an adjustable phase difference: the intensity of the sum swings from four times one beam to zero, and averaging over a random phase leaves just the sum of intensities.

items.name: Young’s double-slit experiment
items.pic: Adjust slit separation, wavelength and screen distance: the fringe spacing follows λL/d, and covering one slit wipes the fringes out leaving a single smooth band.

items.name: Fringe visibility
items.pic: Unbalance the two beams’ intensities or add a random phase jitter: the fringe visibility readout (I_max − I_min)/(I_max + I_min) falls from 1 toward 0.

items.name: Lloyd’s mirror
items.pic: A source and its mirror image interfere on a screen: the fringe at the mirror’s edge is dark, not bright, revealing the half-wave phase flip on reflection.

items.name: Thin-film interference
items.pic: A soap film thins as it drains: reflected colours are computed from the film thickness and spectrum, cycling through bands until the film turns black just before it pops.

items.name: Antireflection coatings
items.pic: Coat glass with a quarter-wave layer of adjustable index and thickness: reflectance at the design wavelength drops to zero when the coating index is √n, and rises at other colours.

items.name: Newton’s rings
items.pic: A curved lens rests on a flat plate: the air gap grows quadratically outward, producing rings whose radii scale as √n, with a dark centre in reflection.

items.name: Michelson interferometer
items.pic: Move one mirror in steps of nanometres: fringes stream past the detector, one per half wavelength, and inserting a glass plate in one arm shifts them by its optical path.

items.name: Mach–Zehnder interferometer
items.pic: Split a beam on two paths and recombine: a phase plate in one arm swings the light between the two output ports, with the port intensities summing to the input.

items.name: Fabry–Pérot interferometer
items.pic: Raise the mirror reflectivity: the transmission peaks sharpen dramatically (finesse grows like π√R/(1 − R)) while staying at the same frequencies, resolving two close spectral lines.

items.name: Dielectric mirrors (Bragg stacks)
items.pic: Stack alternating quarter-wave layers of high and low index: the reflectance in a band approaches 1 as layers are added, and the band’s width depends on the index contrast.

items.name: Temporal coherence
items.pic: Feed a Michelson with light of adjustable bandwidth: fringe visibility falls off as the path difference exceeds the coherence length c/Δν, which shrinks for white light.

items.name: Fourier-transform spectroscopy
items.pic: Scan a Michelson mirror and record the interferogram for a spectrum you draw: its Fourier transform recovers the spectrum, with resolution set by the scan length.

items.name: Spatial coherence (van Cittert–Zernike)
items.pic: Illuminate double slits with an extended incoherent source: widening the source or the slit separation washes out the fringes, and the visibility traces the Fourier transform of the source shape.

items.name: Stellar interferometry
items.pic: Separate two telescope mirrors viewing a star of adjustable angular size: the fringes vanish at a baseline of about 1.22λ/θ, from which the star’s diameter is read off as Michelson did.

items.name: Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity correlations
items.pic: Two detectors record the fluctuating intensity of thermal light: their correlation shows excess coincidences at zero delay that fall off with separation, measuring coherence without phase-stable optics.

items.name: Experiments and calculations relative to physical optics
items.pic: Recreate Young’s card experiment: split a narrow sunbeam with a thin slip of card and see fringes form inside the shadow, vanishing the moment either edge is screened; measure the fringe spacing for each colour and recover the wavelengths in his table, from red to violet.

chapters.title: Quantum statistics
chapters.summary: Letting particle number fluctuate gives the grand canonical ensemble, in which identical quantum particles occupy single-particle states according to the Fermi–Dirac or Bose–Einstein distribution, reducing to Boltzmann statistics when the gas is dilute compared with its thermal wavelength. Degenerate fermions fill a Fermi sea with pressure even at zero temperature, explaining electronic heat capacities, Pauli paramagnetism, Landau diamagnetism and semiconductors. Bosons condense into a single state below a critical temperature — in three dimensions and in traps but not in two — and helium-4 becomes superfluid.

refs: Schroeder, An Introduction to Thermal Physics

items.name: Gibbs factor and grand partition function
items.pic: A small system exchanges energy and particles with a reservoir: the simulated histogram of (N, E) matches e^{−(E − μN)/kT}, with μ set by the reservoir.

items.name: Particle-number fluctuations
items.pic: Count particles in an open sub-volume of a gas: the variance of N equals kT ∂⟨N⟩/∂μ, Poissonian for an ideal gas and suppressed or enhanced for quantum gases.

items.name: Fermi–Dirac distribution
items.pic: Occupancy of a single fermion state versus energy: a step at μ at zero temperature, smeared over a few kT as temperature rises, never exceeding 1.

items.name: Bose–Einstein distribution
items.pic: Occupancy of a boson state versus energy diverges as the energy approaches μ, compared on the same axes with Fermi–Dirac and Boltzmann curves.

items.name: Classical limit of quantum statistics
items.pic: Lower the density or raise the temperature: when occupancies are all small, Fermi–Dirac, Bose–Einstein and Boltzmann curves merge, shown with a degeneracy-parameter slider.

items.name: Quantum concentration and thermal wavelength
items.pic: Compare the interparticle spacing with the thermal de Broglie wavelength for air, electrons in copper and a cold atom cloud: quantum effects appear where the wave packets overlap.

items.name: Density of states
items.pic: Histogram the energies of particle-in-a-box states in one, two and three dimensions: the density of states grows as E^{−1/2}, constant and E^{1/2}, converging to the smooth formulas.

items.name: Degenerate Fermi gas
items.pic: Fill states up to the Fermi energy: energy and pressure stay large at zero temperature, and for electrons in metals the Fermi temperature of tens of thousands of kelvin makes room temperature effectively cold.

items.name: Sommerfeld expansion: electronic heat capacity
items.pic: Only electrons within kT of the Fermi level can be excited: the computed heat capacity is linear in T, tiny compared with equipartition, and dominates the lattice contribution at low T.

items.name: Pauli paramagnetism
items.pic: A magnetic field shifts spin-up and spin-down Fermi seas: only electrons near the Fermi level flip, giving a weak, temperature-independent susceptibility instead of Curie’s law.

items.name: Landau diamagnetism
items.pic: Quantize electron orbits into Landau levels and sum the free energy: a small diamagnetic susceptibility appears — one third of the Pauli value — which classical physics forbids.

items.name: Semiconductors: intrinsic carriers
items.pic: Place the Fermi level in a band gap: thermally excited electrons and holes grow as e^{−E_g/2kT}, so conductivity rises steeply with temperature, unlike a metal.

items.name: Bose–Einstein condensation
items.pic: Cool a boson gas at fixed density: below T_c the excited states can no longer hold all the particles, and the ground-state fraction rises as 1 − (T/T_c)^{3/2}.

items.name: No condensation in two dimensions
items.pic: Repeat the condensation calculation with a dimension switch: in 2D the excited states can absorb any number of particles at any positive T, so the condensate fraction stays zero.

items.name: Condensates in harmonic traps
items.pic: Trapped atoms have a density of states growing as E²: the condensate fraction follows 1 − (T/T_c)³, and the cloud’s density shows a sharp central peak emerging from a broad thermal cloud.

items.name: Superfluid helium-4
items.pic: The heat capacity of liquid helium spikes in a λ shape at 2.17 K; below it the liquid flows without viscosity, and the ideal-gas condensation estimate of 3.1 K is marked for comparison.

chapters.title: Symmetries and conservation laws
chapters.summary: Symmetries act on Hilbert space as unitary or antiunitary operators (Wigner’s theorem), and those commuting with the Hamiltonian give conserved quantities and degeneracies. Translations are generated by momentum, rotations by angular momentum, and parity splits states into even and odd with selection rules to match. Discrete translation symmetry gives Bloch’s theorem and energy bands; time reversal is antiunitary, and for half-integer spin it forces Kramers degeneracy.

refs: Griffiths & Schroeter, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics (3rd ed.)

items.name: Wigner’s theorem
items.pic: Apply maps to qubit states and check which preserve all transition probabilities: they are rotations of the Bloch sphere (unitary) or rotations composed with a reflection (antiunitary), nothing else.

items.name: Symmetries give conservation laws
items.pic: Break a potential’s symmetry with a slider: the expectation of the corresponding generator, flat in the symmetric case, starts to drift in proportion to the breaking.

items.name: Translation operator
items.pic: Apply e^{−iap/ħ} to a wave function via its Fourier transform: it slides rigidly by a, and a periodic potential’s Hamiltonian commutes with translations by one lattice spacing.

items.name: Parity
items.pic: Reflect a wave function through the origin: even and odd parts are separated and drawn, and parity eigenvalues ±1 appear as the only possibilities.

items.name: Bound states of symmetric potentials have parity
items.pic: Eigenstates of a symmetric well alternate even and odd with energy; tilt the well and they lose definite parity as the symmetry slider departs from zero.

items.name: Parity selection rules
items.pic: Compute dipole matrix elements ⟨f|x|i⟩ between eigenstates: the table has zeros wherever initial and final parities agree, with a colour code making the checkerboard visible.

items.name: Bloch’s theorem
items.pic: Eigenstates of a periodic potential are plane waves times periodic functions: slide the crystal momentum k and the periodic part and phase advance per cell are shown.

items.name: Kronig–Penney model
items.pic: A lattice of square barriers: the transfer-matrix condition |cos ka| ≤ 1 carves energy into allowed bands and gaps, which widen as the barriers grow.

items.name: Tight-binding chain
items.pic: Atoms coupled by hopping t: the band E(k) = E₀ − 2t cos ka emerges from diagonalizing the chain, with band width 4t and a finite chain’s levels filling it in.

items.name: Bloch oscillations
items.pic: Apply a uniform force to a packet in a band: instead of accelerating forever it oscillates in place as k sweeps the Brillouin zone, with period h/Fa.

items.name: Time reversal is antiunitary
items.pic: Run a packet’s evolution forward, complex-conjugate the wave function and run forward again: it retraces its path to the start; a magnetic field makes the retrace fail.

items.name: Kramers degeneracy
items.pic: Random time-reversal-invariant Hamiltonians for spin ½ particles: every level comes as a pair; add a magnetic field and the pairs split.

items.name: Rotational invariance implies m-degeneracy
items.pic: Levels of a rotationally invariant Hamiltonian come in multiplets of 2l + 1; squash the potential into an ellipsoid and each multiplet fans apart.

chapters.title: Superconductivity
chapters.summary: Below a critical temperature some metals lose all resistance and expel magnetic fields. London’s equations confine the field to a thin surface layer, and flux through a ring is quantized in units of h/2e, revealing paired electrons. Ginzburg–Landau theory distinguishes type I from type II superconductors with their vortex lattices. BCS theory builds the pairs from a phonon-mediated attraction, predicting an energy gap and the isotope effect; the condensate’s phase coherence gives the Josephson effects behind SQUIDs and superconducting qubits, and the cuprates remain a challenge.

refs: Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics

items.name: Zero resistance and the critical temperature
items.pic: Cool a mercury wire: its resistance drops abruptly to zero at 4.2 K, as in Kamerlingh Onnes’s data, and a current set running in a superconducting ring shows no decay on any timescale you choose.

items.name: London equations and the penetration depth
items.pic: The magnetic field inside a superconducting slab decays as e^{−x/λ_L} with λ_L of tens of nanometres; a superfluid-density slider sets λ_L and thin films let field through.

items.name: Flux quantization in units of h/2e
items.pic: Thread flux through a superconducting ring: single-valuedness of the condensate phase allows only multiples of h/2e, and the measured steps are compared with the h/e that single electrons would give.

items.name: Ginzburg–Landau theory
items.pic: A free energy in the order parameter with a temperature slider: above T_c the minimum is at zero, below it a ring of minima appears, and the coherence length and penetration depth are computed.

items.name: Type I and type II superconductors
items.pic: The Ginzburg–Landau ratio κ = λ/ξ decides the sign of the interface energy: below 1/√2 the field is expelled until a single critical field, above it flux enters gradually between H_c1 and H_c2.

items.name: Abrikosov vortex lattice
items.pic: Raise the field on a type II film: vortices each carrying one flux quantum enter and arrange into a triangular lattice whose spacing shrinks as √(Φ₀/B).

items.name: Cooper pairs
items.pic: Two electrons above a filled Fermi sea with an attraction slider: a bound state below 2E_F exists for any attraction, however weak, with binding energy vanishing as e^{−2/(N(0)V)}.

items.name: BCS theory and the energy gap
items.pic: Solve the BCS gap equation self-consistently versus temperature: Δ(T) vanishes at T_c with 2Δ(0)/kT_c ≈ 3.53, compared with tunnelling data.

items.name: Isotope effect
items.pic: Change the ionic mass of mercury isotopes: the computed and measured critical temperatures fall as M^{−1/2}, pointing to phonons as the glue.

items.name: Josephson effects
items.pic: Two superconductors across a thin barrier: a phase-difference slider drives a supercurrent I_c sin φ with no voltage, and a fixed voltage makes the current oscillate at 2eV/h.

items.name: SQUID magnetometer
items.pic: Two Josephson junctions in a ring: the maximum supercurrent oscillates with the threaded flux with period h/2e, so counting fringes measures fields far weaker than the Earth’s.

items.name: High-temperature cuprate superconductors
items.pic: A doping slider walks across the cuprate phase diagram: an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator at zero doping gives way to a superconducting dome peaking above 90 K, far beyond the phonon-mediated BCS estimate shown for comparison.

items.name: The resistance of pure mercury at helium temperatures
items.pic: Cool a mercury thread in the liquid-helium cryostat and plot its resistance against temperature: it follows the smooth fall expected of a pure metal and then, near 4.2 K, drops abruptly to an unmeasurably small value — the first superconductor, recreated from the Leiden measurements.

paper.title: Further experiments with liquid helium. C. On the change of electric resistance of pure metals at very low temperatures etc. IV. The resistance of pure mercury at helium temperatures
paper.venue: Proceedings of the Section of Sciences, KNAW 13 (II): 1274–1276

items.name: Theory of Superconductivity
items.pic: Solve the BCS gap equation as the temperature falls: the gap opens at T_c and grows to Δ(0) = 1.76 kT_c, the electronic specific heat jumps by a factor 2.43 at T_c and then dies away exponentially, and the reader sets the coupling to match measured gaps and specific heats of real superconductors.

paper.title: Theory of Superconductivity

chapters.title: The quantum Fourier transform and Shor’s algorithm
chapters.summary: The discrete Fourier transform on 2ⁿ amplitudes takes only O(n²) gates. It powers phase estimation, which reads an eigenphase into a register, and hence order finding: the period of aˣ mod N shows up as peaks decoded by continued fractions. Elementary number theory turns the period into factors (Shor); the same idea solves discrete logarithms and abelian hidden-subgroup problems, and phase estimation also counts solutions and inverts linear systems.

refs: Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information

items.name: Quantum Fourier transform
items.pic: Feed a basis state into the QFT: the output amplitudes wind around the circle at a rate set by the input, exactly the discrete Fourier transform, with periodic inputs giving sharp peaks.

items.name: The QFT circuit uses O(n²) gates
items.pic: The product formula writes each output qubit as a phase rotation; the circuit is drawn for n qubits with a gate counter, compared with the n2ⁿ operations of an FFT on the same vector.

items.name: Quantum phase estimation
items.pic: Pick an eigenphase φ: the counting register’s output distribution peaks at the nearest t-bit fraction, and adding counting qubits sharpens the peak as predicted.

items.name: Order finding
items.pic: Choose a and N: modular exponentiation is run in superposition, and phase estimation of the multiply-by-a operator gives peaks at s/r for the order r, read off the simulated histogram.

items.name: Continued fractions extract the period
items.pic: Take a measured fraction y/2ᵗ: its continued-fraction convergents are computed by Euclid’s algorithm, and the first denominator that works is the period r.

items.name: Factoring reduces to order finding
items.pic: For random a coprime to N, compute gcd(a^{r/2} ± 1, N): a table shows most choices of a yield a nontrivial factor, with the failures (odd r, or a^{r/2} ≡ −1) highlighted.

items.name: Shor’s factoring algorithm
items.pic: Shor’s period finding for N = 15 or 21: amplitudes after the QFT peak at multiples of 2ᵗ/r, classical post-processing finds the factors, and a gate counter shows polynomial scaling in log N.

items.name: Discrete logarithm
items.pic: A two-register version of period finding: the function aˣ b^y mod p is periodic on a lattice in (x, y), and the 2D Fourier peaks reveal the logarithm.

items.name: Hidden subgroup problem
items.pic: A finite abelian group is drawn with the cosets of a hidden subgroup coloured; Fourier sampling returns characters trivial on the subgroup, and Simon, Shor and discrete log are shown as special cases.

items.name: Quantum counting
items.pic: Phase estimation on the Grover iterate reads out its rotation angle, from which the number of marked items is estimated, with the error shrinking as counting qubits are added.

items.name: HHL algorithm for linear systems
items.pic: Phase estimation exposes the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, a conditional rotation divides by them, and the success probability falls as the condition-number slider grows — with the caveats on input and output shown.

items.name: Quantum algorithms: discrete logarithms and factoring
items.pic: Factor N = 15 or 21 on a simulated quantum register: modular exponentiation entangles two registers, the quantum Fourier transform turns the hidden period r into sharp peaks at multiples of 2ⁿ/r, and continued fractions recover r and then the factors, with qubit counts and classical costs compared as N grows.

paper.title: Algorithms for quantum computation: discrete logarithms and factoring
paper.venue: Proceedings 35th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (IEEE): 124–134

chapters.title: The equivalence principle
chapters.summary: All bodies fall the same way, so a freely falling laboratory is locally indistinguishable from one floating in empty space. Einstein turned this into a principle: gravity can be transformed away at a point, and only tidal effects remain. Light must then bend and clocks lower in a gravitational field must run slow — effects measured in a laboratory tower, in flying atomic clocks, and every day by GPS — and the weak-field spacetime metric emerges, with free fall as the path of greatest proper time.

refs: Schutz, A First Course in General Relativity
Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity

items.name: Universality of free fall
items.pic: Drop a feather, a hammer and a test mass in vacuum with separate sliders for inertial and gravitational mass: only when the two masses are proportional do all bodies fall together.

items.name: Eötvös torsion-balance tests
items.pic: A torsion balance with two materials hangs in Earth’s gravity and centrifugal field; a hypothetical material difference η twists the beam by a computed angle, compared with today’s bound η < 10⁻¹³.

items.name: Einstein’s equivalence principle
items.pic: An observer in a sealed elevator runs experiments; toggle between resting on Earth and accelerating at g in deep space and every readout is identical, while cutting the cable makes the lab perfectly inertial.

items.name: Local inertial frames
items.pic: Freely falling labs at different places around Earth: zoom into one and residual drifts between test particles appear only when the lab is made large or the experiment long.

items.name: Tidal acceleration as the signature of gravity
items.pic: A cloud of free particles falling toward Earth stretches radially and squeezes sideways; no choice of falling frame removes the deformation, whose rate is plotted against the tidal tensor.

items.name: Light bends in an accelerating elevator
items.pic: A light beam crosses an accelerating elevator: in the elevator frame its path curves downward by gL²/(2c²), the first hint that light falls in gravity.

items.name: Gravitational redshift (Pound–Rebka)
items.pic: Light climbs a 22.5 m tower inside an accelerating rocket; the Doppler shift from the speed the rocket gains in transit equals gh/c², matching the Pound–Rebka readout.

items.name: Gravitational time dilation
items.pic: Clocks stacked at different heights tick at rates 1 + gh/c²; a height slider and a potential map show higher clocks running ahead by an amount that accumulates over time.

items.name: GPS clock corrections
items.pic: A satellite clock gains about 45 μs per day from altitude and loses about 7 μs from speed; an orbit-radius slider shows where the two cancel, and switching off corrections lets the position error grow kilometres per day.

items.name: Hafele–Keating flying clocks
items.pic: Clocks flown east and west around the rotating Earth combine kinematic and gravitational shifts; the computed gains and losses are compared with the 1971 measurements.

items.name: Weak-field metric
items.pic: A spacetime diagram near a mass with clock ticks spaced by √(1 + 2Φ/c²): the falling apple’s worldline is drawn, and Φ is computed from a draggable mass distribution.

items.name: Free fall maximizes proper time
items.pic: Throw a ball up and catch it after a fixed time; drag control points to reshape its worldline and the proper-time readout peaks exactly on the Newtonian parabola.

items.name: Ehrenfest paradox: the rotating disk
items.pic: Spin a disk covered in small rulers: rim rulers contract and radial ones do not, so the measured circumference over diameter climbs above π as the spin slider rises.

chapters.title: Stellar structure and energy
chapters.summary: A star is a self-gravitating ball of gas in hydrostatic equilibrium; the virial theorem ties its thermal energy to its gravitational energy, so losing energy makes it hotter. Its structure follows from a few equations — hydrostatics, mass continuity, energy transport by radiation or convection, and nuclear energy generation by the pp chain or CNO cycle, made possible by quantum tunnelling. Polytropes give quick models, the Eddington luminosity caps how bright a star can be, and the standard solar model was vindicated by solar neutrinos once neutrino oscillations were understood.

refs: Carroll & Ostlie, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics

items.name: Hydrostatic equilibrium of a star
items.pic: Shells of a model star: pressure gradient and gravity arrows balance in each shell; perturb the balance and the star oscillates back on the dynamical timescale.

items.name: Virial theorem for stars
items.pic: A contracting gas sphere: the bars for thermal energy K and gravitational energy U keep 2K + U = 0, so half of the energy released by contraction is radiated and half heats the star.

items.name: Negative heat capacity of self-gravitating systems
items.pic: Remove energy from a star or an N-body star cluster: the simulation heats up and its particles speed up, the opposite of a box of gas, with temperature plotted against total energy.

items.name: Dynamical, Kelvin–Helmholtz and nuclear timescales
items.pic: For a star of chosen mass, the three timescales are computed and shown on a log axis: about half an hour, tens of millions of years and ten billion years for the Sun.

items.name: Kelvin’s age-of-the-Sun problem
items.pic: Gravitational contraction can power the Sun for tens of millions of years, yet geology and evolution need billions; adding nuclear energy extends the lifetime bar to fit.

items.name: Polytropes and the Lane–Emden equation
items.pic: Integrate the Lane–Emden equation for an index slider n: the first zero gives the stellar radius, the density profile grows more centrally concentrated with n, and n = 5 never reaches zero.

items.name: Energy transport by radiative diffusion
items.pic: The temperature gradient needed to carry the luminosity through opacity κ is computed shell by shell; raising the opacity steepens it until convection takes over.

items.name: Schwarzschild criterion for convection
items.pic: Lift a parcel adiabatically: if it ends up hotter and lighter than its surroundings it keeps rising; sliding the actual gradient past the adiabatic one switches convection on.

items.name: Eddington luminosity
items.pic: Radiation pressure on electrons pushes out while gravity on protons pulls in; a mass slider sets L_Edd = 4πGMc/κ, and a star above it loses its outer layers in the simulation.

items.name: Proton–proton chain and CNO cycle
items.pic: The reaction networks are animated with the energy released at each step; energy generation versus central temperature is plotted for both, crossing near 17 million K (about 1.3 solar masses).

items.name: Quantum tunnelling and the Gamow peak
items.pic: The falling Maxwell–Boltzmann tail and the rising tunnelling probability multiply into a narrow Gamow peak; a temperature slider shifts and broadens it, showing why fusion works far below the classical barrier.

items.name: Standard solar model
items.pic: A simple structure integration produces the Sun’s temperature, density and luminosity profiles, with the radiative core and convective envelope marked and the predicted surface values compared with observations.

items.name: Solar neutrino problem
items.pic: Predicted and measured detection rates for chlorine, gallium and water detectors disagree by factors of two to three; switching on neutrino oscillations closes the gap.

items.name: Energy Production in Stars
items.pic: Run the proton–proton chain and the carbon–nitrogen cycle side by side as a core-temperature slider moves: the energy output per gram rises roughly as T⁴ for the chain but as about T¹⁸ for the cycle, so the Sun runs on protons while hotter, heavier main-sequence stars switch to carbon as a catalyst.
