chapters.title: Viscous flow and the Navier–Stokes equations
chapters.summary: Real fluids resist shearing: in a Newtonian fluid the stress is linear in the rate of strain, the fluid sticks to walls, and Euler’s equation gains a diffusion term to become the Navier–Stokes equations. The Reynolds number measures inertia against viscosity, and dimensional analysis shows that flows with the same Reynolds number are scaled copies of one another. Exact solutions — Couette, Poiseuille, the impulsively started plate, the Stokes layer, decaying and stretched vortices — show vorticity diffusing and energy being dissipated.

items.name: Newtonian viscosity
items.pic: Slide the top plate of a fluid layer: the velocity profile becomes linear, the drag on the plate equals μU/h, and a shear-thinning toggle shows a non-Newtonian fluid departing from the line.

items.name: Stress tensor in a moving fluid
items.pic: Rotate a small square cut from a sheared flow: the traction on each face is computed from the stress tensor, normal and tangential parts change with angle, and the principal directions appear as eigenvectors.

items.name: No-slip condition
items.pic: Flow past a plate with a slip/no-slip toggle: with no slip a thin layer of vorticity forms at the wall and diffuses outward; with slip the flow stays irrotational and frictionless.

items.name: Navier–Stokes equations
items.pic: A lid-driven square cavity is solved live: lowering the viscosity strengthens the primary vortex, shifts its centre and spawns secondary corner eddies.

items.name: Reynolds number and dynamic similarity
items.pic: Three flows past cylinders with different sizes, speeds and viscosities but equal Reynolds number are simulated: rescaled, their streamlines coincide exactly; change one Re and they part.

items.name: Dimensional analysis: the Buckingham Π theorem
items.pic: List the variables of a problem (drag on a sphere, period of a pendulum): their dimension matrix is shown, its null space gives the Π groups, and scattered data collapse onto one curve when replotted in those groups.

items.name: Couette and Poiseuille flow
items.pic: Sliders for wall speed and pressure gradient: the exact profile — a line plus a parabola — is drawn beside a numerical solution that converges onto it from rest.

items.name: Hagen–Poiseuille law
items.pic: Flow through a pipe with a radius slider: the volume flux scales as R⁴Δp/(μL), so halving a blood vessel’s radius cuts the flow sixteenfold at the same pressure.

items.name: Viscous dissipation of energy
items.pic: A decaying vortex flow in a box: the kinetic energy falls at a rate equal to the integrated dissipation 2μ e_ij e_ij, both computed from the simulation and plotted together.

items.name: Impulsively started plate (Rayleigh’s problem)
items.pic: A plate is jerked into motion: vorticity diffuses into the fluid with an error-function profile whose thickness grows as √(νt), and profiles at different times collapse when plotted against y/√(νt).

items.name: Oscillating plate: the Stokes layer
items.pic: An oscillating plate sends damped shear waves into the fluid; a frequency slider shows the penetration depth √(2ν/ω) and the phase lag growing with distance.

items.name: Lamb–Oseen vortex
items.pic: A line vortex released into viscous fluid spreads its core as √(4νt); the peak swirl speed decays while the circulation far away is unchanged, matching the simulation.

items.name: Burgers vortex
items.pic: Impose an axial stretching strain on a diffusing vortex: the core stops spreading at a radius of order √(ν/α) where stretching balances diffusion, and the strain slider sets the steady core size.

chapters.title: Phase diagrams of mixtures
chapters.summary: With more than one component, the Gibbs phase rule counts how many variables can change while phases coexist. Binary liquid–vapour diagrams explain distillation and azeotropes, partially miscible liquids show upper and lower critical solution temperatures, and solid–liquid diagrams show eutectics and compounds. The lever rule reads phase amounts off a tie line, and the common-tangent construction on the Gibbs energy curve explains it all.

refs: McQuarrie & Simon, Physical Chemistry: A Molecular Approach

items.name: Gibbs phase rule
items.pic: Choose the number of components and coexisting phases: the app counts unknowns and equilibrium conditions to give F = C − P + 2, and on a diagram shows areas, lines and points with 2, 1 and 0 degrees of freedom.

items.name: Pressure–composition diagram of an ideal binary
items.pic: Lower the pressure over a liquid mixture: bubbles appear at the bubble-point line with a vapour richer in the volatile component, and the liquid and vapour compositions are joined by a tie line.

items.name: Lever rule
items.pic: Drag the overall composition along a tie line like a fulcrum on a see-saw: the amounts of the two phases are read out in inverse proportion to the lever arms, checked by a mass balance.

items.name: Fractional distillation and theoretical plates
items.pic: Step up a temperature–composition diagram plate by plate: each vaporize–condense cycle enriches the vapour, and a column-height slider shows how many plates a given separation needs.

items.name: Azeotropes
items.pic: Raise the non-ideality parameter: the boiling curve develops a maximum or minimum where liquid and vapour compositions coincide, and the distillation simulation stalls there — why ethanol cannot be distilled past 96 %.

items.name: Partially miscible liquids and consolute points
items.pic: Shake hexane and nitrobenzene at different temperatures: two layers form inside a dome whose top is the upper critical solution temperature, and a water–triethylamine preset shows a lower one instead.

items.name: Common-tangent construction on G(x)
items.pic: Roll a straight line under a double-well ΔG_mix curve until it touches twice: the touching points are the coexisting compositions, the convex hull of the curve is the true Gibbs energy, and the inflection points mark the spinodal.

items.name: Eutectic phase diagrams
items.pic: Cool a lead–tin melt of chosen composition: the cooling curve shows a slope change at the liquidus and a halt at the eutectic temperature, and the microstructure panel fills with primary crystals then lamellae.

items.name: Compound formation and incongruent melting
items.pic: Add a compound to a binary system: with congruent melting the diagram looks like two eutectic systems side by side; slide its stability down and a peritectic appears where the compound decomposes before melting.

items.name: Zone refining
items.pic: Pass a molten zone along a rod repeatedly: impurities with distribution coefficient k < 1 ride along with the zone, and the computed impurity profile drops by orders of magnitude after a few passes.

items.name: Ternary phase diagrams
items.pic: Drag a point in a triangle whose corners are three pure components: the distances to the sides read out the three mole fractions, and a two-phase region with tie lines shows the lever rule in two dimensions.

items.name: On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances
items.pic: Build a phase diagram from free-energy surfaces: the reader shapes G for each phase of a binary system, Gibbs’ tangent construction picks out the coexisting phases, and counting components and phases anywhere on the diagram confirms F = C − P + 2.

paper.venue: Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences 3: 108–248 (1876) and 343–524 (1878)

chapters.title: Catalysis and enzyme kinetics
chapters.summary: A catalyst opens a lower-barrier pathway without changing the equilibrium it accelerates toward. Enzymes are the supreme example: the Michaelis–Menten mechanism explains their saturation kinetics, kcat/KM measures their efficiency against the diffusion limit, and inhibitors and cooperativity modulate them. On solid catalysts, adsorption isotherms feed Langmuir–Hinshelwood and Eley–Rideal rate laws.

refs: Houston, Chemical Kinetics and Reaction Dynamics
Steinfeld, Francisco & Hase, Chemical Kinetics and Dynamics

items.name: Catalysts lower barriers but leave equilibrium unchanged
items.pic: Add a catalytic pathway with a lower barrier to A ⇌ B: both forward and backward rates rise by the same factor, so the approach to equilibrium speeds up while the final ratio stays fixed.

items.name: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
items.pic: Raise substrate concentration: the initial rate climbs linearly and then saturates at V_max, half reached at K_M, while a stochastic single-enzyme panel shows the enzyme spending more and more time occupied.

items.name: Lineweaver–Burk plots and error distortion
items.pic: Fit noisy Michaelis–Menten data by the double-reciprocal plot and by direct nonlinear fitting: the reciprocal transform magnifies errors at low substrate and biases the parameters, shown by repeated simulated experiments.

items.name: Catalytic efficiency kcat/KM and catalytic perfection
items.pic: Plot kcat/KM for a collection of enzymes against the diffusion limit: a few, like triosephosphate isomerase and carbonic anhydrase, sit right at the ceiling, where every encounter leads to reaction.

items.name: Competitive inhibition
items.pic: Add an inhibitor that competes for the active site: the saturation curve stretches to the right with V_max unchanged, and enough substrate always wins back full speed.

items.name: Uncompetitive and noncompetitive inhibition
items.pic: Switch the inhibitor’s binding target to the enzyme–substrate complex or to both forms: double-reciprocal lines become parallel or intersect on the axis, diagnosing each mechanism.

items.name: Hill equation and cooperativity
items.pic: Raise the Hill coefficient from 1 to 4: the binding curve sharpens from hyperbolic to sigmoidal, the Hill plot slope reads n, and haemoglobin’s oxygen curve is fitted with n ≈ 2.8.

items.name: Temperature optimum of enzymes
items.pic: Heat an enzyme: catalytic rate rises along an Arrhenius curve while a two-state unfolding equilibrium removes active enzyme, and their product gives the bell-shaped activity profile.

items.name: Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism
items.pic: Two gases compete for surface sites and react when adsorbed neighbours meet: the rate rises and then falls as one gas floods the surface, with a maximum at a computed partial-pressure ratio.

items.name: Eley–Rideal mechanism
items.pic: Let a gas-phase molecule strike an adsorbed one directly: the rate saturates with coverage instead of passing through a maximum, distinguishing it from Langmuir–Hinshelwood on the same axes.

items.name: Temperature-programmed desorption
items.pic: Heat a covered surface at a steady ramp: the desorption signal peaks at a temperature set by the binding energy (Redhead analysis), and changing the desorption order changes the peak shape.

items.name: Die Kinetik der Invertinwirkung
items.pic: Fit Michaelis and Menten’s invertase measurements — initial rates of sucrose hydrolysis at a range of sucrose concentrations — with v = V[S]/(K + [S]), dragging V and K, and set their logarithmic-concentration plot beside the double-reciprocal plot that later became standard.

paper.authors: L. Michaelis and Maud L. Menten
paper.title: Die Kinetik der Invertinwirkung

chapters.title: Bonding in polyatomic molecules
chapters.summary: Beyond diatomics, chemists use a ladder of models of rising cost: VSEPR to guess shapes, hybrid orbitals to describe localized bonds, Walsh diagrams to explain why water is bent, and Hückel theory to turn π systems into graph eigenvalue problems. Frontier orbitals and orbital symmetry then predict which reactions go, and crystal-field and Jahn–Teller arguments carry the same ideas to transition-metal complexes.

items.name: VSEPR model of molecular shape
items.pic: Place electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) on a sphere and let them repel numerically: two, three, four, five and six domains settle into line, triangle, tetrahedron, bipyramid and octahedron, and making lone pairs bulkier squeezes the bond angles below 109.5°.

items.name: Hybrid orbitals
items.pic: Mix an s orbital with p orbitals using a slider for the s fraction: the lobe swings and fattens, and the angle between equivalent hybrids follows cos θ = −s/(1−s), passing 180°, 120° and 109.5° at sp, sp² and sp³.

items.name: Walsh diagrams: why water is bent
items.pic: Bend an AH₂ molecule from 180° to 90° and watch the MO energies shift; fill four or eight valence electrons and the total energy curve picks linear BeH₂ or bent H₂O.

items.name: Hückel molecular orbital theory
items.pic: Draw a carbon skeleton as a graph; its adjacency matrix is diagonalized live, the π levels appear as α + xβ with the eigenvector coefficients drawn as lobes on each atom.

items.name: Ethylene, allyl and butadiene in Hückel theory
items.pic: Step through chains of two, three and four carbons: the levels are 2cos(kπ/(n+1)), and the delocalization energy of butadiene is read out against two isolated double bonds.

items.name: Aromatic stabilization of benzene
items.pic: Close a six-carbon chain into a ring and compare the π energy with three localized ethylenes; the extra 2β of stabilization appears, and distorting the ring into alternating bonds shows how it is lost.

items.name: Hückel’s 4n + 2 rule
items.pic: Choose ring sizes from 3 to 10: the Frost circle (a polygon inscribed vertex-down) gives the levels, and filling electrons shows closed shells for 2, 6, 10 and half-filled degenerate pairs — antiaromatic — for 4 and 8.

items.name: Coulson charges and π bond orders
items.pic: For any Hückel molecule the occupied coefficients are summed into charges on atoms and orders on bonds, drawn as bond thickness; bond orders are plotted against measured bond lengths for a set of hydrocarbons.

items.name: Coulson–Rushbrooke pairing theorem
items.pic: Colour the atoms of a skeleton alternately: when the graph is bipartite the levels come in ±x pairs and the charges are uniform; add an odd ring and the mirror symmetry of the spectrum breaks.

items.name: Frontier orbitals: HOMO and LUMO
items.pic: Bring a nucleophile toward different atoms of a conjugated molecule; the predicted site of attack follows the largest LUMO coefficient, shown as a heat map that changes as you edit the skeleton.

items.name: Woodward–Hoffmann rules
items.pic: Close butadiene and hexatriene into rings by conrotation or disrotation: the orbital lobes at the termini either meet in phase or out of phase, and a thermal/photochemical toggle flips which motion is allowed.

items.name: Crystal-field splitting
items.pic: Surround a metal ion with six point charges and compute the d-orbital energies: they split into t₂g and e_g; switch to four charges in a tetrahedron and the pattern inverts and shrinks to about 4/9.

items.name: High-spin and low-spin complexes
items.pic: Slide the field strength for a d⁶ ion: electrons spread out (four unpaired) while the splitting is below the pairing energy, then collapse into the t₂g set, and the magnetic moment readout drops to zero.

items.name: Jahn–Teller theorem
items.pic: Stretch an octahedral Cu²⁺ complex along one axis: for a degenerate d⁹ ground state the energy falls linearly with the distortion, so the symmetric shape is never the minimum, while for d⁸ nothing is gained.

items.name: Peierls distortion and bond alternation in polyenes
items.pic: Lengthen a polyene with equal or alternating resonance integrals: with equal bonds the HOMO–LUMO gap closes as 1/N, but alternation keeps a finite gap — which is why β-carotene is orange rather than metallic.

items.name: The Nature of the Chemical Bond
items.pic: Mix one s and three p orbitals with adjustable weights: as the bond strength (Pauling’s measure, 2 for sp³ against 1.732 for a pure p orbital) is maximized, four lobes swing to the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°; switch to dsp² and get the square-planar complexes the paper predicted.

paper.title: The Nature of the Chemical Bond. Application of Results Obtained from the Quantum Mechanics and from a Theory of Paramagnetic Susceptibility to the Structure of Molecules
paper.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society 53 (4): 1367–1400

items.name: Quantentheoretische Beiträge zum Benzolproblem
items.pic: Draw a ring of n carbon atoms and solve the Hückel determinant: levels α + 2β cos(2πk/n) fill pair by pair, closed shells and extra delocalization energy appear for 2, 6, 10, … π electrons, and the reader compares benzene with cyclobutadiene and cyclooctatetraene.

paper.title: Quantentheoretische Beiträge zum Benzolproblem. I. Die Elektronenkonfiguration des Benzols und verwandter Verbindungen

items.name: Stereochemistry of Electrocyclic Reactions
items.pic: Close a substituted butadiene or hexatriene into a ring by heat or by light: the symmetry of the relevant HOMO decides whether the ends turn the same way (conrotatory) or opposite ways (disrotatory), and the reader checks the predicted cis or trans product for 4n and 4n + 2 electron systems.

paper.authors: R. B. Woodward and Roald Hoffmann
paper.title: Stereochemistry of Electrocyclic Reactions
paper.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society 87 (2): 395–397

chapters.title: Diffraction geometry
chapters.summary: Waves scattered by a periodic array reinforce only in special directions. Bragg's picture of reflection from lattice planes, von Laue's three equations and Ewald's sphere in reciprocal space are three views of the same condition. They explain the Laue, rotating-crystal and powder methods, how X-rays are made, and why small crystallites give broad peaks.

refs: Hammond, The Basics of Crystallography and Diffraction
Giacovazzo et al., Fundamentals of Crystallography

items.name: Diffraction by a grating
items.pic: Shine light on a grating with an adjustable number of slits: principal maxima stay at sin θ = nλ/d while sharpening as N grows, with N − 2 weak subsidiary peaks between them.

items.name: Bragg’s law
items.pic: Reflect X-rays off a stack of planes and rotate the crystal: the path difference 2d sin θ is drawn and the reflected intensity spikes only when it equals a whole number of wavelengths.

items.name: Laue equations
items.pic: Treat each row of atoms as a grating: each row allows scattering on a cone, and only directions where three cones meet survive, drawn as intersecting cones in 3D.

items.name: Bragg and Laue conditions are equivalent
items.pic: Toggle between the plane-reflection and scattering-vector views of one reflection: the condition k′ − k = g is shown to be exactly 2d sin θ = λ, with the same reflections lighting up in both.

items.name: Ewald sphere construction
items.pic: Rotate a reciprocal lattice through a sphere of radius 1/λ: a reflection flashes each time a reciprocal point touches the sphere, and changing the wavelength resizes the sphere.

items.name: Limiting sphere and resolution
items.pic: Show the sphere of radius 2/λ: reciprocal points outside it can never diffract, so shorter wavelengths reach finer d-spacings, and the number of measurable reflections is counted.

items.name: Laue method
items.pic: Illuminate a stationary crystal with white X-rays: a range of Ewald spheres captures many reflections at once, and the spot pattern on a flat film shows the crystal’s symmetry as you rotate it.

items.name: Powder diffraction and Debye–Scherrer cones
items.pic: Average over randomly oriented crystallites: each reflection becomes a cone and a ring on the detector, and the 1D pattern of 2θ peaks is indexed for cubic lattices by the ratios of h² + k² + l².

items.name: Moseley’s law and characteristic X-rays
items.pic: Bombard targets of increasing atomic number: Kα lines appear on top of the bremsstrahlung continuum, and √ν against Z falls on Moseley’s straight line, which predicted missing elements.

items.name: Scherrer equation for crystallite size
items.pic: Shrink the crystallites in a simulated powder: peaks broaden as λ/(L cos θ), and adding microstrain broadens them with a different angular dependence, separated on a Williamson–Hall plot.

items.name: Interferenzerscheinungen bei Röntgenstrahlen
items.pic: Send a white X-ray beam through a zinc-blende crystal and watch the photographic plate fill with Laue spots; turn the crystal to bring the cube axis along the beam and see the fourfold pattern, and find which wavelengths satisfy the three Laue conditions at each spot.

paper.authors: W. Friedrich, P. Knipping and M. Laue
paper.title: Interferenzerscheinungen bei Röntgenstrahlen

items.name: The Diffraction of Short Electromagnetic Waves by a Crystal
items.pic: Explain each spot of the zinc-blende Laue photograph as a mirror reflection of white X-rays from a family of lattice planes: pick a plane (hkl), see which wavelength nλ = 2d sin θ selects, and find that a face-centred cubic lattice, not the simple cubic one first assumed, accounts for the spots that are missing.

paper.title: The Diffraction of Short Electromagnetic Waves by a Crystal
paper.venue: Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 17: 43–57

items.name: The high-frequency spectra of the elements
items.pic: Plot the square root of the Kα frequency for Moseley’s elements from calcium to zinc against their place in the periodic table: the points fall on a straight line, so each element gets a whole number N, and cobalt and nickel take the order their N demands rather than the order of their atomic weights.

paper.title: The high-frequency spectra of the elements

chapters.title: Phase diagrams of alloys
chapters.summary: Binary phase diagrams are the metallurgist's maps: isomorphous, eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic systems each leave characteristic microstructures, read with the lever rule. The iron–carbon diagram underlies all of steel. Free-energy curves explain the diagrams, and the regions where those curves bend the wrong way give spinodal decomposition and ordering.

refs: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering
Porter & Easterling, Phase Transformations in Metals and Alloys

items.name: Binary isomorphous systems
items.pic: Cool a Cu–Ni alloy through the two-phase lens: the first solid is nickel-rich, the liquid and solid compositions slide along the liquidus and solidus, and the last liquid freezes copper-rich.

items.name: Lever rule in alloy microstructures
items.pic: Drag a temperature and overall composition inside a two-phase field: tie-line endpoints give phase compositions, the lever arms give phase fractions, and a micrograph panel shows that many grains of each phase.

items.name: Coring and the Scheil equation
items.pic: Freeze an alloy fast enough that the solid cannot rediffuse: grain centres stay rich in the high-melting component, the Scheil profile is drawn across a grain, and the last liquid freezes far below the equilibrium solidus.

items.name: Eutectic microstructures
items.pic: Pick Pb–Sn compositions left of, at and right of the eutectic: the microstructure panel grows primary dendrites then lamellar eutectic, with phase fractions checked by the lever rule.

items.name: Eutectoid and peritectic reactions
items.pic: Compare a eutectic (liquid → two solids), a eutectoid (solid → two solids) and a peritectic (liquid + solid → new solid) on one schematic diagram, each animated as its microstructure forms.

items.name: The iron–iron carbide diagram
items.pic: Explore the Fe–Fe₃C diagram with a cursor: ferrite, austenite, cementite and the eutectoid at 0.76 % C and 727 °C are labelled, and the steel and cast-iron ranges are shaded.

items.name: Pearlite and proeutectoid phases
items.pic: Slowly cool hypo- and hypereutectoid steels: proeutectoid ferrite or cementite forms at grain boundaries, then the remaining austenite transforms to lamellar pearlite in the proportions the lever rule predicts.

items.name: Phase diagrams from free-energy curves (CALPHAD idea)
items.pic: Slide the temperature and watch G(x) curves for liquid and solid phases shift: common tangents are found automatically, and their touching points sweep out the computed phase diagram below.

items.name: Spinodal decomposition
items.pic: Quench a mixture into the region where G(x) curves downward: a Cahn–Hilliard simulation grows small composition waves into an interconnected pattern, with atoms diffusing uphill against the gradient.

items.name: Order–disorder transitions (Bragg–Williams)
items.pic: Heat a β-brass lattice in a Monte Carlo simulation: the long-range order parameter falls continuously to zero at a critical temperature, compared with the mean-field Bragg–Williams curve.

chapters.title: Stress, rheology and faulting
chapters.summary: Rocks are elastic for seconds, brittle in the cold upper crust and viscous over millions of years. The stress tensor and Mohr's circle describe the loads; the Mohr–Coulomb criterion and Byerlee's law say when rocks break and slide; Anderson's theory predicts which faults form in which stress regimes; and pore-fluid pressure can trigger slip. At depth, power-law creep takes over, which together with friction gives the strength envelope of the lithosphere.

refs: Stein & Wysession, An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure

items.name: Stress in the Earth: lithostatic and tectonic stress
items.pic: Decompose the stress at depth into an isotropic lithostatic part ρgz and a deviatoric tectonic part: principal axes are drawn as arrows on a cube that rotates with the tectonic setting.

items.name: Mohr’s circle for rock stress
items.pic: Rotate a plane through a stressed rock: its normal and shear stresses trace Mohr’s circle, and the plane with the largest shear is shown at 45° to the principal axes.

items.name: Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion
items.pic: Grow the Mohr circle until it touches the failure line τ = c + μσ: the touching point gives the fracture plane at about 30° to the maximum compression for μ ≈ 0.6.

items.name: Byerlee’s law of rock friction
items.pic: Plot shear against normal stress for frictional sliding on faults in many rock types: data collapse onto τ ≈ 0.85σ at low stress and 50 MPa + 0.6σ at high stress, regardless of rock type.

items.name: Anderson’s theory of faulting
items.pic: Choose which principal stress is vertical: normal, thrust or strike-slip faults form at the Mohr–Coulomb angle, drawn in 3D with their typical dips of 60°, 30° and 90°.

items.name: Pore pressure and fault weakening (Hubbert–Rubey)
items.pic: Inject fluid into a stressed fault: the effective normal stress drops, the Mohr circle slides left toward failure, and earthquakes are triggered without any change in tectonic load, as at injection wells.

items.name: Power-law creep of mantle rocks
items.pic: Plot olivine strain rate against stress at mantle temperatures: a slope near 3.5 on log axes with an Arrhenius temperature dependence, giving effective viscosities of 10¹⁹–10²² Pa·s.

items.name: Strength envelope and the brittle–ductile transition
items.pic: Combine frictional strength increasing with depth and creep strength decreasing with temperature: the weaker of the two traces a Christmas-tree profile whose peak marks the brittle–ductile transition, deepening as the geotherm cools.

chapters.title: Waves in rotating, stratified fluids
chapters.summary: Rotation and stratification support a zoo of waves. Gravity waves feel rotation as Poincaré waves; boundaries and the equator trap Kelvin waves; and the β effect gives Rossby waves, which always propagate westward and carry the weather systems of mid-latitudes. Internal waves ride on stratification, and tides and tsunamis are shallow-water waves on planetary scales.

refs: Vallis, Essentials of Atmospheric and Oceanic Dynamics

items.name: Poincaré waves (inertia–gravity waves)
items.pic: Plot the dispersion relation ω² = f² + gHk²: a gap below f appears, and simulated waves of long wavelength slosh at nearly the inertial frequency while short ones behave like ordinary gravity waves.

items.name: Kelvin waves: coastal and equatorial
items.pic: Launch a bump along a wall in a rotating channel: it travels with the coast on its right (north) at √(gH), trapped within a deformation radius, and an equatorial version races eastward along the equator.

items.name: Rossby waves
items.pic: Displace a ring of fluid north–south on a β-plane: PV conservation creates alternating vortices that push the pattern westward, at a speed matching the dispersion relation ω = −βk/(k² + l²).

items.name: Westward phase and eastward energy of short Rossby waves
items.pic: Send a Rossby wave packet across a basin: crests always drift west, while the packet envelope of short waves moves east, drawn with phase and group velocity arrows.

items.name: Internal gravity waves
items.pic: Oscillate a cylinder in a stratified tank: waves radiate along a St Andrew’s cross at an angle fixed by ω/N, with energy moving along the beams and phase across them.

items.name: Ocean tides and amphidromic points
items.pic: Force a rotating basin with the semidiurnal tidal potential: the tide rotates around nodes of zero range (amphidromes), with co-tidal lines radiating like clock hands, as in the North Sea.

items.name: Tsunamis as shallow-water waves
items.pic: Lift a patch of sea floor in a basin of variable depth: the wave crosses the ocean at √(gH) ≈ 700 km/h, slows and steepens on the shelf, and refracts toward shallow headlands.

chapters.title: The ocean, transient warming and sea level
chapters.summary: The ocean holds most of the climate system's heat capacity, so warming lags forcing. A two-layer model — a fast mixed layer over a slow deep ocean — explains the difference between transient and equilibrium response and the warming still in the pipeline. The measured energy imbalance confirms the planet is gaining heat, and that heat raises sea level through thermal expansion while melting ice adds more. El Niño shows the ocean and atmosphere coupled on interannual time scales.

refs: Archer, Global Warming: Understanding the Forecast

items.name: Mixed-layer response time
items.pic: Apply a step forcing to a slab ocean of adjustable depth: temperature relaxes exponentially with time constant C/λ, a few years for a 50 m mixed layer, plotted against the equilibrium line.

items.name: Two-layer model of transient climate response
items.pic: Couple the mixed layer to a deep ocean: warming shows a fast rise to a quasi-equilibrium and a slow creep over centuries, with the two time scales read off the eigenvalues of the 2×2 system.

items.name: Committed warming and the zero-emissions commitment
items.pic: Hold concentrations constant or stop emissions entirely: constant concentrations give continued warming as the deep ocean catches up, while zero emissions give a near-flat temperature as falling CO₂ offsets the lag.

items.name: Earth’s energy imbalance
items.pic: Integrate ocean heat content measurements over time: the slope gives a planetary imbalance of roughly 0.5–1 W/m², and the model shows the imbalance equals forcing minus feedback times warming.

items.name: Sea-level rise from thermal expansion
items.pic: Warm an ocean column with depth-dependent warming: expansion is computed from the equation of state, larger in warm water than near freezing, and the column height change is summed.

items.name: Sea-level contributions from glaciers and ice sheets
items.pic: Stack contributions to sea-level rise since 1900 and under scenarios: thermal expansion, mountain glaciers, Greenland and Antarctica, with Antarctica’s deep uncertainty shown as a widening band.

items.name: El Niño and the Bjerknes feedback
items.pic: Run a recharge-oscillator model: a warm anomaly weakens the trades, which deepens the thermocline in the east and amplifies the anomaly, while slow Kelvin and Rossby wave adjustment turns it around every few years.

items.name: Arctic sea-ice decline
items.pic: Plot September Arctic sea-ice extent since 1979 against cumulative CO₂ emissions: a near-linear decline of about 3 m² of ice per tonne of CO₂, extrapolated to an ice-free summer.

items.name: Atmospheric Teleconnections from the Equatorial Pacific
items.pic: Couple a toy equatorial Pacific: warm the east and the trade winds slacken, upwelling weakens and the east warms further — Bjerknes’ positive feedback — while the Walker circulation he named shifts east; the reader compares the model’s swing with the 1957–58 El Niño the paper analysed.

paper.title: Atmospheric Teleconnections from the Equatorial Pacific

chapters.title: Spatial analysis
chapters.summary: Tobler's first law — near things are more related than distant things — underlies the statistics of space. Spatial autocorrelation quantifies it, Voronoi polygons and interpolation methods exploit it to fill in unsampled places, distance decay and diffusion describe how influence and innovation spread, and John Snow's cholera map is the founding example of reasoning with location.

refs: Snyder, Map Projections — A Working Manual (USGS, public domain)

items.name: Tobler’s first law of geography
items.pic: Scatter sample points over a smooth random field: the correlation between pairs is plotted against their separation and decays with distance, while a shuffled field shows no decay at all.

items.name: Spatial autocorrelation: Moran’s I
items.pic: Paint values on a grid of cells: Moran’s I is computed live, positive for clusters, near zero for random patterns and negative for checkerboards, with a permutation test giving its significance.

items.name: Voronoi (Thiessen) polygons
items.pic: Drop rain gauges on a map: each claims the region closer to it than to any other, the polygons update as gauges are dragged, and the area-weighted rainfall estimate changes accordingly.

items.name: Spatial interpolation: inverse-distance weighting, kriging
items.pic: Interpolate a surface from scattered samples by IDW with an adjustable power and by kriging with a fitted variogram: cross-validation errors are compared, and kriging also maps its own uncertainty.

items.name: Distance decay
items.pic: Plot interactions (phone calls, shoppers, migrants) against distance from a centre: power-law and exponential decay curves are fitted, and their parameters change with transport cost.

items.name: John Snow’s cholera map
items.pic: Plot 1854 cholera deaths in Soho with the water pumps: the Voronoi cell of the Broad Street pump captures the cluster, and switching to walking distances sharpens the match.

items.name: Hägerstrand’s spatial diffusion of innovations
items.pic: Seed an innovation in a few farms and let adopters tell neighbours with a distance-decaying contact field: adoption spreads in a wave, and the cumulative count follows an S-curve.

items.name: Computer Movie Simulating Urban Growth in the Detroit Region
items.pic: Run Tobler’s computer movie: Detroit’s population grows year by year on a grid as each cell responds to its neighbours, nearer ones weighted more — “everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things” — and the reader changes the distance-decay kernel to see the city sprawl or clump.

paper.title: A Computer Movie Simulating Urban Growth in the Detroit Region

chapters.title: Selection and drift together
chapters.summary: In a finite population even a beneficial mutation is usually lost by chance. Branching processes give Haldane’s 2s and Kimura’s diffusion formula gives the full fixation probability, which shows that selection is effectively invisible when |Ns| is small. That idea underlies the nearly neutral and drift-barrier hypotheses; adaptation then proceeds by origin and fixation of mutations, which interfere in asexual populations and accumulate deleterious load through Muller’s ratchet.

refs: Gillespie, Population Genetics: A Concise Guide
Nielsen & Slatkin, An Introduction to Population Genetics

items.name: Branching-process approximation for a new mutant
items.pic: A single new beneficial mutant founds a lineage whose offspring numbers are Poisson with mean 1 + s; most lineages die within a few generations even when s is large.

items.name: Haldane’s fixation probability ≈ 2s
items.pic: Count surviving lineages out of thousands of simulated mutants for several values of s; the survival fraction falls on the line 2s, and the exact branching-process root is also plotted.

items.name: Kimura’s fixation probability
items.pic: Plot u(p) = (1 − e^{−4Nsp})/(1 − e^{−4Ns}) for positive, zero and negative s, and overlay fixation fractions from Wright–Fisher simulations with selection.

items.name: Effective neutrality: |Nₑs| ≪ 1
items.pic: Scan s for fixed N and plot the fixation probability relative to neutral; a flat region around s = 0 of width about 1/N shows where selection cannot be distinguished from drift.

items.name: Nearly neutral theory (Ohta)
items.pic: Mutations of slightly deleterious effect fix often in small populations and rarely in large ones; the substitution rate per year is plotted against population size for several effect distributions.

items.name: Drift-barrier hypothesis
items.pic: Let selection improve a trait such as replication fidelity until further gains fall below 1/Nₑ; the predicted floor of the mutation rate drops with population size, compared with measured rates across taxa.

items.name: Fixation time of a beneficial allele ≈ (2/s) ln(2N)
items.pic: Time sweeps conditioned on fixation for several N and s; the mean fixation times line up with the logarithmic formula, far shorter than the 4N of neutral alleles.

items.name: Origin–fixation rate of adaptive substitution
items.pic: Beneficial mutations arise at rate 2Nμ and each fixes with probability about 2s; the simulated substitution rate is compared with 4Nμs as both N and s vary.

items.name: Distribution of fitness effects
items.pic: Draw a distribution of selection coefficients and shade the effectively neutral band |s| < 1/2N; changing N reclassifies which mutations behave as neutral, deleterious or beneficial.

items.name: Clonal interference
items.pic: In an asexual population, competing beneficial clones are drawn as a Muller plot; raise the mutation supply and simultaneous clones interfere, so the adaptation rate saturates instead of growing linearly.

items.name: Muller’s ratchet
items.pic: Track the least-loaded class of an asexual population; when its expected size N e^{−U/s} is small it is lost by drift, the ratchet clicks, and the clicks get more frequent as N shrinks.

items.name: Evolutionary rescue
items.pic: A population declining after an environmental change can be saved by a resistant mutant; the U-shaped population trajectory appears in some runs, and rescue probability is plotted against initial size.

items.name: A Mathematical Theory of Natural and Artificial Selection, V
items.pic: Haldane’s 2s: a single new mutant with advantage s leaves a Poisson number of offspring with mean 1 + s; iterate the generating function to get the chance its line never dies out and run thousands of simulated lineages — most beneficial mutations are lost by chance, and the surviving fraction tracks 2s.

paper.title: A Mathematical Theory of Natural and Artificial Selection, Part V: Selection and Mutation
paper.venue: Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 23 (7): 838–844

chapters.title: Oscillators, switches and excitability
chapters.summary: Biology is full of clocks and toggles: glycolysis pulses, genes switch on and stay on, hearts and neurons fire and recover. This chapter collects the phase-plane machinery for proving and ruling out cycles, the canonical relaxation oscillator, feedback-loop oscillators with their gain requirements, positive-feedback switches and excitable systems. Phase response curves then describe how oscillators are reset, entrained and synchronized — including Winfree’s strange stimuli that stop a clock dead.

items.name: Bendixson–Dulac criterion
items.pic: Shade the divergence of a planar vector field (optionally multiplied by a Dulac function); where it keeps one sign on a simply connected region, every attempted closed orbit you draw shows a nonzero net flux and fails.

items.name: Van der Pol oscillator and relaxation oscillations
items.pic: Raise the stiffness parameter μ and the near-sinusoidal cycle turns into slow crawls along the cubic nullcline punctuated by fast jumps; the period readout grows linearly with μ as predicted.

items.name: Sel’kov model of glycolytic oscillations
items.pic: Vary the substrate supply rate; within a window bounded by two Hopf points the ATP–ADP concentrations oscillate, and a trapping region drawn on the phase plane shows why a cycle must exist.

items.name: Goodwin oscillator
items.pic: A gene represses itself through two intermediate steps; increase the Hill coefficient of repression and the steady state gives way to sustained oscillations of mRNA, protein and repressor in staggered phase.

items.name: Secant condition for feedback-loop oscillators
items.pic: For a loop of n identical stages the loop gain needed for instability is sec(π/n)ⁿ; drag n and the gain and watch the simulation start oscillating exactly as the point crosses the plotted curve (gain 8 for three stages).

items.name: Bistable switch from positive feedback
items.pic: A self-activating gene with sigmoidal feedback has production and degradation curves crossing three times; pulse the input and the system jumps to the high state and stays there after the pulse ends.

items.name: Excitability
items.pic: Kick a resting system with stimuli of increasing size: small kicks decay at once, but beyond a threshold the trajectory makes a large excursion around the phase plane before returning — an all-or-none response.

items.name: Oregonator model of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction
items.pic: The three-variable Oregonator is integrated with a stiff solver; bromide and bromous acid concentrations show relaxation oscillations, and a colour swatch flips between red and blue at each cycle as in the beaker.

items.name: Phase and the phase response curve
items.pic: Deliver a brief pulse to a limit-cycle oscillator at a chosen phase; the measured advance or delay of the next peak is plotted, and sweeping the pulse timing builds the whole phase response curve.

items.name: Phase singularities and type 0 resetting (Winfree)
items.pic: Map the new phase against old phase for weak and strong pulses; at a critical strength and timing the pulse lands in the “black hole” near the unstable focus and the rhythm stops, as Winfree found for circadian clocks.

items.name: Entrainment and Arnold tongues
items.pic: Force an oscillator periodically and scan forcing frequency and amplitude; regions of 1:1, 1:2 and 2:3 locking appear as tongues computed from the circle map, with quasi-periodic gaps between them.

chapters.title: Food webs and community stability
chapters.summary: Communities are webs of who eats whom. Removing a keystone predator or adding a top carnivore can cascade down to plants, and the size of these effects depends on productivity. May showed that randomly assembled large communities are unlikely to be stable, overturning the intuition that diversity breeds stability; the resolution lies in the non-random structure of real webs — weak links, compartments and characteristic connectance — and in the insurance that diversity gives ecosystem functions.

refs: Begon, Townsend & Harper, Ecology: From Individuals to Ecosystems
MacArthur & Wilson, The Theory of Island Biogeography
Brown et al., Toward a Metabolic Theory of Ecology

items.name: Food webs and trophic levels
items.pic: An editable food web is drawn with species stacked by trophic level, computed from the average path length to basal resources; adding an omnivory link shifts a species to a fractional level.

items.name: Keystone species (Paine)
items.pic: Remove the starfish Pisaster from a simulated intertidal web; mussels monopolize space and diversity collapses, while removing other species of similar biomass changes little.

items.name: Trophic cascades
items.pic: Add or remove the top predator in a three- or four-level food chain; biomass alternates up and down the levels, as with wolves, elk and willows or sea otters, urchins and kelp.

items.name: Exploitation ecosystems and the green-world hypothesis
items.pic: Raise primary productivity in a food-chain model; new trophic levels are added one by one and equilibrium plant biomass rises in steps only when the number of levels is odd.

items.name: Community matrix and local stability
items.pic: Compute the Jacobian of a multispecies equilibrium and display its eigenvalues; perturb the community and watch it return or diverge as predicted by the rightmost eigenvalue.

items.name: May’s stability–complexity criterion
items.pic: Fill a random community matrix with S species, connectance C and interaction strength σ; the eigenvalues fill a disc of radius σ√(SC), and stability is lost as soon as the disc crosses the self-regulation line.

items.name: Diversity–stability paradox
items.pic: Plot the probability of stability against species richness for random webs (falling) alongside field observations of more stable diverse grasslands (rising), the tension May’s result created.

items.name: Weak interactions stabilize food webs
items.pic: Shift the distribution of interaction strengths toward many weak links and few strong ones at fixed mean; the fraction of stable random webs rises sharply, as McCann argued.

items.name: Niche model of food-web structure
items.pic: Species get niche values on a line and eat everything in a range below them; generated webs reproduce the chain lengths and omnivory of real webs better than random graphs.

items.name: Connectance and food-chain length
items.pic: Compare real food webs on a plot of links against species; links per species stays nearly constant, and food chains rarely exceed four or five links.

items.name: Intraguild predation and omnivory
items.pic: A predator eats both a prey and that prey’s competitor; coexistence requires the intraguild prey to be the better resource competitor, mapped as a band in productivity space.

items.name: Biodiversity and ecosystem function: the insurance effect
items.pic: Communities of species with asynchronous responses to environmental noise give total biomass whose coefficient of variation falls with richness, the portfolio effect.

items.name: Food Web Complexity and Species Diversity
items.pic: Paine’s removal experiment at Mukkaw Bay: take the starfish Pisaster out of a rocky-shore food web and the mussels and barnacles it ate take over the space, shrinking a 15-species system to 8 — remove or restore the top predator in a simulated intertidal patch and watch diversity respond.

paper.title: Food Web Complexity and Species Diversity

items.name: Will a Large Complex System be Stable?
items.pic: May’s random communities: draw an S-species community matrix with connectance C and interaction strength σ and plot its eigenvalues — they fill a disc of radius σ√(SC) — and watch the system flip from almost surely stable to almost surely unstable as σ√(SC) crosses 1.

paper.title: Will a Large Complex System be Stable?

chapters.title: Spike trains and neural coding
chapters.summary: Neural responses are variable, so coding is statistical. Firing rates, Poisson and renewal processes, Fano factors and spectra describe spike trains; tuning curves, reverse correlation and linear–nonlinear–Poisson models describe how stimuli drive them. Decoding asks how well an observer can read a stimulus back, bounded by Fisher information, and efficient-coding arguments explain why response curves match the statistics of the world. Noise models make firing itself probabilistic and can even help detection.

items.name: Firing rate and the peri-stimulus time histogram
items.pic: Repeat a stimulus many times and stack spike rasters; binning across trials gives the PSTH, and changing the bin width trades time resolution for noise.

items.name: Poisson spike trains
items.pic: Generate homogeneous and inhomogeneous Poisson spike trains; interspike intervals are exponential and spike counts in windows are Poisson, checked against histograms.

items.name: Fano factor and coefficient of variation
items.pic: Compare a Poisson train, a regular train with refractoriness and a bursting train; Fano factor and CV are read out, falling below or rising above 1 respectively.

items.name: Renewal processes, survivor function and hazard
items.pic: Draw an interspike-interval density; its survivor function and hazard are computed, and a hazard that is zero during refractoriness then rises reproduces the measured interval histogram.

items.name: Spike-train autocorrelation and power spectrum
items.pic: Compute the autocorrelation and power spectrum of a recorded spike train; refractoriness carves a dip at low lags and a trough in the spectrum, and oscillatory firing shows a peak.

items.name: Tuning curves
items.pic: Rotate a bar of light and record a model V1 neuron; mean rate against orientation traces a bell-shaped tuning curve with error bars from trial-to-trial variability.

items.name: Spike-triggered average and reverse correlation
items.pic: Drive a model neuron with white noise and average the stimulus preceding each spike; the spike-triggered average converges to the neuron’s linear filter as spikes accumulate.

items.name: Linear–nonlinear–Poisson model
items.pic: Filter a stimulus, pass it through a static nonlinearity and generate Poisson spikes; recover both stages from simulated data and compare predicted and actual PSTHs.

items.name: Receptive fields: Gabor and difference-of-Gaussians
items.pic: Convolve natural images with centre–surround and Gabor receptive fields; responses highlight edges and oriented features, and drifting gratings map out spatial-frequency tuning.

items.name: Population-vector decoding
items.pic: Motor-cortex neurons with cosine tuning each vote with their preferred direction weighted by rate; the summed vector points close to the true reach direction, with errors shrinking as more neurons are added.

items.name: Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound for population codes
items.pic: For a population of tuning curves, Fisher information is computed as a function of stimulus; the variance of a decoder across trials stays above 1/I_F, and is most precise on tuning-curve flanks.

items.name: Maximum a posteriori decoding
items.pic: Combine Poisson likelihoods from a population with a prior over stimuli; the posterior is drawn for each trial, and its peak outperforms the population vector when tuning is uneven.

items.name: Efficient coding and histogram equalization (Laughlin)
items.pic: The response curve that maximizes information for a noisy neuron with bounded output is the cumulative distribution of natural contrasts; it matches the fly interneuron data Laughlin recorded.

items.name: Time-rescaling theorem for spike trains
items.pic: Rescale time by the integrated conditional intensity of a fitted model; if the model is right the rescaled intervals are unit exponential, checked by a Kolmogorov–Smirnov plot against the diagonal.

items.name: Escape noise and the noisy integrate-and-fire neuron
items.pic: Let a neuron fire stochastically with a rate that rises steeply with voltage; interval distributions broaden, and diffusive input noise and escape noise give matching histograms.

items.name: Stochastic resonance
items.pic: A subthreshold periodic input alone never makes the neuron fire; add noise and spikes lock to the signal, with signal-to-noise ratio peaking at an intermediate noise level.

items.name: Receptive Fields and Functional Architecture in Cat Cortex
items.pic: Hubel and Wiesel’s bench: sweep a bar of light across a simulated cortical cell’s receptive field and hear its spikes; a simple cell fires only for the right orientation over its excitatory strip, a complex cell for the right orientation anywhere in its field, and an electrode track through the cortex steps through orientation and ocular-dominance columns.

paper.authors: D. H. Hubel and T. N. Wiesel
paper.title: Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat’s visual cortex

chapters.title: Probabilistic phylogenetics
chapters.summary: Treating substitution as a continuous-time Markov process turns tree building into statistics. Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm computes the likelihood of a tree in linear time; reversibility makes the root irrelevant; rate variation among sites matters. The bootstrap and Bayesian MCMC give measures of confidence, likelihood methods stay consistent where parsimony fails, and gene trees need not match species trees.

refs: Durbin, Eddy, Krogh & Mitchison, Biological Sequence Analysis

items.name: Likelihood of a tree
items.pic: For a single alignment column on a small tree, enumerate all ancestral states and sum their probabilities; the likelihood of each candidate topology is compared.

items.name: Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm
items.pic: Partial likelihood vectors are passed up the tree node by node; the root value matches brute-force enumeration while the operation counter grows only linearly with taxa.

items.name: Reversibility and the pulley principle
items.pic: Slide the root anywhere along the tree under a reversible model; the likelihood readout stays constant, while a non-reversible model makes it change.

items.name: Rate heterogeneity across sites
items.pic: Draw site rates from a gamma distribution with shape α; small α makes most sites nearly invariant and a few fast, and ignoring it biases branch lengths downward.

items.name: Bootstrap support for clades
items.pic: Resample alignment columns with replacement and rebuild the tree each time; the percentage of replicates containing each clade is written on its branch.

items.name: Bayesian phylogenetics by MCMC
items.pic: A Metropolis–Hastings chain proposes branch-length and topology changes; the trace of log-likelihood stabilizes and posterior clade probabilities accumulate.

items.name: Likelihood is consistent in the Felsenstein zone
items.pic: On the same long-branch simulation where parsimony fails, the maximum-likelihood tree converges to the truth as sites accumulate, plotted side by side.

items.name: Gene trees versus species trees
items.pic: Simulate gene genealogies inside a species tree with short internal branches; a sizeable fraction of gene trees disagree with the species tree through incomplete lineage sorting.

items.name: Evolutionary Trees from DNA Sequences
items.pic: Felsenstein’s pruning on a four-taxon tree: conditional likelihoods flow from the tips to the root site by site; drag branch lengths and watch the log-likelihood respond, move the root to confirm the pulley principle, and compare the maximum likelihoods of the three unrooted topologies.

paper.title: Evolutionary trees from DNA sequences: A maximum likelihood approach

chapters.title: Proofreading and robust signalling
chapters.summary: Molecular recognition is noisy, yet translation and immune recognition make astonishingly few errors: kinetic proofreading spends energy to square the error rate. Signalling circuits achieve a different kind of robustness — outputs that do not depend on protein levels — through bifunctional enzymes and the structural theorems of chemical reaction network theory. Kinase cascades and receptor binding set how much signal gets through.

refs: Alon, An Introduction to Systems Biology

items.name: Kinetic proofreading (Hopfield–Ninio)
refs: Alon: Kinetic Proofreading and Conformational Proofreading
items.pic: Correct and wrong substrates bind an enzyme and must survive an irreversible delay step before acting; add delay steps and the wrong-to-right product ratio falls geometrically.

items.name: Proofreading squares the error at an energetic cost
refs: Alon: Kinetic Proofreading and Conformational Proofreading
items.pic: Plot error rate against energy dissipated per product for zero, one and two proofreading steps; the error approaches f², f³ while speed and energy costs rise.

items.name: Conformational proofreading
refs: Alon: Kinetic Proofreading and Conformational Proofreading
items.pic: A recognizer that must deform to bind trades binding strength for specificity; scanning the deformation energy shows an optimum where discrimination between right and wrong targets is greatest.

items.name: Absolute concentration robustness (Shinar–Feinberg)
items.pic: For a network with deficiency one and two non-terminal complexes differing in one species, vary every total concentration; that species’ steady state stays exactly fixed in the readout.

items.name: Bifunctional enzymes make two-component output robust
items.pic: In an EnvZ–OmpR-like circuit the sensor both phosphorylates and dephosphorylates the regulator; doubling either protein’s level leaves the phosphorylated output unchanged, unlike a design with a separate phosphatase.

items.name: Deficiency-zero theorem (Feinberg)
items.pic: Draw a reaction network; its complexes, linkage classes and deficiency are computed, and when the deficiency is zero and the network weakly reversible every simulation converges to a unique positive steady state per conservation class.

items.name: Signal amplification in kinase cascades
items.pic: For a cascade of weakly activated kinases the output amplitude and duration are computed tier by tier; amplification is high only when phosphatases are slow, as the readout of signal gain shows.

items.name: Receptor–ligand dose–response and EC50
items.pic: Plot receptor occupancy and downstream response against log ligand; spare receptors and amplification shift the response EC50 below the binding Kd, shown as two offset sigmoids.

chapters.title: Oxygen transport and blood
chapters.summary: Almost all oxygen in blood rides on hemoglobin, whose sigmoidal binding curve — a textbook case of cooperativity — loads oxygen in the lungs and unloads it in tissues. Acidity, CO₂, temperature and 2,3-BPG shift the curve to tune delivery; fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide shift it the other way. The Fick principle measures cardiac output from oxygen consumption, and feedback through erythropoietin keeps the red-cell mass in line.

refs: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

items.name: Oxygen content: bound versus dissolved
items.pic: Break arterial oxygen content into hemoglobin-bound and dissolved parts as P_O₂ varies; dissolved oxygen is a thin sliver, and anaemia shrinks the bound part at normal P_O₂.

items.name: Oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve
items.pic: Plot saturation against P_O₂ with the Hill fit (n ≈ 2.7, P50 ≈ 27 mmHg); the steep middle section unloads oxygen at tissue pressures while the flat top protects loading in the lungs.

items.name: Adair and MWC models of hemoglobin
items.pic: Fit the dissociation curve with the four-step Adair scheme and with the two-state MWC model; the successive binding constants increase, showing cooperativity mechanistically.

items.name: Bohr effect
items.pic: Lower pH or raise CO₂ and the dissociation curve shifts right; at a fixed tissue P_O₂ the extra oxygen released is shaded and read out.

items.name: Haldane effect
items.pic: Plot CO₂ content against P_CO₂ for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood; deoxygenated blood carries more CO₂, so unloading oxygen in tissues helps pick up CO₂.

items.name: 2,3-BPG and adaptation to altitude
items.pic: Raise red-cell 2,3-BPG and the curve shifts right; at altitude compare oxygen delivered with and without the shift for a given arterial P_O₂.

items.name: Fetal hemoglobin’s left-shifted curve
items.pic: Overlay fetal and maternal dissociation curves at placental P_O₂; the fetal curve’s higher saturation at the same pressure lets oxygen flow from mother to fetus.

items.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
items.pic: Replace a fraction of binding sites with CO; the remaining curve both shrinks and shifts left, so oxygen delivery falls far more than the lost capacity alone suggests.

items.name: Myoglobin versus hemoglobin: hyperbola and sigmoid
items.pic: Myoglobin’s hyperbolic curve sits to the left of hemoglobin’s sigmoid; follow oxygen handed from capillary hemoglobin to muscle myoglobin at low P_O₂.

items.name: Fick principle for cardiac output
items.pic: Measure oxygen uptake and the arterial–mixed-venous content difference; cardiac output is their ratio, and the readout tracks a simulated exercise test.

items.name: Oxygen delivery and extraction
items.pic: Delivery is cardiac output times arterial content; lower delivery and extraction rises to hold uptake constant until a critical delivery below which uptake falls.

items.name: Krogh tissue cylinder
items.pic: Solve the diffusion–consumption equation around a capillary; tissue P_O₂ falls with radius and toward the venous end, and a lethal corner appears when consumption is raised.

items.name: CO₂ transport and the chloride shift
items.pic: Follow CO₂ entering a red cell: carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate, which leaves in exchange for chloride; the proportions carried as bicarbonate, carbamino and dissolved are shown as bars.

items.name: Erythropoietin feedback and red-cell production
items.pic: Lower oxygen delivery and the kidney releases erythropoietin; red-cell mass recovers over weeks after a maturation delay, and lengthening the delay produces oscillations.

items.name: Einfluss der Kohlensäurespannung auf die Sauerstoffbindung
items.pic: Recreate the paper’s figure: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves of dog blood measured at several carbon-dioxide tensions; raising CO₂ shifts the curve to the right, so tissue rich in CO₂ unloads more oxygen at the same partial pressure — slide P_CO₂ and read off the extra oxygen delivered between lung and tissue.

paper.authors: Chr. Bohr, K. Hasselbalch and August Krogh
paper.title: Ueber einen in biologischer Beziehung wichtigen Einfluss, den die Kohlensäurespannung des Blutes auf dessen Sauerstoffbindung übt

chapters.title: Pharmacodynamics: receptors and dose–response
chapters.summary: What a drug does to the body starts with binding to receptors. Occupancy theory and the Emax/Hill model give sigmoid concentration–effect curves characterized by potency and efficacy; partial and inverse agonists, spare receptors and the operational model explain why effect is not simply occupancy. Antagonists shift curves in characteristic ways that Schild analysis and the Cheng–Prusoff relation quantify, and combinations are judged against additivity.

refs: Rowland & Tozer, Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
Goodman & Gilman, The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

items.name: Receptor occupancy theory (Clark)
items.pic: Ligand and receptor bind by mass action; fractional occupancy follows C/(C + K_D), drawn on linear and log-concentration axes with K_D marked.

items.name: Emax model and the Hill equation for drug effect
items.pic: Fit effect data with E = E_max·Cⁿ/(EC50ⁿ + Cⁿ); the Hill coefficient sets steepness, and the 20–80% effect range of concentrations is shaded.

items.name: Potency versus efficacy
items.pic: Compare two drugs: one with lower EC50 (more potent) and one with higher E_max (more efficacious); their curves cross, showing why potency alone does not rank drugs.

items.name: Log dose–response curves
items.pic: Replot a hyperbolic dose–response on a log-dose axis; it becomes a symmetric sigmoid that is nearly linear between 20% and 80% of maximum.

items.name: Full, partial and inverse agonists
items.pic: With constitutive receptor activity present, full agonists raise activity to the top, partial agonists to an intermediate ceiling and inverse agonists below baseline.

items.name: Operational model of agonism and receptor reserve
items.pic: Raise the transducer ratio τ: the effect EC50 moves left of the binding K_D; irreversibly removing receptors first shifts the curve right before lowering its maximum.

items.name: Del Castillo–Katz two-state receptor model
items.pic: A receptor binds ligand and then isomerizes to an active state; efficacy is the isomerization constant, and the occupancy and response curves separate as it grows.

items.name: Competitive antagonism and the Schild equation
items.pic: Add increasing antagonist concentrations: agonist curves shift right in parallel; the Schild plot of log(dose ratio − 1) against log antagonist is a line of slope 1 crossing at pA₂.

items.name: Cheng–Prusoff equation: IC50 to Ki
items.pic: Measure an inhibitor’s IC50 against different radioligand concentrations; IC50 rises linearly with ligand, and K_i = IC50/(1 + L/K_D) is constant across experiments.

items.name: Non-competitive antagonism depresses E_max
items.pic: An irreversible or allosteric antagonist lowers the agonist’s maximal effect without shifting EC50 (unless spare receptors exist), contrasted with the competitive parallel shift.

items.name: Allosteric modulators
items.pic: A modulator at a separate site multiplies agonist affinity or efficacy by cooperativity factors; positive modulators shift the curve left and saturate, giving a ceiling to their effect.

items.name: Binding kinetics: on-rate, off-rate and residence time
items.pic: Two drugs with the same K_D but different k_off are washed out; the slow-off drug keeps receptors occupied long after plasma levels fall.

items.name: Tolerance, tachyphylaxis and desensitization
items.pic: Repeated doses down-regulate receptors in a feedback model; the effect of the same concentration shrinks over doses, and the dose–response curve shifts right.

items.name: Drug combinations: isobolograms and Loewe additivity
items.pic: Plot dose pairs of two drugs that give the same effect; points on the straight additivity line, below it (synergy) or above it (antagonism) are classified.

items.name: The Reaction between Acetyl Choline and Muscle Cells
items.pic: Clark’s concentration–action curves: the response of frog heart or rectus abdominis to acetylcholine follows Kx = y/(100 − y), the hyperbola of a drug occupying receptors by mass action; fit K to the data, see the curve become a symmetric sigmoid on a logarithmic axis, and compare with a curve the occupancy law cannot fit.

paper.title: The reaction between acetyl choline and muscle cells

items.name: Some Quantitative Uses of Drug Antagonists
items.pic: The Schild plot: add increasing antagonist concentrations, measure how far each shifts the agonist curve (the dose ratio r), and plot log(r − 1) against log[B]; a straight line of slope 1 marks competitive antagonism and its intercept gives pA₂ — test a competitive and a non-competitive antagonist side by side.

paper.authors: O. Arunlakshana and H. O. Schild
paper.title: Some quantitative uses of drug antagonists
paper.venue: British Journal of Pharmacology and Chemotherapy 14 (1): 48–58

chapters.title: Bias
chapters.summary: Systematic errors do not shrink with sample size. Selection bias arises from who enters or stays in a study, information bias from how exposure and outcome are measured; each has classic forms such as the healthy-worker effect, recall bias and survivorship bias. Quantitative bias analysis asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain a result away.

items.name: Random versus systematic error
items.pic: Repeat a study many times at increasing size; random error narrows the spread of estimates while a systematic error keeps their centre away from the truth.

items.name: Selection bias
items.pic: Let study participation depend on both exposure and outcome; the estimate among participants departs from the population value, explained by a collider in the causal diagram.

items.name: Healthy worker effect
items.pic: Compare mortality of a workforce with the general population; workers look healthier because the sick are less likely to be employed, masking a real occupational hazard.

items.name: Non-differential misclassification biases toward the null
items.pic: Misclassify exposure with the same sensitivity and specificity in cases and controls; the observed risk ratio slides toward 1 as accuracy falls.

items.name: Recall bias
items.pic: Mothers of affected infants recall exposures more completely than control mothers; differential misclassification inflates the odds ratio, which the simulation quantifies.

items.name: Survivorship bias (Wald’s bombers)
items.pic: Bullet holes are plotted only on aircraft that returned; armouring where holes are dense is wrong, since planes hit elsewhere did not come back, as the full simulated fleet shows.

chapters.title: Magnetic resonance imaging
chapters.summary: Nuclear spins in a magnetic field precess at the Larmor frequency and can be tipped by radio-frequency pulses; their relaxation back to equilibrium, described by the Bloch equations, gives tissue contrast through T1 and T2. Magnetic field gradients make frequency depend on position, so the signal is the Fourier transform of the image sampled along trajectories in k-space. Sampling rules, symmetry, coil arrays and sparsity determine how fast images can be made; BOLD and diffusion contrast extend MRI to function and microstructure.

refs: Prince & Links, Medical Imaging Signals and Systems
Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging

items.name: Net magnetization and Boltzmann polarization
items.pic: Spins align slightly more often with the field than against it; the net magnetization is computed from the Boltzmann factor and is only a few parts per million at 1.5 T.

items.name: Bloch equations
items.pic: Integrate the magnetization vector in 3D through an RF pulse and relaxation; in the rotating frame a 90° pulse tips it into the transverse plane where it decays and regrows.

items.name: T1 and T2 relaxation
items.pic: Longitudinal magnetization recovers with T1 and transverse magnetization decays with T2; curves for fat, white matter and fluid are plotted with their characteristic times.

items.name: Free induction decay and T2*
items.pic: Spins in an inhomogeneous field dephase faster than T2; the received signal decays with T2*, shown as a fan of spinning arrows spreading apart.

items.name: Spin echo
items.pic: A 180° pulse at time TE/2 reverses the dephasing; the spins refocus into an echo at TE whose amplitude decays only with true T2, the runners-on-a-track picture animated.

items.name: Image contrast from TR and TE
items.pic: Choose repetition and echo times on a grid; the computed signal of different tissues produces T1-weighted, T2-weighted or proton-density images of a brain phantom.

items.name: Slice selection with gradients and shaped RF pulses
items.pic: A gradient makes resonance frequency vary with position; a sinc-shaped RF pulse with limited bandwidth excites only a slab, whose thickness changes with gradient strength.

items.name: k-space: frequency and phase encoding
items.pic: Trace the k-space trajectory as gradients are applied; each sampled point is a Fourier coefficient, and filling k-space line by line then inverse transforming yields the image.

items.name: Field of view and wrap-around aliasing
items.pic: Increase the spacing between k-space samples; the field of view shrinks below the object and parts of it wrap onto the opposite side of the image.

items.name: Partial Fourier from Hermitian symmetry
items.pic: Acquire just over half of k-space and fill the rest by conjugate symmetry; the image is nearly unchanged for real objects and degrades when phase errors are introduced.

items.name: Parallel imaging (SENSE)
items.pic: Undersample k-space so the image aliases, then use the different sensitivity maps of several receiver coils to unfold each pair of overlapping pixels.

items.name: Compressed-sensing MRI
items.pic: Sample k-space randomly at a fraction of the Nyquist rate; zero-filled reconstruction shows noise-like aliasing that sparsity-promoting iterative reconstruction removes.

items.name: BOLD contrast in functional MRI
items.pic: Neural activity raises blood flow beyond oxygen demand; deoxyhemoglobin falls, T2* lengthens and the signal rises a few percent with the delayed haemodynamic response.

items.name: Diffusion MRI (Stejskal–Tanner)
items.pic: A pair of gradient pulses dephases spins that move between them; signal falls as e^{−bD}, and measuring along many directions reveals fibre orientation in white matter.

items.name: Image Formation by Induced Local Interactions
items.pic: Lauterbur’s first zeugmatogram: two capillaries of water in a magnetic-field gradient give an NMR signal whose spectrum is their projection; rotate the gradient through four angles, back-project the four profiles and the two tubes appear — add angles and objects and see more projections sharpen the image.

paper.title: Image Formation by Induced Local Interactions: Examples Employing Nuclear Magnetic Resonance

items.name: Brain MRI with Contrast Dependent on Blood Oxygenation
items.pic: Ogawa’s rat-brain images at high field: in gradient-echo images the veins turn dark when the blood is deoxygenated and fade when it is oxygenated, because paramagnetic deoxyhaemoglobin shortens T₂*; set blood oxygenation and echo time and watch vessel contrast appear — the effect that became functional MRI.

paper.authors: S. Ogawa, T. M. Lee, A. R. Kay and D. W. Tank
paper.title: Brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast dependent on blood oxygenation
paper.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 87 (24): 9868–9872

chapters.title: Frequency response and filtering
chapters.summary: The frequency response tells how much each frequency is amplified and delayed, which is what filtering means. Ideal brick-wall filters turn out to be non-causal, and the Paley–Wiener criterion says exactly how sharp a causal filter can be. Bode plots, first- and second-order building blocks, minimum-phase systems and the deep link between gain and phase complete the picture.

items.name: Frequency response of an LTI system
items.pic: Drive a black-box filter with sinusoids of a chosen frequency and read off gain and phase from the input and output traces; the points fall on the computed |H(jω)| and ∠H(jω) curves.

items.name: Ideal low-pass, high-pass and band-pass filters
items.pic: Pass music through brick-wall filters with draggable cutoffs: the spectrum is chopped, and the audio button plays the result.

items.name: The ideal low-pass filter is non-causal
items.pic: The impulse response of an ideal low-pass is a sinc extending to minus infinity; truncating and delaying it to make it causal leaves ripples in the frequency response.

items.name: Paley–Wiener criterion for causal filters
items.pic: Design a magnitude response by dragging points: the integral of |log|H||/(1 + ω²) is computed, and any response that is exactly zero over a band is rejected as unrealisable.

items.name: Linear phase and distortionless transmission
items.pic: Send a pulse through filters with flat magnitude but different phase curves: linear phase just delays it, while curved phase distorts its shape.

items.name: Group delay and the dispersion of a pulse
items.pic: A chirped wave packet passes through a dispersive filter: frequencies arrive at different times according to the group-delay curve, and the packet spreads.

items.name: Bode plots
items.pic: Drop poles and zeros on a real axis: the log-magnitude asymptotes bend by ±20 dB/decade at each, and the exact curve hugs them, with phase steps of ±90° smeared over two decades.

items.name: First-order systems: time constant and bandwidth
items.pic: Halve the time constant of a first-order system: the step response rises twice as fast and the bandwidth on the Bode plot doubles.

items.name: Second-order systems: resonance and damping
items.pic: Lower the damping ratio of a second-order system: the step response rings and the frequency response sprouts a resonant peak, linked as one parameter changes.

items.name: Minimum-phase systems and all-pass factors
items.pic: Reflect a zero from the left to the right half-plane: the magnitude response is unchanged, but the phase lag grows and the step response dips the wrong way first.

items.name: Bode’s gain–phase relation and the Hilbert transform
items.pic: Sketch the log-magnitude of a minimum-phase system; its phase is computed from the magnitude alone and matches the true phase, while a non-minimum-phase example deviates.

items.name: Rise time versus bandwidth
items.pic: Shrink a filter’s bandwidth and measure the 10–90% rise time of its step response: their product stays near a constant across filter families.

items.name: Ringing of sharp filters
items.pic: Make a filter’s cutoff sharper and watch its step response develop Gibbs-like ringing that refuses to go away, while a gentle filter has none.

chapters.title: Routh–Hurwitz and the root locus
chapters.summary: Closed-loop stability comes down to whether a polynomial has roots in the right half-plane. Routh's array answers that question from the coefficients alone, without computing a single root, and also tells how far a gain can be raised. The root locus shows instead how every closed-loop pole moves as the gain increases, and simple geometric rules let us sketch it by hand and design compensators on it.

refs: Franklin, Powell & Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems

items.name: Closed-loop characteristic polynomial
items.pic: Edit numerator and denominator polynomials of a loop: the characteristic polynomial d + kn is formed and its roots plotted as the gain slider moves.

items.name: Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion
items.pic: Type a polynomial and watch the Routh array fill in row by row; the number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of right-half-plane roots, confirmed by the computed roots.

items.name: All coefficients positive: necessary, not sufficient
items.pic: A polynomial with all positive coefficients can still have unstable roots once its degree is three or more — a slider finds one, and the Routh array flags it.

items.name: Routh special cases and imaginary-axis crossings
items.pic: Tune a gain until a whole row of the Routh array vanishes: the auxiliary polynomial gives the frequency at which the roots cross the imaginary axis.

items.name: Stability range of a gain
items.pic: For a loop with a free gain, the Routh conditions are solved for k; the stable interval is shaded on a number line and checked against a simulation at each end.

items.name: Root locus
items.pic: Sweep the gain from zero to infinity: closed-loop poles leave the open-loop poles and travel to the open-loop zeros or to infinity, leaving coloured trails.

items.name: Angle and magnitude conditions
items.pic: Drag a test point around the s-plane: the sum of angles from zeros minus poles is displayed and turns red at exactly 180°, where the point is on the locus and the required gain is read out.

items.name: Root-locus sketching rules
items.pic: Toggle each rule — real-axis segments, asymptote angles and centroid, breakaway points, departure angles — to overlay its prediction on the computed locus.

items.name: Roots move continuously with the gain
items.pic: Draw a small circle around a closed-loop pole and nudge the gain: Rouché’s theorem guarantees the circle still contains exactly one root, which the animation confirms.

items.name: Lead compensation on the root locus
items.pic: Place a lead zero and pole to bend the locus leftward through the desired region of the s-plane; the step response improves as the locus passes through the shaded spec region.

items.name: Lag compensation for steady-state accuracy
items.pic: Add a lag pole–zero pair close to the origin: the low-frequency gain rises and the steady-state error falls while the locus near the dominant poles barely moves.

items.name: Conditionally stable systems
