items.pic: A locus dips into the right half-plane and back out: the loop is stable for large and small gains but unstable in between, so reducing the gain can destabilise it.

items.name: Kharitonov’s theorem
items.pic: Give each coefficient an uncertainty interval: checking just four special polynomials certifies stability of the whole family, verified by plotting roots of thousands of random members.

chapters.title: Second-order circuits
chapters.summary: With one capacitor and one inductor, energy can slosh back and forth between electric and magnetic form, and the circuit can oscillate. The series RLC circuit obeys exactly the equation of a damped mass on a spring, so the same three regimes appear — overdamped, critically damped and ringing. The state-variable view, with capacitor voltages and inductor currents as coordinates, prepares the ground for control theory.

refs: Agarwal & Lang, Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits
Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics

items.name: Series RLC circuit: the second-order equation
items.pic: Step the source of a series RLC circuit: the capacitor voltage is simulated live, with R, L and C sliders, and the characteristic roots are plotted in the complex plane beside the waveform.

items.name: Natural frequency and damping ratio
items.pic: Drag the roots in the s-plane: their distance from the origin is ω₀ and the cosine of their angle is ζ; the corresponding R, L, C and step response update together.

items.name: Overdamped, critically damped and underdamped responses
items.pic: Sweep R through the critical value: two real roots merge and split into a complex pair, and the step response changes from sluggish to fastest-without-overshoot to ringing.

items.name: LC tank: undamped oscillation
items.pic: Bar meters for ½CV² and ½LI² trade energy back and forth at twice the oscillation frequency while their sum stays constant; add a little resistance and the total decays.

items.name: Parallel RLC circuit
items.pic: The parallel circuit is the dual of the series one: increasing R reduces damping, and the two circuits are shown side by side with matched responses.

items.name: Electromechanical analogies
items.pic: A mass–spring–damper and a series RLC circuit run in lockstep: mass ↔ inductance, spring compliance ↔ capacitance, damping ↔ resistance, with one parameter panel driving both.

items.name: State variables: capacitor voltages and inductor currents
items.pic: The RLC state (v_C, i_L) moves on a phase plane while the time-domain traces scroll; spirals, nodes and the critically damped case are traced from draggable initial conditions.

items.name: Ringing on digital edges
items.pic: A fast logic edge drives a trace with parasitic inductance and load capacitance: overshoot and ringing appear, and a small series damping resistor tames them.

chapters.title: Storage
chapters.summary: Storage decouples when energy is produced from when it is used. Batteries are electrochemical cells whose voltage comes from reaction free energies, whose usable capacity falls at high discharge rates, and whose life depends on how deeply they are cycled. Pumped hydro, compressed air, flywheels, supercapacitors and hydrogen fill other niches, and the Ragone plot maps them all by energy and power density.

refs: Tester et al., Sustainable Energy: Choosing Among Options
MacKay, Sustainable Energy — Without the Hot Air

items.name: Energy capacity, power capacity and round-trip efficiency
items.pic: Charge and discharge a generic store: its energy rating sets how long it can run and its power rating how fast, and round-trip losses are shaded on the energy flow.

items.name: Cell voltage from free energy: the Nernst equation
items.pic: Vary the state of charge of a cell: the open-circuit voltage computed from ΔG and the Nernst equation drifts with concentration, matching the plateau and tails of a measured discharge curve.

items.name: Battery as a source with internal resistance
items.pic: Draw increasing current from a battery: terminal voltage sags and internal heating grows as I²R, so fast charging and discharging waste a growing fraction of the energy.

items.name: Peukert’s law
items.pic: Discharge a lead-acid battery at different currents: run time falls faster than 1/I, following I^{−k} with a Peukert exponent near 1.2, while lithium-ion cells stay close to k = 1.

items.name: State of charge and C-rate
items.pic: A battery gauge is estimated by coulomb counting; charging at 1C fills it in an hour, at 0.2C in five, and a voltage-based estimate is compared and seen to drift.

items.name: Cycle life and depth of discharge
items.pic: Cycle a cell between different state-of-charge windows: capacity fade per cycle grows with depth, so shallow cycling delivers more total lifetime energy.

items.name: Pumped hydro storage
items.pic: Pump water uphill at night and release it at the evening peak: the stored energy mgh and round-trip efficiency near 75% are computed for a reservoir of chosen size and height.

items.name: Compressed-air storage
items.pic: Compress air into a cavern adiabatically or isothermally: the work stored and the heat lost are compared on a p–V diagram, showing why storing the heat of compression matters.

items.name: Flywheel storage
items.pic: Spin up a flywheel until hoop stress reaches the material’s strength: the maximum energy per kilogram scales with strength over density, ranking steel against carbon fibre.

items.name: Supercapacitors
items.pic: A supercapacitor stores ½CV²: its voltage falls linearly during constant-current discharge, delivering huge power for seconds but little energy compared with a battery of the same mass.

items.name: Hydrogen round trip: electrolysis and fuel cells
items.pic: Follow a kilowatt-hour through an electrolyser, compressor, storage tank and fuel cell: losses at each stage leave about a third, compared with a battery round trip on the same chart.

items.name: The Ragone plot
items.pic: Place storage technologies on log axes of energy density against power density: discharge time is constant along diagonals, and dragging a requirement point shows which technologies qualify.

chapters.title: Beams: internal forces and bending stresses
chapters.summary: A beam carries transverse loads by developing internal shear forces and bending moments, related to the load by two simple differential equations. If plane sections stay plane, bending stress varies linearly across the depth, which explains why I-beams put their material far from the neutral axis. Shear stresses, the shear centre, composite and unsymmetric sections, and plastic hinges complete the picture.

items.name: Shear-force and bending-moment diagrams
items.pic: Drag point loads and distributed loads along a beam: the shear and moment diagrams redraw live, with the maximum moment marked.

items.name: Load, shear and moment: dV/dx = −q, dM/dx = V
items.pic: The area under the load curve between two points equals the jump in shear, and the area under the shear diagram equals the change in moment — both shaded and read out as the points are dragged.

items.name: Plane sections remain plane
items.pic: Bend a rubber beam with a grid drawn on its side: vertical lines stay straight and rotate, so fibres stretch on one side, shorten on the other and keep their length on the neutral axis.

items.name: Flexure formula: σ = −My/I
items.pic: Apply a bending moment: the stress profile across the depth is a straight line through zero at the centroid, and the readout compares the extreme fibre stress with My/I.

items.name: Second moment of area and the parallel-axis theorem
items.pic: Drag rectangles to build a cross-section: the centroid and the second moment of area update live, with each part’s own term and its parallel-axis term shown as stacked bars.

items.name: Section modulus: why I-beams
items.pic: Reshape a fixed amount of material from a square to a tall rectangle to an I-section: the section modulus, and hence bending strength, climbs as material moves away from the neutral axis.

items.name: Shear stress in beams: τ = VQ/Ib
items.pic: Stack planks without glue and they slide over one another when bent; glue them and the shear stress needed to stop the sliding is plotted over the depth, parabolic for a rectangle and concentrated in the web of an I-beam.

items.name: Shear flow in built-up beams
items.pic: Bolt flanges to a web: the shear flow along the joint sets the bolt spacing, which tightens where the shear force is large near the supports.

items.name: Shear centre
items.pic: Load a channel section through its centroid and it twists; slide the load point until the twisting stops, which happens at the shear centre outside the section.

items.name: Composite beams and the transformed section
items.pic: Bond a steel strip to a timber beam: the section is transformed by widening the steel by the modular ratio, the neutral axis shifts toward it, and the stress profile jumps at the interface.

items.name: Unsymmetric bending
items.pic: Bend an angle section with a vertical load: the neutral axis tilts away from horizontal, toward the principal axis of the section, and the beam deflects sideways as well as down.

items.name: Plastic hinges and the shape factor
items.pic: Increase the moment past first yield: the plastic zones grow inward from the outer fibres until the section becomes a hinge; the ratio of plastic to yield moment is 1.5 for a rectangle and about 1.15 for an I-beam.

chapters.title: Dynamics
chapters.summary: Moving a robot quickly takes torques that depend on inertia, gravity and the coupling between joints. The equations of motion can be derived from the Lagrangian or computed recursively link by link with Newton–Euler, and both give the standard form with a configuration-dependent mass matrix. Its structural properties — positive definiteness, passivity — are what make robot control provably stable.

refs: Siciliano et al., Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

items.name: Newton–Euler equations of a single rigid body
items.pic: Apply a wrench to a free rigid body: its twist evolves under the spatial inertia matrix, and with no wrench the angular momentum stays fixed while the body tumbles.

items.name: Equations of motion of an open chain
items.pic: A two-link arm swings under gravity while the terms M(q)q̈, the velocity-product terms and g(q) are plotted separately and summed to the applied torques.

items.name: The mass matrix
items.pic: The kinetic energy of the arm is drawn as an ellipse in joint-velocity space that changes shape with configuration; its matrix stays symmetric positive definite everywhere.

items.name: Skew-symmetry of Ṁ − 2C (passivity)
items.pic: Along any simulated motion, the quantity q̇ᵀ(Ṁ − 2C)q̇ is plotted and stays at zero to numerical precision, while the energy changes only through applied torques.

items.name: Recursive Newton–Euler inverse dynamics
items.pic: Velocities and accelerations propagate outward link by link, then forces and torques propagate back inward — animated as two sweeps — and the joint torques match the Lagrangian result.

items.name: Task-space (operational-space) dynamics
items.pic: Push the end-effector in different directions: the effective inertia felt at the tool is an ellipse that changes with the arm’s posture.

items.name: Gearing and reflected inertia
items.pic: Raise the gear ratio of a joint: the motor’s rotor inertia appears multiplied by the ratio squared, swamping the link inertia and decoupling the joints.

items.name: Coriolis and centripetal coupling between joints
items.pic: Spin the shoulder of a two-link arm quickly with the elbow motor off: the forearm swings outward and lags because of velocity-product torques, plotted live.

items.name: Constrained dynamics
items.pic: Make the end-effector slide along a wall: the constraint force needed is solved at each step and drawn as an arrow normal to the wall, and removing the wall frees the motion.

chapters.title: Stability and control
chapters.summary: An aircraft is statically stable in pitch if a nose-up disturbance produces a nose-down moment, which depends on where the centre of gravity sits relative to the neutral point. Dynamically, its motion splits into a handful of characteristic modes — the slow phugoid, the quick short-period oscillation, the Dutch roll and the spiral — whose eigenvalues pilots feel as handling qualities. Fly-by-wire and aeroelasticity show where control theory and structures meet the airframe.

refs: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students

items.name: Longitudinal static stability
items.pic: Plot pitching moment against angle of attack for the whole aircraft: a negative slope pushes the nose back after a gust, and moving the centre of gravity aft flattens the slope.

items.name: Neutral point and static margin
items.pic: Slide the centre of gravity along the fuselage: the static margin to the neutral point is displayed, and the trimmed aircraft becomes unstable when the centre of gravity passes it.

items.name: Trim and the role of the horizontal tail
items.pic: Adjust tail incidence or elevator angle until the total pitching moment is zero at the desired lift coefficient; the trim point slides along the moment curve.

items.name: The phugoid mode
items.pic: Disturb an aircraft’s speed: it trades altitude and speed back and forth in a long, lightly damped oscillation whose period is close to Lanchester’s π√2 V/g.

items.name: The short-period mode
items.pic: Pulse the elevator: angle of attack and pitch rate respond in a fast, well-damped oscillation, and the linearised model’s eigenvalues are plotted beside the phugoid pair.

items.name: Directional (weathercock) stability
items.pic: Yaw an aircraft with a gust: the vertical fin produces a restoring moment like a weathervane, and shrinking the fin until the yawing-moment slope changes sign makes the aircraft diverge.

items.name: Lateral modes: roll subsidence, spiral and Dutch roll
items.pic: Perturb the lateral motion: the eigenvalues of the lateral equations split into a fast roll mode, a slow spiral mode and an oscillatory Dutch roll, each animated on a model aircraft.

items.name: Dihedral effect
items.pic: Raise the wing dihedral: a sideslip now produces a restoring roll moment, which stabilises the spiral mode but makes the Dutch roll worse, shown by eigenvalues moving as dihedral changes.

items.name: Relaxed static stability and fly-by-wire
items.pic: Move the centre of gravity behind the neutral point to cut trim drag: the bare airframe diverges, but a feedback controller on pitch rate places the closed-loop poles back in the stable region.

items.name: Flutter
items.pic: A wing section with bending and twisting springs sits in an airflow: as speed rises the two modes’ frequencies approach, merge, and a growing oscillation sets in at the flutter speed.

items.name: Some Aeronautical Experiments
items.pic: Fly the Wrights’ glider: twist the wing tips to restore lateral balance instead of shifting the pilot’s body, trim with the forward elevator, and compare the lift actually obtained in a measured wind with the lift promised by Lilienthal’s tables, as Wilbur reported.

paper.title: Some Aeronautical Experiments
paper.venue: Journal of the Western Society of Engineers, December 1901 (address of 18 September 1901)

chapters.title: Externalities, public goods and the commons
chapters.summary: Markets misfire when an action has costs or benefits that no price records. The chapter shows how externalities lead to too much or too little activity, and how corrective taxes, bargaining over clearly assigned property rights, and tradable permits can repair the damage. It then explains why goods that are non-rival or non-excludable, such as lighthouses, fisheries and pastures, tend to be underprovided or overused.

items.name: Externality
items.pic: An upstream mill’s output slider raises a downstream fishery’s losses; the private and social marginal cost curves are drawn and pull apart as an external-damage slider rises.

items.name: Overproduction under a negative externality
items.pic: The market settles where demand meets private cost, beyond the social optimum where demand meets social cost; the deadweight-loss triangle over the excess units is shaded and measured.

items.name: Pigouvian tax
items.pic: Set a per-unit tax: the deadweight loss shrinks to zero exactly when the tax equals marginal damage at the optimum, and overshooting opens a new triangle on the other side.

items.name: Positive externalities and corrective subsidies
items.pic: Vaccination with a spillover slider: social marginal benefit lies above private demand, too few people get vaccinated, and a subsidy equal to the spillover restores the efficient rate.

items.name: Coase theorem
items.pic: A rancher and a farmer bargain over herd size: give the right to either party with a toggle and the bargain lands on the same efficient herd, with payments flowing the opposite way; raise a transaction-cost slider and the outcome starts to depend on who holds the right.

items.name: Efficient pollution abatement
items.pic: Firms with different abatement-cost curves must cut total emissions by a target: a uniform standard is compared with the split that equalizes marginal abatement costs, and the total cost of each is read out.

items.name: Cap-and-trade
items.pic: Two firms share a cap and trade permits until their marginal abatement costs meet: the permit price equals the equivalent Pigouvian tax, and changing the initial allocation of permits changes only who pays whom.

items.name: Public goods and common resources
items.pic: A rivalry-by-excludability grid: drag a good (an apple, a toll road, a fishery, a lighthouse) into a cell and a small simulation tests whether one more user depletes it and whether non-payers can be kept out.

items.name: Samuelson condition for public goods
items.pic: Individual marginal-benefit curves are added vertically for a public good (horizontally for a private good, by toggle); the efficient quantity is where the vertical sum meets marginal cost.

items.name: Free riding
items.pic: A simulated voluntary-contribution game: each of n players gives only until their own marginal benefit equals cost, so total provision falls far below the Samuelson level and the gap widens as the n slider grows.

items.name: Tragedy of the commons
items.pic: Herders keep adding cows to a shared pasture while the average product exceeds a cow’s cost, overshooting the optimum where the marginal product equals cost; the pasture’s rent is plotted falling to zero, and a sole-owner toggle restores the optimum.

items.name: Network externalities
items.pic: Willingness to pay rises with the share of adopters, so the demand curve is hump-shaped; animated adoption from different starting shares collapses to zero or climbs to the high equilibrium, with the critical mass marked.

items.name: Prices vs quantities (Weitzman)
items.pic: Abatement costs are uncertain: draw a cost shock and compare the deadweight loss of a fixed emissions tax with that of a fixed cap; the tax wins when marginal damage is flatter than marginal abatement cost, and tilting the damage curve flips the winner.

items.name: Lindahl equilibrium
items.pic: Two citizens each pay a personal share of the cost of a park: adjust the shares until both demand the same size, and that size satisfies the Samuelson condition; a misreport toggle shows how understating your valuation lowers your share, the free-rider problem in a new form.

items.name: The Problem of Social Cost
items.pic: Coase’s cattle-raiser and farmer: each extra steer tramples more crops (his table: 1, 3, 6 and 10 tons lost for herds of one to four steers); toggle who is liable for the damage and let the two bargain, and the herd size comes out the same either way, until a transaction-cost slider makes bargaining too costly and the legal rule starts to decide the outcome.

paper.title: The Problem of Social Cost

items.name: The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure
items.pic: Two consumers share one public good: their marginal rates of substitution add vertically rather than horizontally, and the efficient quantity sits where the sum equals the marginal rate of transformation; then ask each to report a valuation that sets their tax share and watch the reported sum fall short as each understates, the signalling problem Samuelson flagged.

paper.title: The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure

chapters.title: The open economy in the long run
chapters.summary: In an open economy saving need not equal domestic investment; the gap is the current account. Exchange rates translate prices between countries; over long periods purchasing-power parity holds roughly, and interest-rate differences should be offset by expected currency movements. Both relationships fail in revealing ways — prices of non-traded goods rise with productivity, and high-interest currencies tend not to depreciate as predicted.

items.name: Current account, capital flows and the balance of payments
items.pic: A country’s saving and investment bars with the gap labelled as the current account; editing either one shows the matching capital inflow or outflow.

items.name: Nominal and real exchange rates
items.pic: Convert a basket priced in two currencies: the real exchange rate moves with the nominal rate and with relative inflation, with historical pairs plotted.

items.name: Purchasing-power parity
items.pic: Big Mac prices converted at market exchange rates; deviations from parity are large, and a long-run panel shows them shrinking only slowly over decades.

items.name: Uncovered interest parity
items.pic: Invest at home or abroad without hedging: the interest differential must equal expected depreciation; enter rates and an expected exchange-rate path to check.

items.name: The forward-premium puzzle and the carry trade
items.pic: Regress realized depreciation on interest differentials: the slope is near zero or negative instead of one, and a carry-trade strategy earns steady profits punctuated by crashes.

items.name: The small open economy with perfect capital mobility
items.pic: The world interest rate fixes investment; a domestic fiscal expansion now crowds out net exports instead of investment, shown in linked saving–investment and exchange-rate panels.

items.name: The Balassa–Samuelson effect
items.pic: Price levels against income per head across countries slope upward: productivity growth in traded goods raises wages and the prices of non-traded services, explained in a two-sector model.

chapters.title: Options: payoffs and parity
chapters.summary: Options give the right but not the obligation to buy or sell, so their payoffs are kinked. Without any model of the stock price, arbitrage alone pins down a great deal: put–call parity, price bounds, convexity in the strike, and the fact that an American call on a non-dividend stock should never be exercised early. Combinations of options build almost any payoff shape, and option prices across strikes reveal the market’s risk-neutral distribution.

refs: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives

items.name: Calls and puts: payoffs and profits
items.pic: Drag the strike and premium; hockey-stick payoff and profit diagrams for long and short calls and puts update, with breakeven points marked.

items.name: Put–call parity
items.pic: Stack a call and a bond on one diagram and a put and the stock on another: the payoff lines coincide for every terminal price, so C + Ke^{−rT} = P + S.

items.name: Arbitrage bounds on option prices
items.pic: The band between max(S − Ke^{−rT}, 0) and S where any call price must lie; enter a price outside the band and the page produces the arbitrage.

items.name: Never exercise an American call early (no dividends)
items.pic: Compare exercising now (S − K) with the call’s lower bound S − Ke^{−rT}: the bound is always higher before expiry, and adding a dividend creates an early-exercise region.

items.name: Option prices are convex in the strike
items.pic: Plot call prices against strike; a butterfly spread’s cost is a second difference that must be non-negative, and a dented price curve produces a free butterfly.

items.name: Option strategies: spreads, straddles, butterflies
items.pic: Build a position from a palette of calls, puts and stock; its payoff diagram is the sum of the pieces, and named strategies can be loaded and edited.

items.name: Breeden–Litzenberger: densities from option prices
items.pic: Take the second derivative of call prices with respect to strike; the risk-neutral density appears, and market prices with a skew give a left-skewed density.

items.name: Protective puts and portfolio insurance
items.pic: Stock plus put gives a floor; simulated return distributions with and without the put show the cost of the insurance as a shifted, truncated histogram.

items.name: Equity as a call on the firm (Merton)
items.pic: Firm assets evolve randomly; equity holders get max(V − D, 0) at maturity, so equity is a call and debt a risk-free bond minus a put, with the implied default probability read off.

chapters.title: Evolution, learning and congestion
chapters.summary: Evolutionary game theory replaces rational players with populations whose strategies spread according to payoff. An evolutionarily stable strategy resists invasion by rare mutants; under replicator dynamics such strategies are stable rest points and stable rest points are Nash equilibria, while Rock–Paper–Scissors cycles. In finite noisy populations, fixation probabilities and stochastic stability select among equilibria. Potential and congestion games always have pure equilibria reached by best-response dynamics, but selfish routing can be inefficient — Braess’s paradox and the price of anarchy quantify how much.

refs: Osborne, An Introduction to Game Theory

items.name: Evolutionarily stable strategy
items.pic: Inject a small fraction of mutants playing another strategy into a population; the incumbent is stable if it earns more against the mix, checked for every mutant on a slider of invasion sizes.

items.name: Hawk–Dove game
items.pic: Vary the value of the resource V and the cost of fighting C; the stable proportion of hawks V/C is computed and reached by a simulated population.

items.name: ESS and Nash equilibrium
items.pic: For random symmetric games, all symmetric equilibria are listed and tested for evolutionary stability: every ESS is an equilibrium, every strict equilibrium is an ESS, and some games have no ESS at all.

items.name: Replicator dynamics
items.pic: Strategy shares on the simplex flow in proportion to their payoff advantage; the vector field and trajectories are drawn for a chosen 3 × 3 game.

items.name: ESS are asymptotically stable under the replicator dynamics
items.pic: The relative entropy from an ESS to the current state is plotted along trajectories; it decreases steadily, acting as a Lyapunov function, and fails to for non-ESS equilibria.

items.name: Rock–Paper–Scissors cycles
items.pic: Tune the win and loss payoffs of Rock–Paper–Scissors; replicator trajectories spiral inward, cycle on closed orbits or spiral out to the boundary, as for side-blotched lizards.

items.name: Fixation probabilities in finite populations
items.pic: Run a frequency-dependent Moran process for a 2 × 2 game in a population of N; the probability that one mutant takes over is compared with the neutral value 1/N to decide whether selection favours it.

items.name: Stochastic stability selects the risk-dominant equilibrium
items.pic: Players best-respond with rare mistakes in a Stag Hunt; the long-run time fractions concentrate on the risk-dominant convention as the mistake rate goes to 0, matching the stationary distribution of the perturbed chain.

items.name: Potential games and best-response dynamics
items.pic: For a game with an exact potential, each improving move raises the potential, drawn as a height map; best-response dynamics climb it and stop at a pure equilibrium.

items.name: Rosenthal: congestion games have pure equilibria
items.pic: Players choose routes whose costs depend on usage; Rosenthal’s potential is computed and decreases with every selfish switch until no one can improve.

items.name: Braess’s paradox
items.pic: Add a zero-cost shortcut to a road network carrying selfish traffic; at the new Wardrop equilibrium everyone’s travel time rises, and deleting the road restores the better outcome.

items.name: Price of anarchy for selfish routing is 4/3
items.pic: For networks with linear latencies, the cost of the selfish equilibrium is divided by the optimal cost; random instances never exceed 4/3, and Pigou’s two-link example attains it.

chapters.title: Well-being and the two selves
chapters.summary: The experiencing self lives through moments; the remembering self keeps score and makes decisions, and it judges episodes by their peak and their end while largely ignoring duration. People also adapt to good and bad fortune more than they expect. How income relates to happiness — a satiation point, a log-linear relation, or national averages that do not rise at all — has been fought over with ever larger data sets.

refs: Wilkinson & Klaes, An Introduction to Behavioral Economics

items.name: Experienced versus remembered utility
items.pic: Draw a moment-by-moment pain curve for an episode; its area (experienced utility) is compared with the retrospective rating predicted from the curve’s shape.

items.name: The peak–end rule
items.pic: Two colonoscopy-style pain profiles: the longer one with a gentler end has more total pain but a better remembered rating, computed as the average of peak and end.

items.name: Duration neglect (the cold-hand experiment)
items.pic: Sixty seconds in cold water versus ninety seconds with a slightly warmer last thirty: most participants choose to repeat the longer trial, and the area and peak–end readouts show why.

items.name: Hedonic adaptation
items.pic: Life satisfaction around marriage, widowhood and disability from panel data: some events show return to baseline, others lasting shifts, unlike the strong set-point claim.

items.name: The focusing illusion
items.pic: Rate how happy Californians are compared with Midwesterners, then see the survey data showing almost no difference; asking about weather first exaggerates the gap.

items.name: Affective forecasting and the impact bias
items.pic: Predicted versus actual happiness after tenure decisions or elections: forecasts overshoot in both directions and the bars show how quickly the actual gap closes.

items.name: The Easterlin paradox (contested)
items.pic: Within a country richer people are happier, but national average happiness over decades is flat in some series; toggling in more countries and years (Stevenson–Wolfers) restores a log-income slope.

items.name: Income and well-being: satiation or log-linear?
items.pic: Emotional well-being against log income from the 2010 and 2021 studies and their 2023 adversarial collaboration: the plateau appears only for the least happy group.

chapters.title: Organization, depth and size
chapters.summary: Before we recognise objects we must group features and separate figure from ground; the Gestalt laws describe the grouping cues the visual system uses, and bistable figures show those choices flipping. Depth comes from binocular disparity and from pictorial cues, and the depth we infer feeds back into the size we perceive, which is the root of several famous illusions. Modern accounts treat this as probabilistic inference that weights each cue by its reliability.

refs: Macmillan & Creelman, Detection Theory: A User’s Guide

items.name: Figure–ground segregation
items.pic: Rubin’s vase with adjustable border shape, contrast and symmetry: report which region looks like the figure and see how convexity and smallness tip the balance.

items.name: Gestalt grouping by proximity
items.pic: A dot lattice whose row and column spacings you drag; the perceived grouping flips from rows to columns as the spacing ratio crosses about one.

items.name: Grouping by similarity
items.pic: Pit colour similarity against proximity in the same lattice; sliders for colour difference and spacing locate the point where the two cues balance.

items.name: Good continuation and contour integration
items.pic: A path of aligned Gabor patches hidden among random ones pops out; jitter the orientations and watch the path dissolve at a measurable angle.

items.name: Closure and illusory contours
items.pic: Pac-man inducers create a Kanizsa triangle; rotate the inducers out of alignment and the bright illusory edges vanish.

items.name: Common fate
items.pic: A field of random dots in which a subset moves coherently; the moving subset groups into a shape, and a coherence slider finds your threshold for seeing it.

items.name: Bistable perception: the Necker cube
items.pic: Press a key whenever the cube flips; your dominance durations form a skewed histogram, and adding shading cues biases one interpretation.

items.name: Binocular disparity and stereopsis
items.pic: A top-down view of two eyes fixating a point; drag objects nearer or farther and their images shift on the two retinas by the computed disparity, with the horopter drawn.

items.name: Random-dot stereograms (Julesz)
items.pic: Generate a random-dot stereogram from a depth map you draw; with free fusion or red–cyan glasses a hidden shape floats out, though neither image contains it.

items.name: Monocular depth cues
items.pic: Toggle occlusion, relative size, texture gradient, height in the field and motion parallax one at a time in a 3D scene and rate how deep it looks.

items.name: Size constancy and Emmert’s law
items.pic: Project an afterimage onto surfaces at different distances: its perceived size scales with distance while its retinal size is fixed, as the computed size–distance relation shows.

items.name: Müller-Lyer illusion
items.pic: Adjust a shaft until it matches a fins-in shaft; your error is measured as fin angle and length vary, and the depth (“carpentered world”) explanation is shown alongside its contested cross-cultural evidence.

items.name: Ponzo illusion
items.pic: Two equal bars between converging rails; remove the rails or the texture and the illusion shrinks, measured with a matching slider.

items.name: Ebbinghaus (Titchener) circles
items.pic: A central disc ringed by large or small discs; drag the inducers’ size and distance and match the centre to record how size contrast distorts it.

items.name: The Ames room
items.pic: A top view and the peephole view of a trapezoidal room: people walking along the back wall seem to grow and shrink, and the top view shows the real distances.

items.name: The moon illusion
items.pic: The moon’s angular size is constant (measured by a ruler overlay) while its perceived size changes from horizon to zenith; compare the apparent-distance and angular-size-contrast explanations.

items.name: Bayesian cue combination (Ernst–Banks)
items.pic: Visual and haptic estimates of a bar’s height with adjustable noise: the combined estimate lands at the reliability-weighted average and its variance is smaller than either cue’s.

chapters.title: Conformity, opinion dynamics and synchrony
chapters.summary: People conform to visible majorities, and simple models of opinion change reproduce consensus, persistent disagreement or polarization depending on whom people are willing to listen to. Whether online networks create echo chambers is an empirical question with mixed answers. Collective rhythm — clapping audiences, flashing fireflies — is another kind of coordination, explained by coupled oscillators.

refs: Easley & Kleinberg, Networks, Crowds, and Markets (free online)

items.name: Asch’s conformity experiment
items.pic: Judge line lengths after hearing several confederates give the same wrong answer; your conformity is compared with the original rates and with the effect of a single dissenter.

items.name: The voter model
items.pic: Each step a random person copies a random neighbour’s opinion; on a lattice domains coarsen slowly, and the probability that an opinion wins equals its initial share.

items.name: Bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
items.pic: People average only with those within a confidence bound ε; opinions over time split into one, two or several clusters as you vary ε (Hegselmann–Krause).

items.name: Axelrod’s culture model
items.pic: Neighbours who share some cultural traits interact and become more alike; the grid freezes into regions, and the number of surviving cultures depends on traits and features.

items.name: Echo chambers and polarization (mixed evidence)
items.pic: A bounded-confidence model with an unfollow rule produces separated clusters; beside it, survey and platform studies that find much more cross-cutting exposure than the model implies.

items.name: Pluralistic ignorance
items.pic: Everyone privately dislikes a norm but believes others support it; a threshold model with public versus private opinions shows the norm persisting until a few defections tip it.

items.name: Synchronized clapping and fireflies
items.pic: A population of clappers as coupled oscillators: raise the coupling past the critical value and the order parameter jumps, as in audiences that fall into unison.

items.name: Studies of Independence and Conformity
items.pic: Asch’s line-judgment task: match a standard line to one of three comparison lines after a group of confederates has answered unanimously and wrongly on 12 of 18 trials; his 123 subjects went along on 36.8% of those trials, against errors under 1% when judging alone, and about a quarter never yielded; take the test against a simulated majority, then give yourself one dissenting partner and watch yielding collapse.

paper.title: Studies of Independence and Conformity: I. A Minority of One against a Unanimous Majority

chapters.title: Weighted voting and power
chapters.summary: In councils where members cast different numbers of votes, voting weight is a poor guide to influence. Power indices measure how often a member is pivotal or critical in forming winning coalitions: Shapley–Shubik counts orderings, Banzhaf counts swings. They reveal members with weight but no power, and justify Penrose’s square-root rule for fair weights in two-tier systems.

items.name: Yes–no voting systems and weighted voting
items.pic: Set weights and a quota; every subset of voters is listed as winning or losing, with minimal winning coalitions highlighted.

items.name: Trade robustness characterizes weighted systems
items.pic: Enter a voting system as a list of winning coalitions (e.g. the U.S. federal system); the page searches for a trade among winning coalitions that makes both losing, proving no weights exist.

items.name: Shapley–Shubik power index
items.pic: All orderings of voters are enumerated (or sampled); the pivotal voter in each ordering is coloured, and each member’s share of pivots is its index.

items.name: Banzhaf power index
items.pic: For every winning coalition, members whose departure would make it lose are marked critical; the normalised counts give the Banzhaf index, compared with Shapley–Shubik.

items.name: Weight is not power: the 1958 EEC Council
items.pic: Weights 4, 4, 4, 2, 2, 1 with quota 12: Luxembourg’s single vote is never critical, so its power is exactly zero, and you can search for the quota that would give it power.

items.name: Penrose’s square-root law
items.pic: Two-tier voting where each country’s delegate follows its citizens’ majority: giving delegates weights proportional to √population equalizes each citizen’s Banzhaf power, checked numerically.

items.name: The power of the U.S. president
items.pic: Model the House, Senate, president and veto override as a yes–no system; the president’s Shapley–Shubik share (a few percent) is compared with a single senator’s and representative’s.

items.name: Voter power in the Electoral College
items.pic: Compute the Banzhaf power of a voter in each state under winner-take-all: large states give their voters more power per head, the opposite of the usual small-state claim.

items.name: Minimal winning coalitions and Gamson’s law
items.pic: Parties with seat counts form governments: Riker’s minimal-winning prediction lists candidate coalitions, and cabinet portfolios in real coalitions are plotted against seat shares.

items.name: The paradox of new members
items.pic: Add a new member to a weighted council and recompute: some existing members’ power indices rise, even though the total is now shared among more players.

items.name: A Method for Evaluating the Distribution of Power
items.pic: Voters line up in random order and the one whose vote first makes the coalition winning is pivotal: animate the orderings for a weighted body you edit, count pivots, and reproduce the paper’s examples, the United Nations Security Council, where the five permanent members’ vetoes hold nearly all the power, and the President, Senate and House passing a bill.

paper.authors: L. S. Shapley and Martin Shubik
paper.title: A Method for Evaluating the Distribution of Power in a Committee System

chapters.title: Stable and stationary populations
chapters.summary: If age-specific rates stay fixed, any closed population settles into a stable state with constant growth rate r and a fixed age distribution — Lotka’s result, which lets demographers infer a population’s structure from its rates alone. A stable population’s age pyramid depends far more on fertility than on mortality. The stationary population (r = 0) links births, deaths and life expectancy by simple identities, and later work relaxed stability to variable rates.

refs: Preston, Heuveline & Guillot, Demography: Measuring and Modeling Population Processes

items.name: The stable population model
items.pic: Under constant rates the projected pyramid stops changing shape and just scales; a toggle overlays the analytic stable distribution on the projected one.

items.name: Lotka’s intrinsic growth rate from a life table
items.pic: Plot ∫ e^{−ra} l(a) m(a) da against r for a real human schedule; the curve falls monotonically and crosses one at a unique r, read off live as you edit fertility.

items.name: r ≈ ln(NRR) / T for human populations
items.pic: Scatter the exact r against ln NRR / T for every country’s schedule; points hug the diagonal, and the error grows only for very high fertility.

items.name: The stable age distribution c(a) = b e^{−ra} l(a)
items.pic: Build the stable pyramid from a survival curve and r; raising r tilts the pyramid into a wide-based triangle, lowering it below zero inverts the top.

items.name: Fertility, not mortality, shapes the age pyramid (Coale)
items.pic: Change fertility and mortality separately in a stable population: lowering mortality barely changes the mean age (it saves the young as much as the old), while lowering fertility ages the population sharply.

items.name: Stationary-population identities: b = d = 1/e₀
items.pic: Set r = 0 and see the pyramid become the survival curve on its side; the crude birth and death rates both equal 1/e₀, and the mean age of the living matches its formula.

items.name: Lotka’s renewal equation and convergence to stability
items.pic: Births computed from the renewal equation oscillate in damped waves of generation length before settling on e^{rt}; the complex roots that govern the waves are plotted in the plane.

items.name: Variable-r relations (Preston–Coale)
items.pic: For a non-stable population, compute age-specific growth rates from two censuses; the generalized formula c(a) = b exp(−∫₀ᵃ r(x)dx) l(a) reproduces the observed age distribution exactly.

items.name: Weak ergodicity under changing rates
items.pic: Two different starting pyramids subjected to the same sequence of time-varying rates converge toward each other, though neither settles into a fixed shape.

items.name: The two-sex problem
items.pic: Male- and female-based projections of the same population disagree on r; a marriage-squeeze slider shows how a harmonic-mean pairing function reconciles them.

items.name: A Problem in Age-Distribution
items.pic: Start a population from any age pyramid with fixed age-specific fertility and survival: births oscillate in dying waves while the age distribution converges to the stable shape c(a) = b e^(−ra) l(a), with r the real root of their characteristic equation; edit the starting pyramid to see that the destination does not depend on it.

paper.authors: F. R. Sharpe and Alfred J. Lotka
paper.title: A Problem in Age-Distribution

items.name: How the Age Distribution of a Human Population Is Determined
items.pic: Two sliders, fertility and mortality, drive a stable population’s pyramid: raising fertility turns it from a column into a broad triangle, while lowering mortality, which mostly saves infants and children, barely changes its shape and can even make the population younger; compare the stable pyramids with observed ones from the 1950s.

paper.title: How the Age Distribution of a Human Population Is Determined
paper.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology 22: 83–89

chapters.title: Rhythm and meter
chapters.summary: Rhythm organizes sound in time much as scales organize it in pitch. A steady pulse grouped hierarchically becomes meter, and rhythms laid around a repeating cycle become necklaces whose evenness, oddity and syncopation can be measured. Polyrhythms turn out to be frequency ratios slowed below the threshold of pitch, Euclid’s algorithm generates many of the world’s timelines, and groove lives in small, systematic departures from the grid.

refs: Benson, Music: A Mathematical Offering (free online)
Rossing, Moore & Wheeler, The Science of Sound
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm

items.name: Pulse and tempo
items.pic: Tap along with a click and see your tempo and its stability plotted live; slide the click from 30 to 300 bpm and feel where a pulse stops being a beat, too slow to connect or too fast to follow.

items.name: Meter as a hierarchy of beats
items.pic: A dot grid of metrical levels (subdivision, beat, bar) for 3/4, 4/4, 6/8 and 12/8: switch meters and hear the same pulse train accented differently, with each onset’s metrical weight drawn as a column of dots.

items.name: Rhythms as necklaces
items.pic: A cyclic rhythm drawn as onsets around a circle of n steps with a sweeping playhead; rotate the necklace to hear the pattern start elsewhere, and click steps to add or remove onsets.

items.name: Polyrhythm as a frequency ratio
items.pic: Two click trains in the ratio 3:2 (or 4:3, 5:4) speed up continuously, and once they pass about 20 clicks per second the polyrhythm turns into a sustained fifth (fourth, major third) that you hear and see in the spectrum.

items.name: Euclidean rhythms (Bjorklund’s algorithm)
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: Choose k onsets among n steps and step through Euclid’s remainder algorithm as it spreads them out: the tresillo E(3,8), the cinquillo E(5,8) and other timelines emerge, each looping audibly and matching the maximally even pattern.

items.name: The rhythmic oddity property
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: A timeline on a 12- or 16-step necklace with its diameters drawn: the property holds when no two onsets split the cycle into equal halves, a checker lights as you drag onsets, and Central African timelines pass while many others fail.

items.name: Measuring syncopation
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: A rhythm on a metrical-weight grid scores a Longuet-Higgins–Lee syncopation wherever a note on a weak position is followed by silence on a stronger one; drag onsets or rotate the clave and watch the score track the felt off-beatness.

items.name: Swing and microtiming
items.pic: A drum loop with a swing slider from straight 1:1 through triplet 2:1 to dotted 3:1 and a separate microtiming-jitter control; hear the groove change and see each onset’s deviation from the grid plotted.

items.name: Tempo estimation by autocorrelation
items.pic: The onset-strength signal of a drum recording and its autocorrelation: peaks at the beat period and its multiples appear, the tracker picks one, and a click locked to the estimate plays over the loop, half- and double-tempo mistakes included.

items.name: Additive meters and aksak rhythms
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: Group a fast pulse into cells such as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+2+2+3, drawn as long and short beats on a necklace and played with accents, and compare 2+2+3 with the Euclidean rhythm E(3,7).

items.name: Phasing: rhythmic beats
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: Two copies of one pattern loop at slightly different tempi and drift through every rotation against each other, as in Steve Reich’s phase pieces; slide the tempo difference and watch the phase offset grow like the phase between beating tones.

items.name: Hypermeter
items.pic: Extra rows of metrical dots group whole bars into 2-, 4- and 8-bar hypermeasures above a melody; insert or delete a bar and watch the hypermetric count shift until a strong bar lands where a weak one should be, and hear the phrase stretch or stumble.

items.name: Hemiola
refs: Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm
items.pic: Six beats heard as two bars of 3/4 or regrouped as three groups of two (one bar of 3/2): switch the accents at a cadence and hear the meter broaden, with the dot grid redrawing its strong beats and the 3:2 ratio of the two groupings displayed.

chapters.title: Contrast, constancy and colour appearance
chapters.summary: The colour you see depends on its surroundings. Lateral inhibition sharpens edges and pushes neighbouring colours apart, while thin patterns blend with their neighbours instead; Albers built a whole course on making one colour look like two. Above all the visual system discounts the illuminant, which keeps a lemon yellow at dawn and noon — and occasionally splits the internet over the colours of a dress.

refs: Conway, Burgiel & Goodman-Strauss, The Symmetries of Things

items.name: Lateral inhibition and centre–surround cells
items.pic: Convolve an image with a difference-of-Gaussians receptive field whose surround strength you set: edges brighten and darken in the response map.

items.name: Mach bands
items.pic: A luminance ramp between two plateaus shows illusory light and dark stripes at the knees; the computed centre–surround response reproduces them, and they vanish if the surround weight is zero.

items.name: Simultaneous contrast (Chevreul)
items.pic: Two identical grey squares on different surrounds look different; drag one square across the boundary to prove they are the same, and change surround hue to tint the grey.

items.name: Albers: one colour as two, two as one
items.pic: Albers’ exercise: choose two grounds that make one ochre look like two different colours, then find grounds that make two different colours match; the CIELAB values are shown.

items.name: Bezold spreading (assimilation)
items.pic: Interleave thin black or white lines with a red field: thin lines pull the red toward themselves while thick ones push it away; a width slider finds the crossover.

items.name: Chromatic adaptation and colour constancy
items.pic: Render a still life under candlelight, daylight and shade: raw pixel colours change drastically while adapted colours stay put.

items.name: The von Kries adaptation transform
items.pic: Scale L, M and S independently so the scene’s white becomes white: apply it to a photo shot under the wrong white balance and read the error before and after.

items.name: Land’s retinex and Mondrian experiments
items.pic: Land’s colour Mondrian under three adjustable projectors: two patches sending identical light to the eye still look red and green, and retinex ratios across edges predict the names.

items.name: The dress: illuminant ambiguity
items.pic: Assume a bluish shadow or a warm light and discount it: the same photo pixels resolve as white-gold or blue-black, with the assumed illuminant on a slider.

items.name: Hue shifts with luminance and purity (Bezold–Brücke, Abney)
items.pic: Raise the intensity of a fixed-wavelength light and its hue drifts toward blue or yellow; add white and it bends along the curved Abney lines plotted in xy.

items.name: Helmholtz–Kohlrausch: saturated colours look brighter
items.pic: A saturated red and a grey of equal luminance: adjust the grey until they look equally bright and read how far above the photometric match you landed.

items.name: Lightness illusions: the checker-shadow
items.pic: Adelson’s checkerboard: squares A and B have the same pixel value; drag a connecting bar to see it, and remove the cylinder’s shadow to dissolve the illusion.

items.name: Equiluminance: when colour loses depth and motion
items.pic: Tune a red–green pattern until the two have equal luminance: edges shimmer, depth cues flatten and drift slows, as Livingstone traced to the luminance pathway.

items.name: De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs
items.pic: Chevreul’s demonstration: two strips of different colours laid side by side each shift, along their shared edge, toward the complement of the other; the reader picks the pair, sees the shift predicted on a colour circle as the neighbour’s complement added, masks the border to reveal the true colours, and lays out a tapestry-like pattern to see why the Gobelins dyes looked wrong in context.

paper.title: De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs

chapters.title: Shells, membranes and form-finding
chapters.summary: Thin curved surfaces carry load through their shape, not their thickness, which lets a few centimetres of concrete span tens of metres. Saddle surfaces such as the hyperbolic paraboloid are both easy to build from straight lines and stiff; tensile membranes and cable nets must be anticlastic to stay taut. Because good shapes are hard to guess, designers from Gaudí to Frei Otto found them with hanging models and soap films, and engineers now do the same with computers.

items.name: Shells: strength from curvature
items.pic: Load a flat plate and a curved shell of the same thickness: the plate bends far more, while the shell carries the load by in-plane membrane forces.

items.name: The hyperbolic paraboloid
items.pic: Sweep a straight line along two skew lines to generate a hypar; rotate it to see both rulings and the arch and cable directions, as in Candela’s shells.

items.name: Anticlastic surfaces and tensile membranes
items.pic: Pretension a fabric between masts and anchors: only surfaces curving opposite ways in two directions stay taut, and a flat region flutters in the wind simulation.

items.name: Minimal surfaces and soap-film models
items.pic: Stretch a simulated soap film between draggable wire frames: it relaxes to zero mean curvature, reproducing the forms Frei Otto used for the Munich Olympic roofs.

items.name: Hanging models (Gaudí, Isler)
items.pic: Hang a net of strings with weights, as Gaudí did for the Colònia Güell, then invert it: the resulting vault is compression-only under the modelled loads.

items.name: Force-density method for cable nets
items.pic: Set a force-to-length ratio on each cable of a net and solve the linear system: changing densities reshapes the net, with equilibrium residuals shown at every node.

items.name: Dynamic relaxation
items.pic: Start a gridshell or membrane from a flat mesh and let pseudo-dynamics with damping settle it into equilibrium, with the kinetic-energy trace dropping to zero.

items.name: Gridshells
items.pic: Lift a flat lattice of timber laths into a doubly curved shell, as at Mannheim (1975): the lattice shears to fit, and bracing makes it stiff.

items.name: Tensegrity
items.pic: A three-strut tensegrity prism: struts float without touching, held by cables; slacken one cable and the structure collapses, tighten it and pretension stiffens it.

items.name: Pneumatic structures and the Laplace–Young relation
items.pic: Inflate a membrane over a span: internal pressure balances tension times curvature, Δp = T(1/R₁ + 1/R₂), and lowering pressure lets snow load dent the roof.

items.name: Thinness of shells: span-to-thickness ratios
items.pic: Compare span-to-thickness ratios of the Pantheon, a Candela hypar, an Isler shell and an eggshell; the buckling knockdown factor sets how thin each can safely be.

chapters.title: Meaning: semantics and pragmatics
chapters.summary: The meaning of a sentence is computed from the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined, and can be modelled as the conditions under which it is true. Quantifiers, scope and presupposition show how much structure that computation needs. Much of what we communicate is not said but implied, through Grice’s maxims of cooperative conversation, and many utterances are actions rather than descriptions.

refs: Fromkin, Rodman & Hyams, An Introduction to Language
Ladefoged & Johnson, A Course in Phonetics
Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (free draft)

items.name: Sense and reference (Frege)
items.pic: “The morning star” and “the evening star” point to the same planet on a sky diagram but through different descriptions; substituting them in belief reports changes truth values.

items.name: Compositionality
items.pic: Click nodes of a syntax tree to see the meaning computed bottom-up, each node combining its daughters’ meanings by function application.

items.name: Truth conditions and models
items.pic: A small world of shapes and colours that the reader edits: sentences such as “every red square is big” are evaluated true or false live.

items.name: Generalised quantifiers
items.pic: Venn diagrams of A and B with draggable counts: “every”, “some”, “no”, “most”, “exactly three” are evaluated as relations between sets, and conservativity is checked.

items.name: Scope ambiguity
items.pic: “Every student read a book”: two logical forms are computed, and a model where only one is true is constructed to tell them apart.

items.name: Entailment and presupposition
items.pic: Apply negation, questioning and “if” to “John stopped smoking”: the entailment that he doesn’t smoke now disappears, while the presupposition that he used to survives.

items.name: Grice’s cooperative principle and maxims
items.pic: Dialogue snippets with replies that obey or flout quantity, quality, relation and manner; tag each and see what the hearer infers.

items.name: Scalar implicature
items.pic: On a scale some < most < all, “some” implicates “not all”; then cancel it (“some, in fact all”), which a true entailment would not allow.

items.name: Speech acts and performatives (Austin, Searle)
items.pic: Classify utterances (“I promise…”, “Can you pass the salt?”) by force; the “hereby” test and felicity conditions are checked one by one.

items.name: Deixis and indexicals
items.pic: The same sentence “I’m here now” uttered by different speakers at different places and times maps to different propositions on a timeline map.

items.name: Prototypes and fuzzy categories (Rosch)
items.pic: Rate how good an example of “bird” a robin, penguin and ostrich are; ratings and reaction times show graded membership rather than a crisp definition.

items.name: Basic colour terms (Berlin and Kay)
items.pic: A Munsell chip array: map colour-term foci of languages with 2 to 11 terms, which cluster around shared focal colours in the World Color Survey order.

items.name: Distributional semantics and word vectors
items.pic: Build co-occurrence vectors from a pasted text, reduce them to 2-D and see semantically similar words cluster; cosine similarities appear on hover.

items.name: Vagueness in natural-language predicates
items.pic: Collect judgements of “tall” for heights from 150 to 200 cm: the acceptance curve is a smooth sigmoid, with no sharp cut-off to be found.

items.name: Cours de linguistique générale
items.pic: Saussure’s sign and its value: each word is a card joining a sound-image to a concept, and its value is set by its neighbours; the reader removes or adds words in a small field (English sheep and mutton against French mouton, the kinship or colour terms of two languages) and watches the remaining words’ territories grow or shrink, then switches between the synchronic slice and the diachronic axis of the same system.

paper.title: Cours de linguistique générale
paper.venue: ed. Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye; Lausanne and Paris: Payot, 1916

items.name: Über Sinn und Bedeutung (On Sense and Reference)
items.pic: Frege’s puzzle as a diagram of names, senses and referents: the reader builds “the Morning Star is the Evening Star”, sees both senses lead to Venus so the identity is true yet informative, swaps co-referring names inside “believes that …” and watches the truth value change, and tests a sentence with an empty name (Odysseus), which has a sense but no truth value, the seed of presupposition.

paper.title: Über Sinn und Bedeutung
paper.venue: Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik 100: 25–50

chapters.title: Bayesian epistemology
chapters.summary: Bayesians model belief as probability and learning as conditionalisation. Dutch-book arguments claim that degrees of belief violating the probability axioms expose one to sure loss, and Bayes’ theorem gives a precise account of when evidence confirms a hypothesis and by how much. The approach explains the base-rate fallacy, but faces problems of its own, including old evidence and the paradoxes of the lottery and the preface.

refs: Resnik, Choices: An Introduction to Decision Theory

items.name: Interpretations of probability
items.pic: One coin, three readings: a long-run frequency plot, a propensity of the setup, and a betting rate; the tool shows where they agree and where they come apart.

items.name: Bayes’ theorem
items.pic: A unit square split by hypothesis and evidence with draggable proportions: the posterior is the shaded fraction of the evidence column, computed live.

items.name: The base-rate fallacy
items.pic: A test 99% accurate for a disease with 1-in-1000 prevalence: a crowd of 10,000 icons shows that most positives are false, and the prevalence slider changes that.

items.name: Dutch-book argument for probabilism
items.pic: Enter credences in A and not-A that sum to more than 1: the bookie constructs bets you would accept at those rates and shows a guaranteed loss in every world.

items.name: Conditionalisation
items.pic: Learn evidence E and zero out the worlds where it fails; renormalising the rest gives the new credence, and a diachronic Dutch book is built against any other update rule.

items.name: Confirmation as probability raising
items.pic: Pick a hypothesis and an evidence pattern: confirmation is shown as the jump from prior to posterior, and different measures of its size are compared.

items.name: Likelihood ratios and the weight of evidence
items.pic: Feed in evidence items one by one: log-odds move by the log likelihood ratio of each, and items with a ratio of 1 leave belief untouched however suggestive they seem.

items.name: Washing out of the priors
items.pic: Two agents with very different priors about a coin’s bias watch the same flips: their posteriors merge as data accumulate, with the gap plotted against sample size.

items.name: The problem of old evidence
items.pic: Mercury’s perihelion was known before general relativity: if P(E) = 1 already, conditionalising changes nothing, shown on the probability square collapsing to one column.

items.name: The lottery paradox
items.pic: In a fair 1000-ticket lottery, believe of each ticket that it will lose (probability 0.999); the conjunction of those beliefs contradicts the certainty that one ticket wins.

items.name: The preface paradox
items.pic: An author believes each of 300 claims at 99%: the probability that all are true is computed as about 5%, so the preface’s admission of error is rational.

chapters.title: Steam, iron and the Industrial Revolution
chapters.summary: The first steam engines used atmospheric pressure to pump water from mines. Watt’s separate condenser cut their fuel use dramatically, and rotary motion and governors put them to work driving factories. Cheap coke-smelted iron, precision boring and machine tools made bigger and better engines possible, while engineers’ indicator diagrams and Carnot’s analysis began the science of heat engines.

refs: Cardwell, Wheels, Clocks, and Rockets: A History of Technology
Usher, A History of Mechanical Inventions

items.name: Savery’s and Papin’s steam devices
items.pic: Condense steam in a closed vessel: the pressure drop sucks water up, limited to about 10 m by the atmosphere; Papin’s cylinder raises a weight with a piston.

items.name: The Newcomen atmospheric engine
items.pic: Cycle a Newcomen engine: steam fills the cylinder, a cold jet condenses it, and atmospheric pressure drives the piston down to rock the beam and pump; heat wasted reheating the cylinder is tallied.

items.name: Coke smelting of iron (Darby)
items.pic: Replace charcoal with coke in a blast furnace: fuel cost per tonne and the forest area saved are computed, and furnace size can grow.

items.name: The cylinder-boring machine (Wilkinson)
items.pic: Bore a cylinder with the cutter supported at both ends: the out-of-roundness falls from a shilling’s thickness to a fraction of it, and steam leakage past the piston drops accordingly.

items.name: Watt’s separate condenser
items.pic: Toggle between condensing in the cylinder and in a separate cold vessel: the cylinder stays hot, and coal per unit of work falls by roughly two thirds.

items.name: The rotative engine: sun-and-planet gear and governor
items.pic: Couple the beam to a flywheel through sun-and-planet gearing, then add the centrifugal governor: under changing mill load the speed drifts less with the governor on.

items.name: Watt’s parallel motion linkage
items.pic: Animate Watt’s linkage: the coupler midpoint traces a nearly straight line through the stroke, with deviation from straightness plotted.

items.name: The indicator diagram
items.pic: Trace pressure against piston position over a cycle: the enclosed area is the work per stroke, and changing cut-off reshapes the loop.

items.name: High-pressure steam (Trevithick, Evans)
items.pic: Raise boiler pressure: engine size per horsepower shrinks enough to move on wheels, while boiler-wall stress rises toward the bursting limit.

items.name: Carnot’s analysis of heat engines
items.pic: Run an ideal engine between a hot and a cold reservoir: its efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h is compared with real engines from Newcomen to modern turbines on one chart.

items.name: Puddling and rolling (Cort)
items.pic: Stir molten pig iron in a reverberatory furnace to burn off carbon, then pass it through grooved rolls: output per worker is compared with hammering.

items.name: The Bessemer converter
items.pic: Blow air through molten iron: carbon content falls over minutes while the heat of oxidation keeps the bath molten; the price of steel drops on a timeline.

items.name: The screw-cutting lathe and standard threads
items.pic: Gear a lathe’s lead screw to the spindle: change gears to cut any pitch, and the thread error is copied from the lead screw onto the work.

items.name: Interchangeable parts
items.pic: Assemble muskets from random parts made to tolerances of different widths: the fraction that fit without filing rises sharply as tolerances tighten.

chapters.title: The Malthusian world
chapters.summary: Before about 1800, technological progress raised the number of people rather than their living standards: higher income raised births or lowered deaths until income fell back. English real wages show the pattern over six centuries, most dramatically after the Black Death, when labour became scarce and wages doubled. World population nonetheless grew faster than exponentially over the long run, a pattern that models of population-driven innovation try to explain.

items.name: Malthusian dynamics in pre-industrial economies
items.pic: Birth and death rates as functions of income cross at the subsistence wage: perturb population or income and watch the economy return to the same income.

items.name: Technology raises population, not income
items.pic: Shift the technology level up: income jumps, then decays back to subsistence as population rises to a new, higher equilibrium.

items.name: English real wages, 1200–1800
items.pic: Real wages of builders against population for England: the points trace a downward-sloping curve that shifts only slowly before 1800.

items.name: Hyperbolic growth of world population
items.pic: Fit N(t) = C/(t₀ − t) to world population estimates: von Foerster’s 1960 fit put the singularity on 13 November 2026, and the data bend away from it after the 1960s.

items.name: The Black Death as an SIR epidemic
items.pic: Spread an SIR model across a map of 1347–51 Europe with travel along trade routes: arrival dates and final mortality near a third to a half are compared with the record.

items.name: After the plague: the golden age of labour
items.pic: English population and real wages from 1300 to 1600: the population crash moves the economy up the wage curve, and wages slide back as numbers recover.

items.name: Preventive checks: the European marriage pattern
items.pic: Raise the age at first marriage and the share never marrying: fertility falls and the Malthusian equilibrium income rises, as in north-western Europe.

items.name: Survival of the richest (contested)
items.pic: Surviving children by testator wealth in English wills: the rich had more, and a toggle compares Clark’s cultural-transmission reading with critics’ alternatives.

items.name: The Little Ice Age and the seventeenth-century crisis
items.pic: Reconstructed temperatures, harvests and recorded revolts in the 1600s on one timeline, with the correlation and its sensitivity to the choice of dates.

items.name: Seven Centuries of the Prices of Consumables
items.pic: The paper’s chart rebuilt from its index: a basket of consumables priced in southern England from 1264 to 1954 and a building craftsman’s daily wage, their ratio plotted as a real-wage index; the reader zooms to the high plateau after the Black Death, the long sixteenth-century fall and the rise after 1800, and sets population beside it to see the Malthusian inverse relation.

paper.authors: E. H. Phelps Brown and Sheila V. Hopkins
paper.title: Seven Centuries of the Prices of Consumables, Compared with Builders’ Wage-Rates

items.name: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026
items.pic: The paper’s fit redone: estimates of world population from year 1 to 1958 are plotted against time and the reader fits the hyperbola N = C/(t₀ − t)^k by dragging t₀, landing near 2026 with k close to 1; the actual population since 1960 is then overlaid and peels away from the curve as growth slowed.
